The Dayz mod was the reason I finally bought a gaming PC. I had always been a console gamer since I was a kid but I  never saw a game that intrigued me as much as the mod. When I got into it finally it waseverything I expected, a new, engaging experience on a kind of alien system to me that was not like any other game I'd ever played. I was always stressed out in the game but I loved it for being so different and exciting even when doing nothing. I figured the standalone was going to be amazing, eventually. I knew it was an alpha and that there would be time needed to grow and develope.
I should've seen the writing on the wall when Rocket said in an interview in 2012 I think that there was no reason the standalone shouldn't be out by Christmas that year and if it wasn't then they seriously screwed up. I don't expect it to be perfect, even still. it's an alpha. Games are often in development for years before the public is even really aware of them. Some people take the fact that it's still an alpha as a crime, I don't really agree. But the developement really seems to be at such a stand still to me that it's crazy. There are so many core things in the game that are never really taken care of while these small, esoteric things are added. It's very confusing. The foundation is very flawed but instead of really working it out and cementing it development just focuses on these branches and leave the core rotten.
I had these amazing hopes for this game but it's really just spun it's tires. it's aggravating enough when the community inside the game is like 85% KOS bur when the game itself seems ti be working against you, it's just not fun anymore. And that's the only thing that really matters to me. It's not fun enough to deal with the constant aggravation it dishes out.

Anyways, considering I'd never heard a word about this game (besides the music) before playing, this game really caught me off-guard with how good it turned out to be. Definately an investment worth making!

There is very little I can say about this game without spoiling it, This game is so rich with story that if i mention that name of the main character i will have ruined the entire game for you. I will have to try to talk about the game itself instead of the story.
as you'd expect there are several endings in the game which sucks because you have to play the game several times to see all of the content. Anyways:
the neutral route
This is most likely what you will get the first time playing assuming you haven't looked up the ending like you should.
It has a good story and it is obvious that the gameplay was balanced around this route and the good ending route. Other than that there is not much you can say about this route as there are so many ways to play it that i can't be completely accurate in describing what you will experience
"The good route"
I don't think I am spoiling anything by saying there is a good ending, but I will say that, if you beat the neutral ending, the good ending will be very easy. In fact, if you go this route the game gives stuff to you and it's almost impossible to lose. It works because of how you get this route and it keeps an appropriate tone. There is a satisfying ending to this as well
"The bad route"
The bad route has a constant negative tone in the entire thing which is definetely a bit wierd because there are plenty of elements from the good ending that still show up despite that. also the difficulty curve is awful in this mode. At first it starts okay than it curves down until one of the boss fights where it spikes up very high. After that, the gameplay gets easier than it was at the start of the game until you meet the final boss which has the highest spike in difficulty I have ever seen. I guess it's kind of appropriate considering the story of the bad route but I'd feel that it is way too steep for difficulty that only spikes higher during the fight.
Overall:
You could complete the game in 3-8 hours depending on how good you are at games like these and with a great soundtrack, likable characters, and enjoyable (but by no means perfect) gameplay. It is definetely worth playing.

DayZ Standalone is a survival game located in a small country called Chernarus  in Eastern Europe at a time after an infection wiped out the population.  Some of the infected rose again as zombies.  A small percentage of the population was immune (Including the player).
As a survivor, you start out with almost nothing in terms of supplies and must make due with looting houses or making your own food and tools in the wilderness.  You'll have to deal with the many dangers of surviving in a land where society has fallen apart, to include hunger, thirst, disease, hypothermia, etc.  Other survivors can provide safety or danger as they choose, communicating with had gestures, voice chat, and text chat in the local area only.  Having no global chat adds much to the immersion of the survival experience.
The mechanics in this game are the best I've seen in this genre.  The combination of good mechanics mixed with player interaction that can be anything from receiving a bullet to the head out of nowhere to building a small community in an abandoned town makes the immersion the best I've enjoyed in a multiplayer game.  The zombies are really just a part of the ambiance as they are pretty easy to avoid and fairly easy to kill.  They add to the immersion.
The only negative that I've seen is that the map is HUGE.  It takes a long time to get from place to place.  So you'll spend a lot of time running around if chose to just run around and get supplies the whole game.  While this is a common complaint amongst the community, I find it helps even more with the immersion.  When you're running around and see no one for an hour or two and find another player, you might become tense from a possible threat or desperate to see if they can help you out with being low on food or blood.
If you enjoy role play, this game offers many opportunities for it.  You are able to play any way you like.  Shooting other players tends to destroy their equipment.  So holding them up and forcing them to drop their gear is better than putting a bullet through their heart, which could also destroy many items in their pack.  So, you can tie them up with duct tape or handcuffs and then release them if you like.  Or not.  It's just how you want to play.
Overall, I find this game amazing.  The immersion and mechanics alone are pretty awesome.  On top of that, it has pretty good graphics and no loading screens once you get into the game.  I highly recommend this game if you like open worlds or survival games.

So I'm approaching 200 hours and feel like I now have a grasp on what DayZ is all about...
Some of my best video game experiences have happened in DayZ.  And of course, some of my worst gaming experiences have occured whilst playing DayZ.
Encountering other players struggling to find a simple can of food creates such a demanding, desperate atmosphere unlike anything else I've felt in other games.  Without knowing it, DayZ has alot of roleplay.  I would possibly like this game even more if I had a better PC.  It is very graphically intensive.
The main problem with DayZ is...the devs.  I don't know who they are or what they are doing.  But this game is far from BETA let alone a real game.  DayZ at times feels like a scam.  A promise of a future game which will be bug free and ultimately better, but where is this game?  It's almost 2 years into alpha.  Oh yeah, and the new zombie system is awful.  They attack way to fast, and are too glitchy to properly hit them.  Which leads to another thing...the combat system is incredibly clunky.  I didn't know swinging a simple weapon was so diffcult to replicate.
They have sold probably 3+ million copies of this game.  Accounting for over 100 million in profits.  Why do we not have a complete, bug free game??  We are testing if for you, 3+ million testers and still zombies glitch through floors.
Meanwhile, as DayZ "tries" to fix problems, about a dozen other zombie survival games have been release.  Mind you, all of these games have more content than DayZ.  What is the problem devs?!  Writing this post just reminds me of how frustrating the game is.
I was a sole believer that DayZ had the potential to be the best video game ever made.  I'm shying away from that thought now.   Anyway, I would recommend this game before the new zombie update.  We all got trolled on that one.
With all this being said, there isn't much else like DayZ.  It, at the time of release, was an extremely unique game.  Now put to shame by H1Z1, Fading Light, and countless others.  Hell, we might as well all go play Arma 3 DayZ mod now.
I've lost faith in DayZ.  Maybe one day the devs will get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together...

Alright, so i've been questioning myself on whether or not to review this game and all I can come up is...
Find a Demo of this game before you purchase, cause the outcome will be like a double-edged sword. Either you will hate it (which is like one side of the blade), Like it (Another side of the blade), or basically be indifferent towards the purchase of the game in general (In-which is a missed swing).
Let's start with Graphical Details:
If you don't like pixelated graphics, Get out, Get out right now, cause this game is totally not for your Graphics-intolerant eyes. Want to know why it's like this? Because it's cheap and simple, especially for those who lack artistic skills to make something better. Plus, it's more inspired by the retro-classic rpgs like earthbound, and maybe a few other familiar games during the NES days.
Gameplay Mechanics:
Well, The gameplay itself is interesting to say the least, One moment you going through Floating in box using the top-down shooter mechanic, the next moment the game play changes and this differs for each boss, and i'm talking about the defensive side of defensive mechanic, No RNG here, just you, your reflexes, and your perception.
The Offensive side on the other hand actually gives you a choice, Kill all the things? Spare all the things? Or just Play it the way you want to play it, your choice.
Now to the story:
Let's just say, it's more of an experience than something you really want to know from a reviewers stand point, but it's better to play it for yourself, or watch somone else play it in order to get the knowlege of the lore & secrets. Otherwise it's pretty nice on the feels.
So, How would I rate this. 8/10 Go for it.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

Very disappointing game.  The first major flaw is the performance.  I have a pretty beefy computer with a liquid cooled overeclocked processor and 16GB memory and the game runs terribly.  Just loading into the lobby uses 5GB of memory right off the top.  The game has serious chunk loading issues.  It is almost unplayable until you manage to explore the area enough to load it into memory as well.  Even with all of the graphics turned all the way down it took 2 hours before I reliably got more than 1 FPS.  This is a serious issue complained about for years according to multiple forums that is not being fixed.
The gameplay itself is not enjoyable either.  All of the servers, even if they've been recently reset and with a low population, have the resources stripped clean.  On a server reset 5 days ago with 2-15 people playing at any given time it took me hours to find enough hemp to make one piece of clothing.  If you do manage to run into into someone expect to be gunned down by a machine gun while trying to defend yourself with a bow and sharpened stick.  If you want to get better gear, too bad.  There are no more blueprints available, no way to research new gear, and the only way to get new gear is by trading days worth of gathered materials for one upgrade item, and probably be double crossed and gunned down and left with nothing to show for it.
The base building mechanic is seriously flawed as well.  Do you want to tear down one section of wall you just put up?  Well be prepared to use a dozen pickaxes and sit there for 10 minutes hacking away at it.  Want to upgrade a wall?  Well go collect resources for a full day and maybe you can upgrade 1 of your 30 walls.  I've never wanted my money back on a game before until I played Rust.
I want my Money back.....

So I'm approaching 200 hours and feel like I now have a grasp on what DayZ is all about...
Some of my best video game experiences have happened in DayZ.  And of course, some of my worst gaming experiences have occured whilst playing DayZ.
Encountering other players struggling to find a simple can of food creates such a demanding, desperate atmosphere unlike anything else I've felt in other games.  Without knowing it, DayZ has alot of roleplay.  I would possibly like this game even more if I had a better PC.  It is very graphically intensive.
The main problem with DayZ is...the devs.  I don't know who they are or what they are doing.  But this game is far from BETA let alone a real game.  DayZ at times feels like a scam.  A promise of a future game which will be bug free and ultimately better, but where is this game?  It's almost 2 years into alpha.  Oh yeah, and the new zombie system is awful.  They attack way to fast, and are too glitchy to properly hit them.  Which leads to another thing...the combat system is incredibly clunky.  I didn't know swinging a simple weapon was so diffcult to replicate.
They have sold probably 3+ million copies of this game.  Accounting for over 100 million in profits.  Why do we not have a complete, bug free game??  We are testing if for you, 3+ million testers and still zombies glitch through floors.
Meanwhile, as DayZ "tries" to fix problems, about a dozen other zombie survival games have been release.  Mind you, all of these games have more content than DayZ.  What is the problem devs?!  Writing this post just reminds me of how frustrating the game is.
I was a sole believer that DayZ had the potential to be the best video game ever made.  I'm shying away from that thought now.   Anyway, I would recommend this game before the new zombie update.  We all got trolled on that one.
With all this being said, there isn't much else like DayZ.  It, at the time of release, was an extremely unique game.  Now put to shame by H1Z1, Fading Light, and countless others.  Hell, we might as well all go play Arma 3 DayZ mod now.

Oh Steam, you clever bugger. Asking not whether I liked the game, but whether I would recommend it.
When I first played Undertale, I only knew the game by reputation. That reputation was that the game was very Earthbound-like, and for a long time that was enough to make me aggressively interested in NOT playing this game. Then my little cousin says the only thing he wants for Christmas is to watch me play Undertale, and I'm like "well what the hell else am I going to do for the holidays?" And you know what?
I actually kind of enjoyed Undertale... at first.
Since I was essentially coerced into playing Undertale, I took whatever scraps of entertainment I could by deliberately ♥♥♥♥ing around the game at every oppotunity. Dodging the "love pellets," running from the combat tutorial, taking all the candy... it's remarkable just how much effort went into making the game troll-friendly. Even monsters (who I hesitate to call "enemies" since most of them are pretty amicable folk) are essentially puzzles that fight back, and you defend yourself in combat by playing danmaku. Even though I went into this game expecting to hate its guts (and wanting to tear out my own) I found myself strangely compelled by the game.
I never finished it.
I don't know what happened, but once I'd adjusted my expectations from "I am going to hate this game" to "this is actually pretty fun" it abruptly stopped being fun. I cannot really quantify why; my best guess is that once I acclimated to the game's quirky humor, there wasn't enough left to make me want to keep playing. Aside from a slightly interesting mechanic where the gameworld's fate is changed by how much of a murderous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you are, humor and a certain depreciative self-awareness are really all the game has. I ended up uninstalling with a sense of bitterness about the whole experience; I rather wish I had never played Undertale, since the fun parts will shadow everything I ever play or do from here on out.
I would still recommend it, if only because every other person and their cat likes Earthbound and Undertale is basically Earthbound++.

Oh Steam, you clever bugger. Asking not whether I liked the game, but whether I would recommend it.
When I first played Undertale, I only knew the game by reputation. That reputation was that the game was very Earthbound-like, and for a long time that was enough to make me aggressively interested in NOT playing this game. Then my little cousin says the only thing he wants for Christmas is to watch me play Undertale, and I'm like "well what the hell else am I going to do for the holidays?" And you know what?
I actually kind of enjoyed Undertale... at first.
Since I was essentially coerced into playing Undertale, I took whatever scraps of entertainment I could by deliberately ♥♥♥♥ing around the game at every oppotunity. Dodging the "love pellets," running from the combat tutorial, taking all the candy... it's remarkable just how much effort went into making the game troll-friendly. Even monsters (who I hesitate to call "enemies" since most of them are pretty amicable folk) are essentially puzzles that fight back, and you defend yourself in combat by playing danmaku. Even though I went into this game expecting to hate its guts (and wanting to tear out my own) I found myself strangely compelled by the game.
I never finished it.
I don't know what happened, but once I'd adjusted my expectations from "I am going to hate this game" to "this is actually pretty fun" it abruptly stopped being fun. I cannot really quantify why; my best guess is that once I acclimated to the game's quirky humor, there wasn't enough left to make me want to keep playing. Aside from a slightly interesting mechanic where the gameworld's fate is changed by how much of a murderous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you are, humor and a certain depreciative self-awareness are really all the game has. I ended up uninstalling with a sense of bitterness about the whole experience; I rather wish I had never played Undertale, since the fun parts will shadow everything I ever play or do from here on out.
I would still recommend it, if only because every other person and their cat likes Earthbound and Undertale is basically Earthbound++.

Very disappointing game.  The first major flaw is the performance.  I have a pretty beefy computer with a liquid cooled overeclocked processor and 16GB memory and the game runs terribly.  Just loading into the lobby uses 5GB of memory right off the top.  The game has serious chunk loading issues.  It is almost unplayable until you manage to explore the area enough to load it into memory as well.  Even with all of the graphics turned all the way down it took 2 hours before I reliably got more than 1 FPS.  This is a serious issue complained about for years according to multiple forums that is not being fixed.
The gameplay itself is not enjoyable either.  All of the servers, even if they've been recently reset and with a low population, have the resources stripped clean.  On a server reset 5 days ago with 2-15 people playing at any given time it took me hours to find enough hemp to make one piece of clothing.  If you do manage to run into into someone expect to be gunned down by a machine gun while trying to defend yourself with a bow and sharpened stick.  If you want to get better gear, too bad.  There are no more blueprints available, no way to research new gear, and the only way to get new gear is by trading days worth of gathered materials for one upgrade item, and probably be double crossed and gunned down and left with nothing to show for it.
The base building mechanic is seriously flawed as well.  Do you want to tear down one section of wall you just put up?  Well be prepared to use a dozen pickaxes and sit there for 10 minutes hacking away at it.  Want to upgrade a wall?  Well go collect resources for a full day and maybe you can upgrade 1 of your 30 walls.  I've never wanted my money back on a game before until I played Rust.

Very disappointing game.  The first major flaw is the performance.  I have a pretty beefy computer with a liquid cooled overeclocked processor and 16GB memory and the game runs terribly.  Just loading into the lobby uses 5GB of memory right off the top.  The game has serious chunk loading issues.  It is almost unplayable until you manage to explore the area enough to load it into memory as well.  Even with all of the graphics turned all the way down it took 2 hours before I reliably got more than 1 FPS.  This is a serious issue complained about for years according to multiple forums that is not being fixed.
The gameplay itself is not enjoyable either.  All of the servers, even if they've been recently reset and with a low population, have the resources stripped clean.  On a server reset 5 days ago with 2-15 people playing at any given time it took me hours to find enough hemp to make one piece of clothing.  If you do manage to run into into someone expect to be gunned down by a machine gun while trying to defend yourself with a bow and sharpened stick.  If you want to get better gear, too bad.  There are no more blueprints available, no way to research new gear, and the only way to get new gear is by trading days worth of gathered materials for one upgrade item, and probably be double crossed and gunned down and left with nothing to show for it.
The base building mechanic is seriously flawed as well.  Do you want to tear down one section of wall you just put up?  Well be prepared to use a dozen pickaxes and sit there for 10 minutes hacking away at it.  Want to upgrade a wall?  Well go collect resources for a full day and maybe you can upgrade 1 of your 30 walls.  I've never wanted my money back on a game before until I played Rust.

Nearly 1000 hrs in - Review time.
The game is in early alpha, and is in a constant state of development, so I am only going to talk about what DayZ is, and how it brings its idea/concept forward.
- You begin life in a random location, somewhere in the 225km2 expanse. You have a T-Shirt, Jeans, Shoes, a Flashlight and a Battery. There is no pressing 'M' for a map, no tutorial. It begins.
- You will make your way to houses/towns/cities, looking for every and anything to help you survive (food, drink, weaponry, clothing, backpack). You may find something, or nothing, there is no guarentee.
- You will worry about being Hungry, Thirsty, Stuffed (over full), Cold, Hot and Sick (with different sickness types - Cholera, Food Poisoning, Blood Poisoning etc)
- You will find Infected, everywhere. These guys will see and smell you from ages away, and chase you down with the speed and ferocity of a cheetah! - DO NOT APPROACH.
- You will value gear for how much it can carry and how much it can protect from the environment.
- You will cheer at safe water to drink is like it is nectar from the gods!
- You can farm your own food from the land, but finding the equiptment necessary is difficult enough!
- Player interaction in this game, is on a whole new level. The game does not send players into any direction (in terms of how they must play) and every new encounter with another player, is COMPLETELY different!
- Most players are bandits, and bandits are everywhere. Some may want to rob you, others may want to just kill you and eat you. Some will handcuff you and keep you prisoner.
- Sometimes you meet someone nice, you may quickly exchange words/items, you may have an adventure together, or you may part ways instantly.
- The map is amazing. I felt lost for so long, and sometimes, I still find myself wondering where the f**k I am!
- The dev team on this release updates almost monthly (adding a couple weeks sometimes) and when an update comes, it brings big changes. This can completely change "fundamentals" and shakes everything up a little, but Survival = Adaption. Bugs are usually introduced with patches, and that is all part and parcel of the territory we are in. The devs are very quick to make fixes when problems are apparent, and they're in touch with the community 100% of the time.
Summing it up:
All in all, I feel the place that DayZ is in now, since starting (just under) 1000 hrs ago, is a great one.
- The game itself is absolutely immersive. The map is large enough, and with enough locations to keep exploring for what feels forever! (and getting more locations).
- I actually feel a connection to my character, pride in their long lives, and sadness when they die.
- Surviving is not the only point, but thriving.
- Finding other players to have awesome times with, and forming long relationships that last (nothing is more bonding than relying on your friend, and have them relying on you, to make it through!)
11/10 - STILL buying copies for friends and family who see how into it I am! Still recommending it to anyone that listens!

I've been playing DayZ Standalone for nearly 2,000 hours now, which has left me with enough experience with this game to have seen the various sides of the coin. I also want to add that I've only played the Mod for about 2 hours or something, as I was late on the DayZ train, so I won't be comparing DayZ Standalone and DayZ Mod at all.
"Pros"
1. Huge variety in gameplay. There's so much to do in a game such as DayZ Standalone, even if all the features within the game is complete nor in, it has a huge amount of things to do and ways to play the game. Farming, Hunting, PvP, PvE, Roleplay is only some of the bits and bobs available to the players!
2. Active servers. No matter what, you'll always find yourself a server with a handful of people on. Whether you are looking for PvP, PvE or RP! And if playing with less people is what you want, there's usually servers around for that too!
3. Activity around the map has increased. This means that people don't only go to Cherno or Elektro to PvP anymore! You'll even find people up north and in lesser common towns now! Woho!
4. FPS & UI! For a long time the game had horrid FPS, but it has gotten a lot better! And the UI is becoming better and better with time, even if it still has a lot of work to be made on.
"Cons"
1. Hackers. I think it's quite obvious why this is a con.
2. Slow patching. Don't get me wrong, we get patches that comes out quicker than others, but occationally you've got periods where there won't be a patch in many months! This can be a side effect to some people, as some require new content consistantly.
3. Bugs. There's plenty of bugs in the game still, which is expected from a early acess game, however it can tilt you occationally when you run across a field and suddenly get the "you are dead" message due to desync.
4. Lack of Zombies! The amount of Zombies has been increased, however it's nowhere near what people want it to be yet!
(This review was made during patch 0.60)

Since I have heard so many overwhelmingly good reviews about this game as well as noticing it's popularity, I finally decided to test it out for myself a couple of days ago. Truly a good game considering it's an indie game. The characters are well-written and the plot as well as the graphics make the game captivating in an unconventional way; and to be frank, I actually enjoyed the (supposedly intentional) bad puns that appeared frequently through-out the game. The puzzles were fairly easy, though, and the game slightly too short. Also, some dialogues were overly annoying and unneccessary for the plot, but generally the majority of them add up and appear to be really funny and enjoyable to read. I have merely tested out the neutral route as of yet, thus there is more for me to explore in this game before I can make a clear over-all statement.
In short: playing Undertale filled me with determination.

Undertale is probably one of the best games I've ever played in a long time. It may seem like a typical 2d game where you start off easy but as you spend more time playing it you get to understand the great storyline it holds, and how difficult the game can actually get. Accompanied by a lot of characters with a lot of depth, personality-wise, and a lot of hilarious moments, you just get to have so much fun. And finally, you get to choose how the game will end.
Honestly, Undertale is a blast. Everyone should play it.

You've all heard it, this game is amazing, awesome story blah blah blah. Everybody has said it, and although I agree with it entirely, I have my own things to say.
This game seems as the creator (Toby Fox) has put all of his work and creativity into this 6 hour game. And it has payed off so well. Everything, the story, the gameplay, the music, the characters, even the jokes has been pushed to be the best it can be, and it is so confident with itself as well. I wish to become a game developer myself some day, but not I, nor anybody else in this world has or probably will make a game as well thought out and creative as this game.
But enough rambling, let's discuss the things this game gets right.

First of all, the story and characters. This is what makes the game as popular as it is, and I do agree it is amazing, but it isn't perfect. Let's talk about what i like about it. The characters are very well made, they all fit together well in this game world and all have their own unique charm to them. Not a single character or moment feels bland or even forced at all, and the story (the pacifist one at least) is very touching and inspiring.
I rarely cry over movies or video games and this is one of the few occasions I have shed a few tears, but be warned, the feels don't come until the near end of the pacifist route. And the thing is, there is more than one story, you can choose to kill nobody, or you can choose to kill everybody, everybody says that the genocide route makes you feel the most extreme guilt you can feel, but to be honest, I didn't really feel it. I was more interested in the differences and what happens if I WERE to kill everyone, but there comes the main, and honestly only problem I have with this game, the game scolds you for being curious, going against human nature.
Just remember, this is just a game, a bunch of lines of code, you can try to debate it with me but I am not one for being interested in philosophy. Call me a heartless ***hole all you want but I really think it is unhealthy to compare a world of a video game to our own.
Story: 9.1/10
The graphics. Why do I bother talking about this? The damn game is in 16 bits, there isn't much to talk about. But the one thing I can talk about is the sprite work looks pretty good, but it could be better.
Graphics: 7/10
Now the part that I am most particularly fond of is the gameplay. The only thing I will be talking about is the battle gameplay. The battles are great, whether in pacifist or genocide. The game uses concepts from RPGs of old, but also tries to have it's own identity. The main draw in gameplay is the bullet-mini-game-esk sort of battle style. During an enemy's turn, you can dodge attacks that they throw at you rather than just standing there and taking it like an idiot. You, given the right amount of practice and skill, can potentially dodge every single attack in the entire game (that's not scripted of course).
Though I am not one to brag at all (I suck at most video games), I and particularly good at these bullet minigames and have gone through multiple bosses without getting hit, and man is it fun. The boss fights are not too easy, but they aren't too hard, with the exception of the genocide boss battles (those of you who have played the game know what I'm talking about). Another great part of the battle system is the Act, and Mercy options. You can spare any enemy in the entire game, and I seriously mean every single enemy, including bosses. You can be nice to them, be mean to them, intimidate them, strengthen them, and even go on a date with them.
Gameplay: 9.5/10
Conclusion:
After 20 hours of playing this game, I can easily say this is the best Indie game I have ever played. Is it the best game ever made? no. Does it belong in the top ten? Maybe, and since the amount of flaws is so small I can put this as #7 on my list of favorite games ever.
Final rating: 9.7/10

I got this game back in November, but never got the chance to review it. I was debating whether or not to get this after seeing it everywhere, but I eventually decided to check it out after receiving a recommendation from an artist I watch. No regrets were had. This was a great game that combined RPG mechanics with a bullet-hell system and providing a very interesting experience.
The storytelling in this game was superb and the characters were very likable (which pained me when I had to kill them in a "Genocide Run"). The humor also played a part in me enjoying this game. The final aspect that I enjoyed about this game was the music. I found it rather interesting that Toby Fox was able to create most of the music in the game by slowing down or speeding up several tracks.
As stated previously, the storytelling was superb as it changed depending on your actions throughout the game. You can go through the entire game without killing a single monster, or you can kill everything in your path, but suffer the consequences. There is some interesting dialogue that can also occur if you decide to spare monsters and kill some as well and the timing of when you do so can also affect the remainder of the playthrough.
Overall, I thought this was a really good game and I would recommend it to anyone who is thinking of trying it out.

Now, I've gotten to the point where if I spawn near Elektro or Cherno I can get my provisions and at least one gun with matching bullets. 1. Have enough food and water forever
2. Have enough bullets to peg all zombies and bandits
3. Be a pro

Life in a Rust highpop server, trying to win:
Your first month is essentially PvE, learning how to play and build, dodging all the wars and sadistic murderers running around you, learning each new map and adapting to it.  You'll die.  A lot.  By the end of the month, you should have learned what you need to save things (blueprint learning, a small locked building) from one death to the next, and begin aggregating resources.  After getting over how many people kill you on sight, you fall in love with the exploration, the maps, the adrenaline rush of brushing up against someone's territory or a chance encounter in the woods, and getting away with it.

Your second month is joining a clan, getting to know them, getting to work together, learning the rest of the mechanics, plotting out how you will civilize this place and make it your own.  You start to navigate the social hierarchy, and learn how things work in practice amongst the people who have been killing you.
Your third month is being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off that they're not taking it seriously enough to win, moving on to another clan, developing the same sentiment, maybe trying in vain to start your own clan or form an alliance.  You won't succeed.  Because the type of players that you would need to survive, are the type that you can't recruit: hardcore no-lifers.  The rest of the serverpop will experience very rapid churn.  Most of the clans you're dealing with, and the clan members you're dealing with, will have a half life of two or three weeks.  If you work at it there *will* be a conflict with a twelve-year-old clanmember starting drama, if not more than one.  All the others are full of trash-talking 16-year-old sadists who have happened upon a social situation where they have just enough chemistry to stick it out.  Even recruiting them isn't gonna work for you;   They won't play nice.
Maybe, if you're lucky, you can find a group of people you wouldn't mind hanging out with;  But try to put them to work getting into a winning position, and they won't want to hang out with you.  Morale problems preclude the kind of work you need.  The most effective organizations have built such a reputation that they can employ 'slaves' to do their work for them, in exchange to protection and blueprints.  Success requires making the game a fulltime job for someone.
You will probably not go past 90 days.  If you're playing properly / competitively, that's about a thousand hours of gameplay.  Expect to be raided and lose your♥♥♥♥♥♥whenever you go to sleep.  Expect to play a 24h streak when the map resets (weekly), and then go to normal hours for two or three days, then to lose everything because some other group played more than you;  You can either try and rebuild (you won't succeed, you started behind), or quit until the following weekly reset.
Maybe you'll give up on Vanilla Rust and go to a high-gather server.  In that event, you'll get the same 90 day cycle a second time, but with easier to build and destroy structures, massive lag problems, and greater emphasis on 24 hour manning.
It's a brutal game.  It's incredibly immersive.  It will punish anyone that tries to play casually.  A bit like Eve Online, but the Survival gametype, limited serverpop, world reset, and raid dynamic makes it so difficult to form structured organized play that there's no comparison socially;  The playerbase is toxic.  People running around shouting "Allahu Ackbar" with a rifle and killing the nakeds is ubiquitous, worse than any game I've seen.  It's the first MMO I've ever played in which people would just scream "NNEEEEERRRRRRRRRRRRRD" into their mic, as an insult;  A lot of these people are not part of the cultural group I associate with the word 'gamer'.  I wished many times that there was no ingame voicecomms: it seems to make everyone more dickish, and it's amazingly difficult to get everyone to submit to Teamspeak.   Hackers will occasionally pop up and try to sample your tears as you lose a hundred man-hours of work, which they throw away.  Likewise better-organized playergroups than you, but at least that's designed to be part of the game.
This game is everything I wanted in an MMO survival game other than scaling to thousands of players, and an adult playerbase & culture.  It turns out, the level of committment that's required filters out too many people and things, including, eventually, me.  Ultimately, it's a nice place to visit but I wouldn't want to live there.

WEED BUTTER RECIPE
This recipe pro­duces a small amount of cannabis-​​infused butter, or can­nabutter, which can be used in a massive range of recipes to add that extra kick! If your recipe requires more butter than the amounts given here, feel free to mul­tiply up all the amounts.
Ingredients
Baking
•4oz (115g) Butter or Margarine
•1/​8oz (3.5g) Can­nabis buds/​hash OR
•1/​4oz (7g) Can­nabis leaves
Equipment
•Small saucepan
•Wooden spoon
•Sieve (optional)
Method
1.Melt the butter slowly in a pan. Add 1⁄8 oz (3.5g) finely ground can­nabis, and simmer on a low heat for around 30 minutes. This allows the can­nabis to infuse fully into the butter. Take care to keep the heat low, and stir con­tinu­ously as the butter can burn easily.
2.After 30 minutes, pour the butter into a jug or tub. As you do this, if you want to remove the bud/​hash/​leaf, you can pass it through a fine sieve. You won’t be wasting any “good stuff”, since all the THC should have dis­solved into the butter, but if you don’t mind getting green bits in your teeth, you can just as easily leave it in.
3.Allow the can­nabutter to set for around an hour, or until rel­at­ively hard, before using.

WEED BUTTER RECIPE
This recipe pro­duces a small amount of cannabis-​​infused butter, or can­nabutter, which can be used in a massive range of recipes to add that extra kick! If your recipe requires more butter than the amounts given here, feel free to mul­tiply up all the amounts.
Ingredients
Baking
•4oz (115g) Butter or Margarine
•1/​8oz (3.5g) Can­nabis buds/​hash OR
•1/​4oz (7g) Can­nabis leaves
Equipment
•Small saucepan
•Wooden spoon
•Sieve (optional)
Method
1.Melt the butter slowly in a pan. Add 1⁄8 oz (3.5g) finely ground can­nabis, and simmer on a low heat for around 30 minutes. This allows the can­nabis to infuse fully into the butter. Take care to keep the heat low, and stir con­tinu­ously as the butter can burn easily.
2.After 30 minutes, pour the butter into a jug or tub. As you do this, if you want to remove the bud/​hash/​leaf, you can pass it through a fine sieve. You won’t be wasting any “good stuff”, since all the THC should have dis­solved into the butter, but if you don’t mind getting green bits in your teeth, you can just as easily leave it in.
3.Allow the can­nabutter to set for around an hour, or until rel­at­ively hard, before using.

Ignore anybody complaining about hacking, I've played so many hours on this game, on both legacy and the new version. The new version is so much better you can't even compare the games and I've only run into maybe a couple hackers throughout my whole history on the new rust. Anybody complaining about hackers probably played on one of the official servers which don't have people monitoring them and they rely on VAC bans or a lot of reports to deal with hackers. If you join a community server like Rustopia which is vanilla, you will find active admins who also take the initiative and ban anybody suspicous. This includes everybody with a VAC ban on record.
This game is ever evolving with weekly updates and a great dev team which is very responsive. Are you finding you might not have the time to grind out resources to build a giant base which you hope would be able to outlast a raid while you are offline? No worries! There are modded servers! On these modded servers, you can get increased gathering rates. Since most servers wipe weekly, I find it difficult to outlast all the clans as a solo player. And you really can't on community servers. But that is why you join a modded server. With kits and a couple hours of grinding, you could build a castle for yourself.
It's not just the gameplay itself which makes this game so great. The player interaction is key. Being able to engage in conversations with random strangers using your microphone or having rock battles and calling them scum, Rust allows you to be free. I've read some people complaining about 12 year olds screaming on the mic, this isn't an issue. If I ever run into somebody I don't like and I find them annoying, I kill them. Guess what? They won't be annoying anymore.
Rust can and will be a great experience for anybody, whether you enjoying the survival aspect (yes there is one) or the shooting. Rust is for everybody and I would recommend it to everybody. This is a game you want to buy for your friends and you can play together. This game can be a lot of fun if you give it a real chance. Yes, you will die, yes, you will probably die a lot. But after all those deaths you will learn and eventually you can be the one killing. Can you survive this wasteland? Can you make it to the top and build the biggest and the best structures? Will you come out a legend or a mere peasant?

The designers of Dayz have stated from the beginning that this will be slowly developped to the point of perfection. They have clear goals as to the development roadmap and still have to be flexible. Vehicles are not near intergration stage due to the fact that each component added to the vehicle needs to be maintained and correctly used. Once again the programmers need to reduce overhead on the system but still keeps realism.
Weather Effects and health are bieng developed alongside and also this needs to be correctly added.
Give Dayz a year and the bad comments will go away. To create something this intricate takes time and paitience. Go play 7 Days to Die or  Rust and you will see the difference between slow and fast. Good thing come to those that wait.

*DISCLAIMER* I have attempted to avoid spoilers in this review, but if you are on the fence, don't read my full review - or anything else about Undertale for that matter. Just spend the $10 on a (relatively short) true experience like no other in the annals of video gaming.
Undertale starts conventionally, with the obligatory easy early battles and introductory characters. Right from the start, you will notice that something is different - combat is fresher, as attacks involve timing on a meter and defense is akin to a 'bullet hell' game without the shooting. Plot-wise, the humor inherent within the characters' quirks - especially the primary characters - stands out. And both in and out of battle, structured flexibility is what this game is all about, with many paths available through combat and the plot in general. The characters and scenarios provide guidance on your path through, as engaging puzzles fill your time in between battles and plot points. The music, too, succeeds on multiple levels - both fitting the situation in which each track is played like a glove and being very high quality in its own right. As for the graphics - they might not be technically advanced, but with a one-person development team, artistic choices are what matter. In that regard, Undertale's 16-bit graphics and deliberate artistic style, focused on black-and-white contrasts, together represent an effective stylistic decision that also serves as an intentional callback.
Ultimately, more than any other video game, Undertale succeeds because you end up truly caring about its characters. Truly, it is an RPG with a soul - made by one person and sold for ten dollars, the result is perhaps the most uniquely compelling singular experience in video gaming.

Positives: A hardcore 1rst and 3rd person shooter with no radar that has a fun pvp side to it. It is especially fun to go against other players in the large towns because it requires a lot of tactics and skill. Playing as a survivor used to be fun as well but that changed recently.
Negatives: The survival component to the game died in the last patch. Improvised bows and fishing rods don't work. The devs also removed the ability to cook on an open fire without any extra tools (now a cooking pot or pan is required and they aren't easy to find). Ammo is extremely scarce in most towns.
Zombies are now found everywhere (even in the most remote northern towns) and they've gone from being extremely weak to extremely dangerous. As an example, zombies will half ruin your clothing now in about 4-5 hits and you can't outrun them on an open road. In the past, you could at lease dodge them beause they lunged at you when they got close; now, they don't lunge so the strafe dodge technique is pointless. The only way to outwit them is to lead them into dense woods because their tracking goes haywire if you lead them through enough large pine trees. My advice is to stay away from large towns unless you have silenced weapons or any other decently powerful weapon with a lot of ammo.
Unfortunately, I cannot recommend this game in it's current state. The improvised crafting system needs a lot of development and the loot generation system needs to be tweaked so that more loot is generated in larger towns as well as the remote towns. Mining picks and axes need their damage buffed against zombies; it shouldn't take 4-6 direct hits to the chest of a zombie with a fire axe to kill it.  It wouldn't hurt to fix the whole fire cooking mechanic either. If we can't cook directly on a fire, we should be able to place food on a spit over a fire or at least on a stick that we place on the fire.

Life in a Rust highpop server, trying to win:
Your first month is essentially PvE, learning how to play and build, dodging all the wars and sadistic murderers running around you, learning each new map and adapting to it.  You'll die.  A lot.  By the end of the month, you should have learned what you need to save things (blueprint learning, a small locked building) from one death to the next, and begin aggregating resources.  After getting over how many people kill you on sight, you fall in love with the exploration, the maps, the adrenaline rush of brushing up against someone's territory or a chance encounter in the woods, and getting away with it.

Your second month is joining a clan, getting to know them, getting to work together, learning the rest of the mechanics, plotting out how you will civilize this place and make it your own.  You start to navigate the social hierarchy, and learn how things work in practice amongst the people who have been killing you.
Your third month is being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off that they're not taking it seriously enough to win, moving on to another clan, developing the same sentiment, maybe trying in vain to start your own clan or form an alliance.  You won't succeed.  Because the type of players that you would need to survive, are the type that you can't recruit: hardcore no-lifers.  The rest of the serverpop will experience very rapid churn.  Most of the clans you're dealing with, and the clan members you're dealing with, will have a half life of two or three weeks.  If you work at it there *will* be a conflict with a twelve-year-old clanmember starting drama, if not more than one.  All the others are full of trash-talking 16-year-old sadists who have happened upon a social situation where they have just enough chemistry to stick it out.  Even recruiting them isn't gonna work for you;   They won't play nice.
Maybe, if you're lucky, you can find a group of people you wouldn't mind hanging out with;  But try to put them to work getting into a winning position, and they won't want to hang out with you.  Morale problems preclude the kind of work you need.  The most effective organizations have built such a reputation that they can employ 'slaves' to do their work for them, in exchange to protection and blueprints.  Success requires making the game a fulltime job for someone.
You will probably not go past 90 days.  If you're playing properly / competitively, that's about a thousand hours of gameplay.  Expect to be raided and lose your♥♥♥♥♥♥whenever you go to sleep.  Expect to play a 24h streak when the map resets (weekly), and then go to normal hours for two or three days, then to lose everything because some other group played more than you;  You can either try and rebuild (you won't succeed, you started behind), or quit until the following weekly reset.
Maybe you'll give up on Vanilla Rust and go to a high-gather server.  In that event, you'll get the same 90 day cycle a second time, but with easier to build and destroy structures, massive lag problems, and greater emphasis on 24 hour manning.
It's a brutal game.  It's incredibly immersive.  It will punish anyone that tries to play casually.  A bit like Eve Online, but the Survival gametype, limited serverpop, world reset, and raid dynamic makes it so difficult to form structured organized play that there's no comparison socially;  The playerbase is toxic.  People running around shouting "Allahu Ackbar" with a rifle and killing the nakeds is ubiquitous, worse than any game I've seen. I wished many times that there was no ingame voicecomms: it seems to make everyone more dickish, and it's amazingly difficult to get everyone to submit to Teamspeak.   Hackers will occasionally pop up and try to sample your tears as you lose a hundred man-hours of work, which they throw away.  Likewise better-organized playergroups than you, but at least that's designed to be part of the game.
This game is everything I wanted in an MMO survival game other than scaling to thousands of players, and an adult playerbase & culture.  It turns out, the level of committment that's required filters out too many people and things, including, eventually, me.  Ultimately, it's a nice place to visit but I wouldn't want to live there.

Ignore anybody complaining about hacking, I've played so many hours on this game, on both legacy and the new version. The new version is so much better you can't even compare the games and I've only run into maybe a couple hackers throughout my whole history on the new rust. Anybody complaining about hackers probably played on one of the official servers which don't have people monitoring them and they rely on VAC bans or a lot of reports to deal with hackers. If you join a community server like Rustopia which is vanilla, you will find active admins who also take the initiative and ban anybody suspicous. This includes everybody with a VAC ban on record.
This game is ever evolving with weekly updates and a great dev team which is very responsive. Are you finding you might not have the time to grind out resources to build a giant base which you hope would be able to outlast a raid while you are offline? No worries! There are modded servers! On these modded servers, you can get increased gathering rates. Since most servers wipe weekly, I find it difficult to outlast all the clans as a solo player. And you really can't on community servers. But that is why you join a modded server. With kits and a couple hours of grinding, you could build a castle for yourself.
It's not just the gameplay itself which makes this game so great. The player interaction is key. Being able to engage in conversations with random strangers using your microphone or having rock battles and calling them scum, Rust allows you to be free. I've read some people complaining about 12 year olds screaming on the mic, this isn't an issue. If I ever run into somebody I don't like and I find them annoying, I kill them. Guess what? They won't be annoying anymore.
Rust can and will be a great experience for anybody, whether you enjoying the survival aspect (yes there is one) or the shooting. Rust is for everybody and I would recommend it to everybody. This is a game you want to buy for your friends and you can play together. This game can be a lot of fun if you give it a real chance. Yes, you will die, yes, you will probably die a lot. But after all those deaths you will learn and eventually you can be the one killing. Can you survive this wasteland? Can you make it to the top and build the biggest and the best structures? Will you come out a legend or a mere peasant?
I understand it is early access, but the amount of time spent on loading screens was a bit rough.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This game is much more than meets the eye. It's heartwarming, sad, happy, humorous and even downright creepy. All that just depending on how you play the game.
And yes, it's absolutely true. You don't have to kill ANYONE.
Gameplay is quite simple but at the same time very engaging. It's an RPG style combat system with a fun twist to it and during bigger encounters the mechanics change to keep things fresh and interesting. It's so well executed. Instead of having to sit there and take the hits, you can actually attempt to dodge enemy attacks. Different enemies have different kinds of attacks that mostly match the personality of your foe. Overworld is pretty average stuff. Move around towns and dungeons. Random encounters. And lots of fun puzzles.
The soundtrack is godlike. Seriously, I paid 10€ for the game and then 10€ more for the OST and I still feel like I robbed Toby Fox (developer). It's just that good. Some tracks are rearrengements of other tracks but the mood is completely different. I couldn't tell that they were actually the same songs. Major characters have their own themes that really fit them and evolve depending on the situation. For example, one character had a very humorous tune during overworld encounters but during their bossfight, add some drum beat, BAM! It's an awesome boss theme. Just somehow.
Characters feel so nice. I haven't encountered characters that felt just forcefully pasted in. All of them felt like they belonged somewhere, had something going on, had lives of their own. They felt "real" so to say. And it can go much beyond the "talk to the random NPC" stuff but that's a spoiler.
Saying that the game is full of mysteries is an understatement. There's so much to discover and unravel. Although the game is quite short, it should be played more than once. The game encourages you to do that and it's really worth it. I mentioned that it matters how you play the game. If you become really kind and don't kill anyone, the game feels very light-hearted and happy. If you decide to really eradicate everything, the game will let you know that for sure. If you kill here and there, go on about it pretty casually, the game might note you about it and give you something to think. The difficulty of the game depends on how you go on about it really.
So, I really recommend it. It's more of an experience than a game. Ignore all the hype and fandom around it. Like Toby wanted, I'm going to gently recommend it to you. Just don't listen to others and pick up the game. Have a one on one, you and Undertale. Go in as blind as you can. Think outside of the box and never ever get scared. Have determination. And enjoy Undertale.
For the record, I've never felt so happy playing a video game.

Rust... where do I even begin? I used to hate this game because I would spawn with a rock, run around, craft a bow, and die by some guy with an AK-47. I see a lot of people get into this situation where they cannot even build a base. However, that is almost what this game is about.
When one starts to play rust, they must know what they are getting into. There are hundreds of whiny 12-year-old mic-spamers that will make you wish you were deaf. There are random wolves that will eat you when you are almost done with your base. It is a SURVIVAL game. Not survival like DayZ or H1Z1 where you simply have to get lucky and find an OP gun. Rust you have to go about strategically; hiding in bushes as a genocidal helicopter flies overhead, building a small base that you hope no one sees so that you might make it to the end of the server wipe. All-in-all, Rust is not for the faint of heart. You must be patient, wise, and do your research.
You get out of this game what you put in. If you take it as a die-hard survival game, that's the sort of experience you will have. If you want to be a high-powered clan that dominates the server, you have to work for it. If you want to take this game lightly and just to have some fun, you will have some of the funniest experiences in gaming ever. But everything considered, buy this game. You will not regret it.

I played this game for a bit, and I can finally come to the conclusion that this is nowhere near as good as the community makes it out to be. In fact this is probably one of the worst indie RPG games I've ever played, which I didn't expect from a game with an "Overwhemlingly Positive" rating. Here's the things I liked first of all:
Bits and pieces of the soundtrack were very nice to listen to.
Uhh.........well that's about it. Let's move on to the cons:
Let me start off by saying this game falls in the story department, and that's the supposed reason this game is praised. I've watched my friend play the endings of this game and I can say I'm thoroughly unimpressed. The story is cliche and lacking, which I do not like in an RPG. But maybe the gameplay can make up for this, right?
Nope. Battles are tedious as hell. I never feel any reward to killing an enemy either. When you're NOT in battle with an enemy, you're exploring bland and redundant environments. Sometimes you'll get a puzzle that's super easy its not even funny.
What's with the "runs"? In this game you can get multiple different endings. One of them being where you LITERALLY kill NOTHING (known as the pacifist run). Killing monsters to progress your character is the point of an RPG, and I have to let that not happen just so I can get some stupid peaceful ending? Why? The genocide run makes sense. You kill every monster you encounter. The true ending is alright too, you can spare creatures you want and kill those who you think don't deserve to live. But why is the pacifist run so fun for people?

Rust... where do I even begin? I used to hate this game because I would spawn with a rock, run around, craft a bow, and die by some guy with an AK-47. I see a lot of people get into this situation where they cannot even build a base. However, that is almost what this game is about.
When one starts to play rust, they must know what they are getting into. There are hundreds of whiny 12-year-old mic-spamers that will make you wish you were deaf. There are random wolves that will eat you when you are almost done with your base. It is a SURVIVAL game. Not survival like DayZ or H1Z1 where you simply have to get lucky and find an OP gun. Rust you have to go about strategically; hiding in bushes as a genocidal helicopter flies overhead, building a small base that you hope no one sees so that you might make it to the end of the server wipe. All-in-all, Rust is not for the faint of heart. You must be patient, wise, and do your research.
You get out of this game what you put in. If you take it as a die-hard survival game, that's the sort of experience you will have. If you want to be a high-powered clan that dominates the server, you have to work for it. If you want to take this game lightly and just to have some fun, you will have some of the funniest experiences in gaming ever. But everything considered, buy this game. You will not regret it.

Bottom Line:
One of my favorite games now. If you don't read this, spend the $ and I promise you will want to beat it 3-4 times. I have almost 50 hours now on a less than $15 investment. With all the over bloated, unfinished buggy messes that are still going for $60 a pop or more with DLC, you owe it to yourself to play through one of the most elegant experiences in gaming in recent years. Buy this now.
If you wanna know why:
There is NOTHING superfluous about this game. Every element works to strengthen another: every mechanic, piece of audio/visual feedback and the overall plot feel thoroughly and thoughtfully designed.
Almost every encounter in the game contains a novel mechanic to it. (Always pet dogs)
The boss battles are the best of any game this year. I say this because Undertale is the rare game that presents a main gameplay loop and mechanic and then constantly changes how you use it to fight. I don't want to ruin a single mechanic as many are relevant to the story, so suffice to say that each boss fight feels unique and you will rarely (if ever) use the same tactics twice.
The story is extremely rich and at times downright poignant. The content is also seemingly endless. I remember at hour 20 being amazed that I was still finding new content by just making minor decisions differently on subsequent playthoughs.
But the star of this show is the writing and how Mr. Fox was able to create a consistent theme which permeates all interaction in the world of the game. Once again, I won't spoil a single element, but think of a film like Scott Pilgrim vs the World where this wonderful aesthetic is used to enhace the story's themes and conflicts, rather than distract from them.
I could gush endlessly about this one and everyone else here already has, so just take a hint and buy it already.

Interesting game with open-ended possibilities, but difficult to begin.  However, why would one begin with no clothing, armed with only a rock, and the comfort of a torch?  I found myself running around for about an hour trying to bash logs, trees, crates, structures with no idea how to progress.  Other players offered hints, but no certain orientation was apparent on to how to survive.  Other players were naked as well were running aound, whereby three of them killed me with their rock.  Logically,  I should have some knowledge of survival before I begin awakened from pergutory with only my basalt companion to use as a tool.  I understand the need for progression and learning through trial and  error, as well as occasional help from other players, but getting lost (and frustrated) in the beginning seems too much to become comfortable with this game's player dynamics.
I really wanted to like this game fro the start, and perhaps with additional time, I will.  I can understand giving players a leveled playing field to begin so advancement begins at level zero for everyone, however, unless you are very familiar with *How* to progress, it will seem like you are an outsider that will be certainly doomed to respawn over and over unless someone takes you under their wing.  For players new to Rust, apprenticeship may not be easy to obtain unless you know established players or on the off chance meet someone that actually wants to help you understand the world in which you'll spend trying to decipher.  The ability and possibility of building your own structures and crafting items for survival is none the less intriguing.
If Rust had a orientation such as a dream state where you could do some crafting, constructing, hunting, etc where you *remember* what to do, it could loop in new players easier.  Experienced players already know exactly what they need to do when they wake up from their slumber, so it would be great if new players could at least learn some rudimentary things prior to waking up (spawning) in this volatile environment.

Undertale may at first seem like the average rpg, but it is so much more than that! Even though a playthrough takes around 6-8 hours, the way the game is designed makes the characters seem real. It fleshes out all the main characters through dialogue and various items, making it feel like each and every one of your choices are affecting real people(err...monsters?). The gameplay is simple, and is easy to pick up. The music is amazing considering the fact that Toby Fox made it almost all by himself.
The story consists of three main branches (which I will not spoil) that are based on the choices you make in the game. Are you going to kill that froggit? Are you going to "befriend" the loud fish that tried to kill you? Are you going to make a skeleton have a bad time? Every choice you make affects the rest of your playthrough, and even choices you make in other playthroughs will affect you in the future. It really makes you think before making your decision.
Overall, I would say that this game is a must-play for all gamers intrested in rpgs. It may become repetitive at times, but the story more than makes up for it!

My wife and I had a lot of fun playing this game together. Let me tell you a little story that shows why this game can be amazing.
She loaded into the server I was playing on and started at the beach. I on the other hand had no clue where I was and could not find said beach. After about 2 hours we finally found each other. We go to the nearest town and are running through all the houses looting and looking for stuff. We are in a hospital, both looking at something on the ground when I look to my left and see a guy at the end of the hallway. My wife is completely oblivious to his presence until I yell "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥there's a guy!" Before she can finish saying "what" I watch the guy raise his rifle, shoot and kill her! A deadly shootout commenced between me and my wife's murderer. I hit him a couple times and he got me once. He ran out of ammo first and sprinted to the nearest room, closing the door behind him. Understanding what just happened, I switched to my firemans axe and raced to the room. I threw open the door and found him crouching in a corner trying to reload. I quickly brought the axe down on his head, getting my revenge, and finding that all that happened for basically nothing. He had very little gear on him and was just trying to kill us for ours I think. What a great reflection of the community in DayZ.
After the battle, my wife spawns again and I run to find her. An hour later we finally meet up on some railroad tracks near the sea. On my way there I had managed to find a decent pair of handcuffs and was hoping to use them on someone to see how they worked. We began the DayZ shuffle once more. We looted all the buildings trying to find the gear that I couldn't carry after she had died and had to leave on her body. We found a rifle, a decent pistol and minimal ammo. We came along some people and kept our distance after what had happened. No way did we want a repeat and to go through all this again. Both of us became thirsty from all the sprinting around and had used up the remaining water that we had. We went to the nearest well and were filling our bottles and cantenes. Then I remembered that I had those handcuffs and decided to lock up my wife without her permission. Cue bom chica wah wah. She's on her knees not knowing what happened to her, and I'm cracking up. When I told her she laughed and says ok you had your fun now take them off. I didn't realize the error that I made until it was too late. I had never found a key for the handcuffs, and they were in near pristine condition! She was cuffed until she broke them or I could find a key...After about 20 mins of struggling to break them to no avail, we decide to quit out and rejoin. Unfortunately, it killed her! She was so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at me for this and it still comes up everytime we play this game.

Interesting game with open-ended possibilities, but difficult to begin.  However, why would one begin with no clothing, armed with only a rock, and the comfort of a torch?  I found myself running around for about an hour trying to bash logs, trees, crates, structures with no idea how to progress.  Other players offered hints, but no certain orientation was apparent on to how to survive.  Other players were naked as well were running aound, whereby three of them killed me with their rock.  Logically,  I should have some knowledge of survival before I begin awakened from pergutory with only my basalt companion to use as a tool.  I understand the need for progression and learning through trial and  error, as well as occasional help from other players, but getting lost (and frustrated) in the beginning seems too much to become comfortable with this game's player dynamics.
I really wanted to like this game fro the start, and perhaps with additional time, I will.  I can understand giving players a leveled playing field to begin so advancement begins at level zero for everyone, however, unless you are very familiar with *How* to progress, it will seem like you are an outsider that will be certainly doomed to respawn over and over unless someone takes you under their wing.  For players new to Rust, apprenticeship may not be easy to obtain unless you know established players or on the off chance meet someone that actually wants to help you understand the world in which you'll spend trying to decipher.  The ability and possibility of building your own structures and crafting items for survival is none the less intriguing.
If Rust had a orientation such as a dream state where you could do some crafting, constructing, hunting, etc where you *remember* what to do, it could loop in new players easier.  Experienced players already know exactly what they need to do when they wake up from their slumber, so it would be great if new players could at least learn some rudimentary things prior to waking up (spawning) in this volatile environment.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

It is hard to talk about this game without spoiling too much, but it definitely went viral for a reason.
The music, characters, and bullet hell turn based combat system are amazing and I would easily play this game for those reasons alone. But what really makes this game shine is its story, and how the game changes according to how you play it.
There are two major paths, Pacifist or Genocide. They feel COMPLETELEY different, changing events and the world drastically. The game truly makes you feel the path you are taking. Doing a Genocide run after the Pacifist path is a trip, and may not be for the faint of heart.
Note that the game knows what you did, even if you load a previous save.
I loved playing this game, and I would highly recommend it. Definitely go for the extreme endings to get a true feel for it. There are a few spoiler free guides that you can use to get a gist of each path if you need.

Ah Rust. As we all know, steam is very much oversaturated with survival crafting mmo's. however, Rust is by far the most immersive and rewarding experience i've had so far. the game in and of itself is pretty simple. harvest, craft, build, survive. while harvesting and exploring are two fun yet critical components in the game, pvp is inevitable, and is in fact a primary staple of the game. Pvp is the reason for the game's intense difficulty and the sense of panic and paranoia when you know you're being stalked from afar.
In truth, the game is what you make it. the beautiful visuals and environment makes playing for immersion possible. sometimes you just want to get by in your little shack that you've outfitted with spikes and traps and a balcony that you stand guard at defending your home with a bow and arrow. or perhaps you're the type that enjoys banding together with a small gang of raiders armed with revolvers and bone armor, going base to base, busting down walls with your preciously scarce c4 you spent forever crafting. or hell, maybe you're a clan guy, belonging to a large heavily armed compound nestled in a valley rich in resources, keeping your phone close by in case you get a text while you're offline saying that your clan's fortress is getting raided by a rival clan and they need you online now.
just remember, you will rage after losing your base that you spent 3 real life days building. every time you get raided, learn from it. adapt, grow, and improve. its a man eat man world, literally, and you'll realize that after you watch yourself become the manhunter you never thought you'd be.
