undertale is the game that makes me wish for an 'I guess' option, so treat this vote as that.
this game gets a lot of praise everywhere I go, so because it was on sale, I decided to give it a go, and I don't get why it is praised this much.
as always, let me start with the positive points:
+ the battle system is awesome, as a bullet hell fan, I loved it and the variations made it constantly interresting
+ the random encouters are not annoying, and I never needed to farm once
+ the musics were really cool, and I completely understand the praise the game gets around the music
+ this game was a lot shorter than though it would be, and to be honest, I am glad, because it was just the right length for me
while this game as quite a few things going on for him, there are points that didn't work out so well in my opinion:
- a lot of people say that this game hurt their feelings, but it didn't do anything to me, most of the characters were forgetable and they were for the most part a**holes who wanted to either kill me, capture me or stop me from going back to my family (I can only think of 3 who didn't do that: sans, the guy from the lab and the ghost).
- the game has a backstory that didn't interrest me at all, and it didn't make me want to look more into it, as all you do in the entire game is find the barrier to go back home, that backstory is barely mentioned and isn't even used in the main story.
- this kinda goes with my first negative point but the game often made characters appear out of nowhere, makes you kill them and then talks about them as big charaters expecting you to feel bad for killing them. all I knew is that they wanted to kill me, why would I feel bad for defending myself?
this felt like a poor attempt at making the game sad more than anything.
- a lot of feature in the game is almost useless, such as the phone, the spare option and the entire act tab
- the graphics look really cool, but am I really the only one who thinks the main character looks ugly?!?
all in all, this game has a great combat system but a (in my honest opinion) poor story. so I would recommend that you get it when it's on sale only if you like bullet hell games, if you want an interresting story with memorable characters though, I recommend you look for something else.
Final rating: 5.5/10

The game is good, Toby did a great job on it but I felt the game was too short. The only thing I was told by the friend who gifted me the game was to play it by my own personility which meant that I played it with my own decisions. Certain monsters who attacked me of the bat got murdered. Undyne got murdered cause I dispise her attitude and how I could not spare nor woudl she listen. Toriel got the axe cause she challenged my authority in leaving from a kidnapping situation. Thus I showed her how strong I was cause she asked me to. Mettaton got the axe too because not only he was annoying but his creator... I was onto her, she was trying to kill me.
The only characters I enjoyed  was Sans and Papyrus and thus they were spared.
I do not feel like a monster for doing the genocide run and I wanted to puke rainbows and kittens at the pacifist ending.
I feel if the game was longer and had more meat and potatoes, I would have enjoyed the game a bit more. I do not have the "fan boy conviction" some people have with this game. Toby did a great job but I feel the game is over hyped. It was so over hyped that the game I feel is a good start of a game but needs more. I say this because like when you do the genocide run, Flowey makes a comment about how you would kill him if he got in your way or became useless in your goals.
I feel that if there was more build up to each boss fight.  Something to make you feel guilty for killing them because you are a heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Then yes, I could see how the genocide route would do so but to be all honest. The monsters are JUST AS GUILTY as the humans. To declare that all humans are bad is just as bad as the humans who imprisoned them. How can I feel guilty about killing monsters who the first thing walking up to me, even after trying to talk to them. They attack my soul?
Flowey from the start tries to lie to you and tries to kill you. Toriel saves you but how can you trust Toriel who tries to kidnap you and keep you in her home.
The one point I will put out is I like the simple battle system, I do love the music. The music does remind me of Earthbound. The gameplay is great but the storyline could have had more meat and potatoes to it.
I hope that when and if Toby makes anther game or anther Undertale 2: The Surface. That he makes it longer. And we all know that I think Toby could easily make a Undertale 2 where you have many routes, paths and perhaps either side with the humans and imprison the monsters again(genocide route), help the monsters intergrate into society(Pacifist route) or you do nothing and let them duke it out(neutral). Oh and make your decisions affect more.... than they do. I mean I killed Undyne and supposely Alyphs watched it but yet she states she didn't and she doesn't bat an I... I feel the only decision that really affects what I did was the genocide route. I really just felt my decisions only affected who was where and why and hte phone call at the end for the neutral route.
I think everyone should play this game but it's a GOOD game, not a great game.  The game is over hyped. I'm sure within minutes this review will have a billion dislikes cause I'm going against the fan boy crowd.

Undertale is a great game, I enjoyed it and played all three runs. Undertale is an RPG game where you play as a child who has fallen down a mountain into a world of monsters. You travel the underground and adventure to find a way out.The music in this game is outstanding, besides the fact that more than half the songs are remixes or sped up/slowed down versions of 5 songs. The pacifist run will make you hit the feels, and after that you get a happy ending. There are many things that bother me, and I would like to point them out.
1. Toriel knows you for like, 30 minutes and gets WAY too overprotective
2. Toriel is only in 1/10 of the game, yet she's a popular fan-pick
3. The entire ruins part seems a bit boring and is too long
4. The ruins "teach you" how to solve puzzles, even though puzzle solving rarely shows up in the game
(Spoilers Ahead! Skip if you want to play blind!)
5. Sans is EASILY BEAT BY FLOWEY (megalovania anyone?)
6. The fanbase is a bit, well, i'll just describe them as fnaf-like
One of the biggest things I would like to point out is that Undertale has alot of cliche parts in it, and the game in an overall rating deserves a 8.5 because there are still alot of things that make the game boring. when i was in the CORE, I felt like the enemies were just annoying, and Undertale fails to place the "all monsters are unique" in at the best times, so that people will experience it. The main thing that will make you love this game more are the fans. They tell you everything positive, and it makes you enjoy the game more, now that's not a bad thing, but after you're already playing after your 2 runs of the game, you start to feel, it isn't fun, or "I have to go through all of this again? ._."
Overall, Undertale is a good game, but I don't want the parts that make it non-perfect to be covered up.

This is one of the first games in a long time to ever make me cry. And so early on too! When I first started to hear about this game, I was confused on what it was about. So I downloaded the demo and gave it a shot. The demo was fun, but I was intrigued about the rest of the game. I downloaded the game and started my first run as the True Pacifist. Soon after I did neutral, and later I did my least favourite of the bunch, genocide. I have now clocked in 40 hours in this game, and plan to do more. This was definelty my game of the year.

This game...this game touchs my very soul. Its music is powerful, its message is strong. Its cast of characters is amazing. I will forever carry this game and its music with me, where-ever I go. Its part of who I am, what I believe. Its part of my soul, my heart, and my mind. There is so much I wish I could say, but the words just...don't exist for me to convey how I feel. So many strong emotions swell within me. This game may have went silent, but it won't ever die.
Toby, if you are reading this...I would like to thank you for creating this game. There is much I wish to say to you, but I can't find the words for it. What you've made here...its just...perfect in my eyes. The music is so wonderful, the characters...I love it all. I want to thank you ever so greatly Toby. You're game helped me become a better being. You helped me see the errors of my ways, and I thank you for that. I thank you for this game, for its message...for everything.
To end this all...I just want to say this, one final time. Undertale is an amazing game. I loved playing it. I will never do a genocide run. I just don't have the heart or soul to do so. I can't bring myself to harm any of the characters in this game, nor can I see poor Asriel be killed off. I can't bring myself to do it, and I never attemped to do so. I love this game, and I will carry its message with me forever. Through this life, and whatever comes after this.
No matter how old I get, how old this game gets, I will always, always...keep its message known, its story and music heard. I will never drift away from it. This game shall always stay with me, no matter how old I do get. I will treasure it, and love it, as I do now. I don't care, if I will be hated for loving this game, long after its been released, I don't care if I'm made fun of, for my love of it. Because in the end, this game is still with me. I, love this game so very, very much.
Stay DETERMINED....and Goodnight.

; Undertale is a mash-up between a standard RPG and Bullet-hell combat. The story itself is quite interesting and the different routes you can take, not to mention the hidden lore you can find by looking stuff up, makes Undertale an interesting game. I would give it a solid 9/10.
Now for the longer review...
Undertale functions as a very bare-bones RPG. You do not have many stats, consisting of ATK, DEF, Gold, and LV. You may have noticed I did not include HP. In Undertale, you're HP is directly related with your LV. There are no items to increase it, although you can get items to lengthen invincibility frames. When attacked, you will be put into a combat screen. You have 2 choices. These choices are a simple "FIGHT", which is a general 'hit-the-bulls-eye' type of attack, and "SPARE", which can be more complicated at times. The games branching story depends greatly on how much you use each of these methods.
You can guess just by looking at the trailer how the graphics are. It has a very 8-bit feel to it and, in all honesty, pulls it off quite well.
Undertale has many amazing characters in its story. I never got bored of seeing how everyone acted, even the fodder monsters that you fight have a certain personality to them. There are also many interesting quirks to each main character. One being a knight sworn to their duty, another being a anime-loving royal scientist.

Like graphics, not much to say here. The soundtrack is pretty good for what it is and also helps with the 8-bit and RPG feeling. It also does a great job at giving a music that suits your surroundings and
I mean atmosphere... yeah...
A lot of negative reviews have one thing in common(that isn't due to personal preference). It's how you don't gain LV for sparing monsters. They're right. In fact, it is actually impossible to kill something without gaining LV. I'll explain it more in a spoiler, but basically LV doesn't quite stand for "Level" in this game.
Everything else amounts to "bad story"... I'd argue it's good as long as you actually get far enough to enjoy it.
That's just about everything. Now, you may be wondering why I gave this game a 9/10 since I said nothing wrong about it. One reason is because I have a strong belief that no game is perfect. The other reason is the final boss at the end of the Neutral route kinda... Let's just say it was a bit weird for me... It isn't much though. Just get past that and you can see the other 2 routes, which do quite the job at explaining the story.

Okay, I'll write a serious review for my friends and whoever reads this (without any actual spoilers):
Undertale is a well... I don't know if there's an exact word to describe what it is. RPG? Fighter? Bullet hell? Something along the lines of those? Well, with that out of the way, it's one of those games where what you do and how you act can change how your story plays out for you. There are two different kinds of "runs" or "stories". Pacifist, where you befriend and don't fight the monsters you meet (and might even get emotionally attached to), and Genocide (also known as "No Mercy") where you fight all the monsters, almost like an extermination route.
If you do Pacifist first, you'll generally feel bad when you play Genocide, not wanting to kill monsters you've met before. But if you play Genocide first, you might like the game less, but have an easier time killing monsters, because you haven't grown attached to them at all. Your story as the character is that you have fallen into the underground, where monsters were sealed off from the overworld, and you have to find a way to escape.
Now, that's it for explanation, personal opinion time. I liked the game. The people who dislike it often try to compare it to FNAF, because it got so popular so soon. The game had it's fun moments, and gave me quite a few laughs as well. It has "the feels" as some would say, and bosses that will give you a challenge. All in all, I felt the game was satisfying, and would reccomend it to someone that's looking for a game with a good story and a fun play style. (If you're on my friends list and you want to ask me about the game, you can just message me.) Anyway, that's my review. Hope it helped, and I hope you buy the game.

Undertale is an rpg that takes inspiration from Earthbound with its own unique charm and flare. The motto of the game is that you could kill these monsters you face and get EXP like a normal rpg protagonist, or you could spare them all through the game.
Sometimes sparing is frustrating, usually a puzzle on its self figuring out how to do it for certain boses or enemies. Sometimes you just have to hold out against an onslought of attacks. Sometimes its worth it. Sometimes you will feel defeated, and others victorious.
Either way, spare or no spare, the game delivers on character and characters in spades. Te writing is fantastic, cheeky, and doesn't try too hard to "meme" it up. I felt engaged and interested in pretty much every major character in some capacity. I felt terror, fear, sadness, sympathy, and maybe hints of affection. Its hard to draw those feelings out for characters in a video game, especially when most rpgs dance with tired and true tropes we all know.
Undertale alllows for so much more though. No expectation is a solid one when faced with Undertales writing.
The music is a major highlight. The soundtrack with last long on the internet as those tracks you will hear a lot in youtube videos for the next five years. Each track gets its point across fast and well.
The combat is atypical, going for a bullet hell dodging mechanic over swinging swords, although you can still do so if you don't mind drawing blood. Even when choosing the violent route, the attack is a rhythm game, not just an animation. The mechanics of the fight change based on enemy sometimes, making the gameplay feel fresh throughout the playthrough.
My only gripe is the start/tutorial is a bit weak compared to the rest of the game.

Undertale is an over hyped piece of garbage and I have a problem with that. In essesnce because of the cult following this game gets it is impossible to review this game because any negative review will be ignored. But sometimes you just have to try. Undertale has many flaws that get overlooked. The first being the concept for the entire game. That idea of should i really be killing these monsters to level up and and get Xp. That idea gets old after the first area and the game never really compounds on that idea and it kind of just sits there until you complete the first playthrough. That being the second problem, Undertale artificially extends its play time by making the player go back and play the entire game again and try to get a different ending. Most of the time when games do this I don' t mind but those games change dramatically or are at least fun, two things Undertale fails to be, fun and different. The second playthrough is most likely the pacifist playthrough, it was for me, and most of the game was the same except for the dates, the part in the underground lab, and final boss. Other wise it is the same 4 hours of nothing. The third flaw of this game is its play time. it takes 4 hours to beat a single playthrough. With 3 major endings it should take about 12 hours to complete this game and see most of the content in this game. If it wasn't repetitive, awesome bring it on. But no I can't even bring myself to finish the murder run because I can't take the repetitiveness. The next flaw is in the overworld. The entire game looks like it was made in MS-Paint. So it is not pretty but ugly games have never stoped me before. What makes this bad is that all the enemy battle sprites look so good that the overworld seems lack luster and rushed. Finally we have the story. The story just isn't engaging. We follow a young human child, with jaundice, through his many adventures in the same underground monster infested cave as he tries to get home. and that is it.
I mean overall Undertale is not a bad game and it might even be a good game. But it falls short in some pretty key areas and overall leaves a sour taste in my mouth when I am done playing a session. The essense of this game, the moral ddilemma, is something that i just don't care about. The only good thing I i can agree with about this game is that it has a great soundtrack and if that is enough, buy it. Or just follow all the hype and buy it anyways becuase trust me Undertale is a one of a king experience.

Undertale is the perfect example of how a single player story game should be. All of the characters are lovable in their own way. Even Flowey the flower, and ESPECIALLY goatmom (though im pretty sure shes a cow, that's what my friends refer to her as). The story has branching paths based on your decisions and each of your decisions really feel like they matter.
The game has a fairly simple combat system. You choose whether you want to attack, act, use an item, or show your opponents mercy. If you have fulfilled the correct requirements, usually through act, then you can spare your enemy at the cost of the battle's EXP. Regardless of if you choose to attack or act, you must dodge the attacks thrown at you in a similar way to a bullet hell.
Each of the different paths are worth playing, as you only get chunks of the story in each, not the whole story. This gives the game a surprising amount of replayability. The best way most agree to play it is to first do a "pacifist" run. This means never killing a monster and instead attempting to resolve all conflict in other ways. This fills you in on the story the most, and shows you the emotional side of the game. You even get to grow close to the monsters. Hell, if you play your cards right, you get to date a skeleton!
When doing a "genocide" run of the game, you must kill every monster you see. This may be more up the alley of those who have played many JRPGs before, as it will feel fairly similar to them. While less focused on story, this path allows you to fight the two hardest bosses in the game, the hardest of which may be the hardest boss I've had to fight before. The satisfaction of beating these bosses makes all the struggling against them well worth it.
I really can't recommend this game enough to everyone. It has a beautiful story, lovable characters, and extremely fun and challenging boss fights. Really, what more could you ask for in a game? I give Undertale a perfect 10/10.

With over 200 hours put into this game, I have played enough to have been almost everywhere and seen almost everything in the game, including the corners and far reaches (Nice work removing the tents and high loot from Balota and moving it out west where no one will ever bother to look by the way >.>) Despite every zombie that ever walked through a wall, every murderous staircase, and every button you have to press to simply get into a vehicle, I still love you DayZ. This game has the potential to be the best survival/PvP game that ever existed, especially considering the $70 million dollars that was spent on it in the first month of open alpha, but Dean, you are so slow! I know the devs want to stay in their little group of friends and not hire a bunch of programmers that they'll probably never get along with, but I demand progress!
But in all seriousness, I love the work the devs are doing (even if it is at a glacial pace) and I hope to see more content soon.
Now, onto the actual review (finally).
DayZ is perhaps the most realistic survival simulator I've yet seen, and I think that even though the price is steep for an early access game, it is completely worth it. Worth every penny (Millionenschwer!). But be warned! This game requires the utmost patience and a level head. Bandits, zombies, and glitches will kill you at every chance they get! When you get good gear you have to be willing to sacrifice it at a moments notice, because you never know who's around that corner with an M4A1. Starting over is a brutally hardcore process in the game that happens more often than most people are comfortable with. I, however, enjoy the brutality put on by Dean Hall and the devs. They punish you for your mistakes, which would seem bad but makes getting re-equiped that much sweeter! The lack of vehicles in the alpha make this game quite the more to require patience. But I have to admit, there's something peaceful about hiking through Chernarus whilst skyping my friends and playing The Proclaimers - I'm gonna be (500 Miles) in the background. In closing, I once again warn you: THIS GAME IS NOT FOR THE LIGHT OF HEART! DEATH, LAG, AND GLITCHING ARE AROUND EVERY CORNER!

; Undertale is a mash-up between a standard RPG and Bullet-hell combat. The story itself is quite interesting and the different routes you can take, not to mention the hidden lore you can find by looking stuff up, makes Undertale an interesting game. I would give it a solid 9/10.
Now for the longer review...
Undertale functions as a very bare-bones RPG. You do not have many stats, consisting of ATK, DEF, Gold, and LV. You may have noticed I did not include HP. In Undertale, you're HP is directly related with your LV. There are no items to increase it, although you can get items to lengthen invincibility frames. When attacked, you will be put into a combat screen. You have 2 choices. These choices are a simple "FIGHT", which is a general 'hit-the-bulls-eye' type of attack, and "SPARE", which can be more complicated at times. The games branching story depends greatly on how much you use each of these methods.
You can guess just by looking at the trailer how the graphics are. It has a very 8-bit feel to it and, in all honesty, pulls it off quite well.
Undertale has many amazing characters in its story. I never got bored of seeing how everyone acted, even the fodder monsters that you fight have a certain personality to them. There are also many interesting quirks to each main character. One being a knight sworn to their duty, another being a anime-loving royal scientist.

Like graphics, not much to say here. The soundtrack is pretty good for what it is and also helps with the 8-bit and RPG feeling. It also does a great job at giving a music that suits your surroundings and
I mean atmosphere... yeah...
A lot of negative reviews have one thing in common(that isn't due to personal preference). It's how you don't gain LV for sparing monsters. They're right. In fact, it is actually impossible to kill something without gaining LV. I'll explain it more in a spoiler, but basically LV doesn't quite stand for "Level" in this game.
Everything else amounts to "bad story"... I'd argue it's good as long as you actually get far enough to enjoy it.
That's just about everything. Now, you may be wondering why I gave this game a 9/10 since I said nothing wrong about it. One reason is because I have a strong belief that no game is perfect. The other reason is the final boss at the end of the Neutral route kinda... Let's just say it was a bit weird for me... It isn't much though. Just get past that and you can see the other 2 routes, which do quite the job at explaining the story.

Undertale is the perfect example of how a single player story game should be. All of the characters are lovable in their own way. Even Flowey the flower, and ESPECIALLY goatmom (though im pretty sure shes a cow, that's what my friends refer to her as). The story has branching paths based on your decisions and each of your decisions really feel like they matter.
The game has a fairly simple combat system. You choose whether you want to attack, act, use an item, or show your opponents mercy. If you have fulfilled the correct requirements, usually through act, then you can spare your enemy at the cost of the battle's EXP. Regardless of if you choose to attack or act, you must dodge the attacks thrown at you in a similar way to a bullet hell.
Each of the different paths are worth playing, as you only get chunks of the story in each, not the whole story. This gives the game a surprising amount of replayability. The best way most agree to play it is to first do a "pacifist" run. This means never killing a monster and instead attempting to resolve all conflict in other ways. This fills you in on the story the most, and shows you the emotional side of the game. You even get to grow close to the monsters. Hell, if you play your cards right, you get to date a skeleton!
When doing a "genocide" run of the game, you must kill every monster you see. This may be more up the alley of those who have played many JRPGs before, as it will feel fairly similar to them. While less focused on story, this path allows you to fight the two hardest bosses in the game, the hardest of which may be the hardest boss I've had to fight before. The satisfaction of beating these bosses makes all the struggling against them well worth it.
I really can't recommend this game enough to everyone. It has a beautiful story, lovable characters, and extremely fun and challenging boss fights. Really, what more could you ask for in a game? I give Undertale a perfect 10/10.

Alright, so I'm writing this review with the same thoughts as most people who love this game. We all just want everyone to stop bashing it for things that are either out of the developer’s hands, things that the person that bought the game should have thought about beforehand, and/or people that are complaining about things when they have only had 1-10 hours of gameplay.
One thing I would also like to stress, I am not a big fan of the bohemia games. Yes they are some of the most detailed, fluent, and immersive games I've ever seen. But I am more of a hack and slash or RPG kind of gamer. I am only including this so you know that I am not just some bohemia fan boy trying to come at everyone for talking bad about their games.
PROS:
-Can eat people
-THEY HAVE VEHICLES TO DRIVE IN, YES IT HAS HAPPEND ALREADY.
-Great bullet projection and bullet drop. If you are a sniper trying to find some peoples day to ruin, then this lonely and cold game is for you.
-BIGGEST MAP I HAVE EVER HAD THE PLEASURE OF MASSCAREING PEOPLE IN. (Besides Altis)
-Rushes of adrenaline when getting in a combat situation. The feeling is unlike any other. I have NEVER felt the way this game makes me feel when I can hear a bullet *PWHOOSH* past my skull. Most people will also talk about this or maybe they haven’t played the game long enough before actually posting a good review.
-In-depth Graphics. Never seen such beauty in a game when it comes to the floral, weapon design, and the character detail.
-Great party play. Seriously, if you aren't playing this game with friends then you really are not playing Dayz the way it
was meant to be played.
CONS:
-Weapon-sway after running is the biggest ♥♥♥♥♥ you will have to deal with in this game. (Realism at its finest)
-Like previously stated, this game is a PARTY PLAY game. As in, you don't have friends or know how to use the internet? Then this game IS NOT for you.
-Solo play can be boring. I will admit this is another thing that can make the game seem like a walking simulator 2015. You play alone looking for food, weapons, running from the police (AKA the guys with the better guns than you), and then you get shot and just wasted 3-7 hours of your day. It's just the way Dayz goes. How do you make up for it you ask? you grow some balls, get some buddies, AND THEN no one will ♥♥♥♥ with you.
-Poor zombie AI, they are working on this as I write this review.
CHECK IT.
-The loot spawning system needs some work. I haven’t found an M4 since the helicopter update was implemented.
-That's the other con of this game, I CAN'T FIND HELICOPTERS OR POLICE CARS EVER. They are so rare that you will have better luck trying to fist yourself while playing The Can Can with a violin.
Ok, it's not that bad....
The last thing I want to post on this review is that I also see a lot of people complaining about hackers. To be honest, in the 180 some hours of playing this game, I HAVE ONLY MET ONE HACKER. He said "sup." then floated away. Is that so bad?
Lastly, GET THIS GAME AND DON'T TRUST ANYONE.

Being a early access game and still in alpha (they remade the whole game so this stage has been prolonged) many people have avoided it. Honestly this is the best early access game out there. The dev team is amazing and provide frequent updates (no, they have not given up on it and don't seem like they will). It has a healthy player base with new people joining all the time.
The survival aspects are there. You start off naked with only a torch and a rock and you have to move your way up by creating new and better tools and weapons. You face dangers such as the wildlife, a patrol helicopter and most importantly other players. In order to make new items you need to gather wood, stone, metal and sulphur from the enviroment. 'Monuments' and 'rad towns' provide land marks on the map and can be explored in order to find loot such as weapons, tools and blue prints. Each item requires a blue print in order to craft (you have many 'default' blueprints right from the start), the more advanced the item the harder it is to craft and the harder it is to get the blue print.
Rust uses a modular building system that allows players to build whatever their heart's desire. Want to build a shack with one room? You can. Want to build a massive compound with towers and a castle? You can if you put the effort into it. Be aware that people can make explosives in order to raid you. To try and mitigate against this make sure to design your home well. Try and make peace not war with your neighbours unless you want to make it a race to get C4 and blow down the other's base. Don't worry if you can get raided. It happens to everyone and not just once. Try and rebuild in a new area, make new friends and new enemies. Explore the amazing open world.
Rust currently updates biweekly compared to the weekly updates it used to have and each update is either filled with amazing content to keep the game fresh or backend developer stuff to hasten the introduction of new content and provide much needed improvements. The dev team seems to get a lot of crap for not catering to everyone's needs and by being a normal person you would understand that, just isn't possible. I feel this has been caused by the dev team being so good many people have become spoilt brats. I guess that's a good thing. In my opinion this is the best dev team as they work hard and infact do listen to the community. You won't be seeing any DayZ style yearly updates (I still love you DayZ!).
One warning is that Rust takes up a lot of time. Yes, you can jump on and play whenever (you might want to play on modded servers which speed up the process of resource collecting. Each modded server has their own set of features) but to get the most enjoyment out of it, having a weekend/week with little on is the best way to play.
For $20 or the current sale price of $13.39, this game is a no brainer.

-Is "Undertale" great? I think so, yes.
-Does it live up to the hype? While I think it's debatable, I personally believe that it does and I can see why it's so hyped. It's an accessible RPG with a fun and unique combat system. This combined with great music, lovable characters and genuinely funny jokes make this a game that is hard not to enjoy. Long story short, it can easily be a fun experience for both the casual and intense gamer, which I believe lends to why it has gotten so much attention recently: just about anyone can appreciate it and have a good time.
Verdict
"Undertale" is a fun, accessible RPG that can easily appeal to both casual and intense gamers. Unique combat, great tunes and lovable characters make this a must play indie title. However, the RPG elements in this game don't go very deep, so if you're looking for a highly customizable game with multiple play types and character builds or a strategically in depth turn-based combat system look somewhere else.
*P.S. If you're looking at my Steam hours and wondering "Wow! Can I really get that many hours of gameplay out of "Undertale?" The answer is very probably "No." I have nephews and a niece that like to play this game a lot. I would estimate that if you go for all three of the main endings you'll probably get about 10-12 hours of gameplay depending on how much time you take exploring and talking to people.*

In
, Toby Fox and the team of game developers that helped him ask a simple question for rpgs, "
" Without spoiling things, this small question has bigger implications on the funny but sweet world of the game. Death is taken seriously, and just one kill has consequences, as do some story choices along the way. It's given even more gravity when the monsters that are normally rpg cannon fodder are their own fleshed out characters.
The gameplay is a pleasant surprise. The combat isn't reliant on RNGs (random number generators) and instead goes for bullet hell gameplay. So hits only hit if they touch you. The option to attack or act on your turn ads its own little puzzle to the game for players who would rather solve things without violence. The design of the game is thoughtfully done with the player in mind. Sometimes it's still frustrating, but not enough to be completely off-putting.
The graphics, while not for everyone, I think take advantage of the retro look for clean visuals. Some characters don't really mesh with the main visual direction, though, and feel like they were drawn by completely different artists.
The music is surprisngly great. Each song captures the mood of the moment but still leaves you with distinct melodies you'll definitely find yourself humming, like the video game music of yesteryear. It's not just nostalgia-bait, it's actually good. At this rate, I'm probably buying the soundtrack too.
If you want to try an rpg with a distinct take on the genre with the option to solve things peacefully, please try
. Don't look further into it, it's best played blind.

I can recommend this, but don't expect miracles.
It's a fun playthrough and some of the humor is pretty well thought out. There are three endings, but really only two different ways to play through the game. You can follow the rules and get lively character interactions and a happy ending, or go against moral principles and have a very boring playthrough that ends with one of the only difficult battles in the game, but it's worth doing because of the huge difficulty spike at the end.
Sans one of them, there isn't a whole lot of depth to the characters as almost all of them are built out of one (1) quirk they possess and a few of the characters can get annoying very quickly. The writing isn't aware of subtlety, so you won't miss anything unless you're a hardcore narcoleptic dummy or a masher of the Z and X keys as all the spoken material is very clear cut.
Battle mechanics while you're on the defense are a really nice breath of fresh air for RPGs and it would be good if more people added active defense like this in their games. Dodging attacks and taking chances on using health items is exciting and brings back memories of the chance in using guard types from Nintendo's Paper Mario 2. Offense, on the other hand, is a different story. Many people will praise to the moon how you don't have to kill anything and that each encounter is deep and personal, but once you figure out how to beat something through ACT, it becomes a rudimentary experience with every subsequent encounter playing out all too similarly. The FIGHT option is also very shallow, but is somewhat justified in that the game discourages violence.
Credit where it is due, it's pretty darn impressive to see a game like this come out of GameMaker, and most of the music is quite nice. Very few thematic devices are used, and yet there is a great deal of variance to many of the tracks. Some of the megafans are trying to use this as a way to connect characters to one another, which is a load of bull****, so don't buy into that. Just think of it like Banjo Kazooie, Donkey Kong 64 or Wario Land 3 with their stylistic changes without melodic changes.
Overall, you are very likely to enjoy your experience with Undertale, but it is not the best game ever made. Not by a long shot.

Tl;dr: The game’s good, but the fan base is annoying and getting the best content is also annoying.
I wanted to hate this game. I wanted to point out how over rated it is (it still is), and I wanted to tell all of the mega-fans to just calm the !@#$ down about it -- oh wait I still will, CALM THE !@#$ DOWN MEGA-FANS! But I don't hate this game.
In fact, I recommend this game quite a bit, but I can't help but wonder if it would have been nearly as effective or popular if the game's base story was all there was to it. The fact that I went into this game knowing there was a big twist at the end almost ruined it for me, but the amount of charm Undertale's world had, won me over.
However charming the world may be, the thing people often say this game has a "good story" for is its massive meta-narrative, that is unfortunately only given to you in chunks through the game’s other endings.
The worst part is that these endings aren't just a little bit of different text, it's often a new boss, More information on the lore of the game, and other things. I've done all of the endings and they're all great in their own way, but they feel like side-quests that you have to repeat the whole game to do, but the base game just has a few small tweeks.
Although I realize a lot of this could probably be countered by saying that it's just completionist stuff, I'd argue the best parts of the game are in these other endings and the amount of work needed to get to those is asinine. I’m all for putting side content in games, but when you need to play through the whole game again and again just to get to it, it’s really stretching to your patience.
Admittedly, the game allows you to skip some parts during sequental playthroughs, which is good, but I feel like more parts could have used the same treatment in some way. For example, the player could have been given the option to skip puzzles they've already done in previous playthroughs.
But again, I don’t hate Undertale, I really like it and I recommend it to anyone who enjoyed any of the Mother games, or just JRPG’s in general...unless you don't like bullet-hell games...because the battle system uses bullet-hell mechanics for dodging enemies attacks.

In
, Toby Fox and the team of game developers that helped him ask a simple question for rpgs, "
" Without spoiling things, this small question has bigger implications on the funny but sweet world of the game. Death is taken seriously, and just one kill has consequences, as do some story choices along the way. It's given even more gravity when the monsters that are normally rpg cannon fodder are their own fleshed out characters.
The gameplay is a pleasant surprise. The combat isn't reliant on RNGs (random number generators) and instead goes for bullet hell gameplay. So hits only hit if they touch you. The option to attack or act on your turn ads its own little puzzle to the game for players who would rather solve things without violence. The design of the game is thoughtfully done with the player in mind. Sometimes it's still frustrating, but not enough to be completely off-putting.
The graphics, while not for everyone, I think take advantage of the retro look for clean visuals. Some characters don't really mesh with the main visual direction, though, and feel like they were drawn by completely different artists.
The music is surprisngly great. Each song captures the mood of the moment but still leaves you with distinct melodies you'll definitely find yourself humming, like the video game music of yesteryear. It's not just nostalgia-bait, it's actually good. At this rate, I'm probably buying the soundtrack too.
If you want to try an rpg with a distinct take on the genre with the option to solve things peacefully, please try
. Don't look further into it, it's best played blind.

I can recommend this, but don't expect miracles.
It's a fun playthrough and some of the humor is pretty well thought out. There are three endings, but really only two different ways to play through the game. You can follow the rules and get lively character interactions and a happy ending, or go against moral principles and have a very boring playthrough that ends with one of the only difficult battles in the game, but it's worth doing because of the huge difficulty spike at the end.
Sans one of them, there isn't a whole lot of depth to the characters as almost all of them are built out of one (1) quirk they possess and a few of the characters can get annoying very quickly. The writing isn't aware of subtlety, so you won't miss anything unless you're a hardcore narcoleptic dummy or a masher of the Z and X keys as all the spoken material is very clear cut.
Battle mechanics while you're on the defense are a really nice breath of fresh air for RPGs and it would be good if more people added active defense like this in their games. Dodging attacks and taking chances on using health items is exciting and brings back memories of the chance in using guard types from Nintendo's Paper Mario 2. Offense, on the other hand, is a different story. Many people will praise to the moon how you don't have to kill anything and that each encounter is deep and personal, but once you figure out how to beat something through ACT, it becomes a rudimentary experience with every subsequent encounter playing out all too similarly. The FIGHT option is also very shallow, but is somewhat justified in that the game discourages violence.
Credit where it is due, it's pretty darn impressive to see a game like this come out of GameMaker, and most of the music is quite nice. Very few thematic devices are used, and yet there is a great deal of variance to many of the tracks. Some of the megafans are trying to use this as a way to connect characters to one another, which is a load of bull****, so don't buy into that. Just think of it like Banjo Kazooie, Donkey Kong 64 or Wario Land 3 with their stylistic changes without melodic changes.
Overall, you are very likely to enjoy your experience with Undertale, but it is not the best game ever made. Not by a long shot.

Undertale is the best RPG of 2015, maybe of all time. Maybe the best game of 2015. Possibly even the best game of all time. It's that good.
I wasn't sure I would like this game... it seemed like a homage to JRPGs, which I really dislike. So I pretty much ignored everyone saying what a great game Undertale is.
Well, I shouldn't have.
What really makes the game shine are the amazing, tender characters, great music, extremely clever writing and gameplay mechanics that play with you while you play with the game.
There's nothing else really like it, it's just stunning how something so original can be so free of bugs and gameplay flaws.
The battle mechanics are so much better than any of the old JRPGs, though I hear they aren't totally unique. I haven't played any of the games that are said to have similar mechanics (paper mario? IDK).
The only things I don't like about Undertale is it's somewhat short (~6 hours) and some important plot information is too hidden. You need at least two playthroughs, careful searching and listening to npcs, as well making certain choices in order to find out what's really gone on in the past and going on now. It's good that the game doesn't spoonfeed you everything but I feel like some stronger hints could be dropped about a few important optional plot exposition points that I won't spoil.
I also only bought it after I saw some lets plays and streams, which was good because it convinvinced me to buy the game, but also bad because I feel like this game would be somehow better if I went into it completely unknowning. I do recommend going in completely "blind" and not reading any guides, lets plays or wikis, try to be as unspoiled as possible. But even if you've had certain things spoiled, like I did, this is still something you should buy immediately and play.
Play it blind. Changed what RPG means to me.

I was very skeptical about this game at first. It does pay homage to some other JRPG’s of the past and it has a certain charm that I have not seen in many games of this era. I recommend it to any gamer who wants to have a great story unfold with you at the helm and also if you love to pet dogs to the clouds and back. 10/10

(SPOILERS AHEAD IF YOU HAVEN'T PLAYED AT LEAST THE DEMO)
Now that Undertale is making the rounds on various end-of-year Top 10 lists, I figured it was time to share my experience with this game, and why, when I first played it, I would have given it a thumbs-down.
I picked up Undertale in October, after hearing Dodger gush about it on a recent episode of the Co-Optional Podcast. TotalBiscuit and his crew had previously turned me on to Final Fantasy Record Keeper and Life Is Strange, both of which have defined my year in gaming. So, somewhere about the middle of the month, I grab this game- as well as Davey Wreden's The Beginner's Guide- and sat down, ready to break me some fourth walls.
If you've played the Undertale demo, you've gone just as far- actually, a little further- than I did in my first attempt at a playthrough. I came in knowing its status as a Game What Judges You, and was further warned by its Steam summary- "the RPG game where you don't have to destroy anyone." So, I went in ready to cut a swath of love and peace that would make Vash the Stampede shed a tear.
Aside from one unfortunate dummy (thank you, brave soldier, you taught me that the "FIGHT" button is very literal and not a way to access one's diplomacy skills), I behaved like a perfect gentleman through Toriel's guided tour of the Ruins. My stick remained but a rustic fashion accessory as I learned the strange, endearing ways of the monsters that lived amongst the puzzles and leaf-piles. I made an eyeball-monster's day by not picking on him. I complimented a ghost on its fashion sense. I gently respected the personal space of a large fly-like creature. It was a good day.
I eventually proceeded to the point where Toriel was standing guard at the doorway out of the Ruins, heartbroken yet steadfast in her refusal to let me escape to Snowdin and the realms beyond.
The problem was, I didn't want to leave.
I already knew about Flowey's save-reading tricks, and the game, up to this point, had only rewarded me for staying my hand in a conflict. Furthermore, the game had given me no specific reason why my young-child avatar had gotten lost in the mountains in the first place. Why so far from home? Is the realm of humans really a place that they, or I, even wanted to go back to? Especially with Goatmom here offering free room and board for as long as I liked? Sure, she was doting, to the point of being clingy. But, Undertale had challenged me to use the full force of my personal judgment, and that judgment was struggling to find any reason at all to turn down Toriel's generous offer.
Thus, while Toriel stood guard at the gate, waiting to answer a challenge I really didn't want to make, I kept sleeping in my new bed over and over again, thinking I would trigger a cutscene, or a Lavos-style non-standard ending. However, it seems that for all the player reactions I later found Toby Fox had prepared for, there was no acknowledgment of my attempt to actually take Toriel at her word, aside from a few anonymous exhortations of how I was the future of monsters. (Dude, I'm ten years old and hungry, go find another chosen one.)
At this point, I felt I was being railroaded- more so when I found no immediately obvious way to talk Toriel down without a fight. I knew that, even if I killed Toriel and then reloaded the save, that freaking flower- which I'd then mistaken to be the voice of the game creator- would be there to mock my cruelty and my cowardice, even though I was trying desperately to display neither.
So, to spite what I thought was my tormentor, I stopped playing. My story ended with my young-child self chatting with frogs, dancing with slime molds, and developing a taste for snails, with my new guardian hopefully taking the hint after a few days. (With all of the Undertale AUs floating around Tumblr, I sometimes wonder how ConscientiousObjectorTale would play out.)
I could have been a prick at this point and petitioned for a refund- but besides not seeing "ideological disagreement" as worthy grounds to recover ten bucks, I still wanted Toby Fox to have my money. Even with my decision, I liked what he was attempting to do enough that I wanted to see what he would make next- perhaps something a little more elaborate, expanding on the theme of subverting the tropes and trappings of traditional RPGs.
Turns out, he did. And it's called "Undertale".
I stood by my choice, having felt the concept of a game sternly judging the player's actions was becoming old hat three years after Spec Ops: The Line. But I was curious enough to read ahead about the rest of the story, with no concern about spoiling myself on a game I felt I had finished playing. I didn't know who most of the characters were, so the plotline was a pretty massive knot of lore to disentangle, but I soon stumbled across a single fact that started a massive shift in my opinion of this game.
I had presumed Flowey to be the mocking voice of the game creator, shaming the player for having the audacity to fight and kill in a genre chiefly based around fighting and killing. On this, I was massively incorrect.
Flowey the flower's fourth-wall flouting is very, very much canon, and both the reasons why and the implications thereof are
.
This dandelion Deadpool was up to something, and in my search to find out exactly what it was, I began to truly understand the things that have endeared this game to so many people these past few months. I had turned tail and ran to dodge the shots of a satirical game developer, only to later find that his gun was never loaded and I had locked myself right out of his world of wit and wonder.
I'm still working on my own playthrough now, even though I now know everything that happens- in recent weeks, I've sought out as many different Let's Plays and Twitch streams as possible, just to see different people react to the mindfreak that is Undertale's endgame. It's late December now, and this has yet to get old. In addition, I've also read plenty of Undertale AU comics and fan theories, and bought both the original soundtrack and RichaadEB's cover album. Just over two months after I initially dismissed this game as a morality play at the expense of the player, I'm as fully absorbed in the world of Undertale as nearly all of its fans. I'm a bit saddened that I experienced Undertale's best moments second-hand, but I'm overjoyed that my initial cynicism about this game has been proven astonishingly wrong.
Congratulations, Toby Fox. Even on a meta-textual level, you found a way to subvert another player's expectations. Now, if you'll excuse me, I've got a bone to pick with a certain royal guardsman.

Day Z is currently in EA and has been for a longtime. If ever there was a thesis written on hubris in the games industry, this would make a great case study. Essentially, it abused the EA model and used it,, as a cash cow. What BI have done with the millions of gamer's money remains a mystery? Day Z currently resembles an indie game. This despite massive resources, advanced in good faith by an unsuspecting gaming public.
The entire enterprise has been plagued by incompetence and mismanagement. No doubt, the initial success and hype caused poor judgement . One does not have to delve too far to unearth it. The use of an outdated DX9 engine has made the game all but unplayable . The renderer is far behind BI's own public schedule. The AI is a joke and the UI, even worse. A plethora of other promised content has also failed to appear. Those that have, remain largely broken.
Players are increasingly joining its founder, Dean Hall, and abandoning the game. Steam numbers gives testament to that . The arrogance of the developers is all too apparent. There is little appetite to engage with Alpha participants and their input, all but unwelcome. Dissent in their forums is not tolerated. A Stalinist level of censorship is enforced with a hair-trigger ban hammer. One would be forgiven for drawing parallels with another ill fated game, War Z.
In summary the project is fast running out of time and its players , out of patience. Will this unoptimised ugly duckling ever grow up to be a AAA swan?

This game is absolutely incredible. So many people have raved about this game, hyping it up to be the best game of the year, maybe even of all time. I guess what I am getting at is that going into Undertale with unrealistically high expectations might just be inevitable if you haven't been living under a rock for the past few months. Fortunately, I am happy to report that Undertale somehow lives up to what it is hyped to be, just make sure to go into it completely blind.
This is one of those games where the less you know about it the better, so I am just going to end off this short review by saying that Undertale is definitely one of the best games of the 2015, and for $10 you really can't go wrong. Incredible gameplay, awesome art style, phenomenal music and an amazing and surprisingly developed storyline made this game one hell of a package. You can't possibly go wrong with Undertale, no matter how you play it; this game is definitely a must own for any PC gamer.
It's like Skyrim but with some talking flower.

Undertale is the best RPG of 2015, maybe of all time. Maybe the best game of 2015. Possibly even the best game of all time. It's that good.
I wasn't sure I would like this game... it seemed like a homage to JRPGs, which I really dislike. So I pretty much ignored everyone saying what a great game Undertale is.
Well, I shouldn't have.
What really makes the game shine are the amazing, tender characters, great music, extremely clever writing and gameplay mechanics that play with you while you play with the game.
There's nothing else really like it, it's just stunning how something so original can be so free of bugs and gameplay flaws.
The battle mechanics are so much better than any of the old JRPGs, though I hear they aren't totally unique. I haven't played any of the games that are said to have similar mechanics (paper mario? IDK).
The only things I don't like about Undertale is it's somewhat short (~6 hours) and some important plot information is too hidden. You need at least two playthroughs, careful searching and listening to npcs, as well making certain choices in order to find out what's really gone on in the past and going on now. It's good that the game doesn't spoonfeed you everything but I feel like some stronger hints could be dropped about a few important optional plot exposition points that I won't spoil.
I also only bought it after I saw some lets plays and streams, which was good because it convinvinced me to buy the game, but also bad because I feel like this game would be somehow better if I went into it completely unknowning. I do recommend going in completely "blind" and not reading any guides, lets plays or wikis, try to be as unspoiled as possible. But even if you've had certain things spoiled, like I did, this is still something you should buy immediately and play.
Play it blind. Changed what RPG means to me.

Undertale is a weird and fun game. It's an RPG, story-driven, bullet hell, with meaningful decisions and multiple endings. To be honest, it's quite complex to review.
The game is super addicting and the characters have very good personalities. The soundtrack is insanely good, also.
The length of 1 run is about 6-7 hours if you take your time and interact with everything (which is worth it, because there's alot of hidden jokes and such), if you then complete every other possible endings, it pumps up the game length to almost 40 hours!

Undertale would have to be my favourite RPG that was released this year. It has a beautiful soundtrack, great characters, and a decent storyline. However, this game has a few flaws, and I don't feel like naming them all. The bosses were pretty easy for me, but quite the challenge for first time players.
You have a choice: You can kill or give mercy. I find that option unique, since I haven't seen many games with that option (Even though you can just flee from an enemy an not kill them in other video games). However, that choice can haunt you forever. I became too attached to the characters when I spared them to the point where I wouldn't even do Genocide (still haven't done it). I would really recommend this game for those who are fans of EarthBound/MOTHER, for it has a few references they can catch, and it plays in a similar style. It also has a few feels thrown in here and there, so if you like to cry over a video game, this is probably one for you.
If you EVER buy this game, I hope you feel the same way I did. I hope you have a great time playing this, even if you didn't really like it much.
Just keep one thing in mind: Every choice you make affects your gameplay.

-In game purchases  are a bit pricey
-Despite having a decent PC the game has major lag spikes
-Servers tend to be unstable
-The Blueprint system makes it very difficult to progress

The lack of any "COMMON FOE" makes the game purely pvp and maybe thats why the community is crappy but hey.

EDIT: You can tell I was pretty butthurt from a day of getting destroyed in this game when I wrote this but regardless my points still stand.
I am being 100% honest when I say: I could only recommend this game to you if you want to role-play as a fugitive in a free-fire warzone.
Rust was a fun, although very unpolished game when it was initially "released". Then Facepunch decided to start adding more and more guns and explosives and less and less survival oriented items with every new update. This effectively changed Rust from a multiplayer apocalyptic survival game, as it was initially advertised and hyped up to be, into a high-stakes free-for-all PvP-focused first person shooter with survival elements.
It doesn't help at all that the community for this game is the worst and most toxic I have ever seen for any peice of media ever. If you play on a regular server you can only hope to chop down one or two trees and maybe mine one rock before being shot in the face for no reason other than whoever shot you was bored. On the other hand if you play on a low population server and have no human opposition the game is easy and monotonous because its designed to be played with other people. Unless you are playing with a bunch of freinds or you wait for the server you are playing on to get wiped you will never be able to catch up to the other players. Even if you do you will most likely be killed at some point and wind up in the same situation again. I like permadeath in games when I die because I made a mistake or a wasn't skilled enough to handle the situation. I know I can just start over and do better next time. I don't like it when I lose days worth of loot because someone sniped me from a mile away for cutting down his favorite tree and I can't start over because he is still in the sniping spot with my stuff when I respawn.
If not for the community (and micro-transactions in an unfinished game) I might have recommended it. The gunplay and crafting/building mechanics are solid, the graphics are good, and overall it seems like it could have a lot of potential. However games are supposed to be fun, and Rust, in my opinion, is just not.
A once-in-a-lifetime experience that everyone should have the pleasure of enjoying. Takes everything you think you know about gaming and tosses it out of the window.

is a game that makes you care.
From the beginning, it starts off with a rather simple premise. The retro-looking graphics helps to sell that premise, letting the casual person to look at it and assume the story it offers is just as simple. And it is... at first.
The main 'schtick' of the game being 'an RPG where you don't have to destroy anyone' made me ponder for a moment
it's even a gimmick in the first place. RPGs are those games where you kill monsters, get gold and xp, become stronger and save the world, right? Admit it, it's what most people think of when they hear 'RPG', and I wasn't any different.
What marks
as an RPG is that it doesn't diverge from that aspect at all, but instead adds something else. You can, if you truly desire to, kill monsters, get gold and xp, and so on. Obviously the monsters won't enjoy it when you do that to their friends and the story you create changes. Choices matter, and the game will remember what you do, what you don't do, and can be rather startling on how it reminds you of your past decisions.
The characters of
is where the game can make or break it for you. The game tries to instill some compassion for them and make you care for them. Now, I know it sounds bad for some, but it's not overly clumsy or heavy-handed in its approach. It does its best to make you smile. Or cry. Or both, if you're a big softy like me.
The monsters are diverse, funny, quirky, and so on (having drawn a large amount of inspiration from games like Earthbound) ranging from the meek and not-very-terrifying Whimsun to some rather violent and scary monsters. The battle mechanics are just as diverse, requiring good reflexes and judgement. Battle is turn-based, and you have to dodge attacks like a bullet-hell game... most of the time. Depending on the monster, the rules of the battle can change.
sometimes breaks the fourth wall, but it does so tastefully. The plot actually revolves around the fact that Undertale
, and it benefits greatly from not shying away from this fact. After all, this game does quite a bit to change your expectations of what to expect from this 'RPG'.
Who likes 8-bit games with pretty cool music
Who likes diverse, funny NPCs and monsters, and possibly having unexpected feels for them
Who likes having their expectations suddenly subverted in surprising ways
Who likes dodging, platforming, solving puzzles
Who likes being a soft-hearted saint or a cold-blooded murderer... or something in between
Having an appreciation for anime, bad puns, annoying dogs, spiders, skeletons, yelling for emphasis, ghosts, robots, and making friends would be nice, but not necessary. Also, strongly resist any urge to look up a guide until after your first playthrough. Spoilers would wreck a great deal of the experience this game has to offer.
Probably shouldn't let small children play it, though; I'd say kids 13+ wouldn't have a problem playing through it. It's not an overly-long game; a couple of hours and you'd be done unless you're scouring the game for secrets or something. Undertale has quite a few secrets as well, so take some time to smell the flowers.
There's a demo for the game (so you can try before you buy) as well as several YouTubers already having done playthroughs of the game. I'd recommend searching for 'StephenPlays First 20' of Undertale if you'd rather watch someone play the demo without too many spoilers, instead of playing it yourself.

We finish up the day sitting around a fire, with matches supplied by our pacifist quartermaster.
A perfect end to a perfect first day in the DayZ standalone. I recommend the hell out of this game, but only if you're mature enough to handle constant and inevitable loss, as well as the typical Alpha hiccups. Come in with a positive attitude and a love for a challenge; the little personal challenges and stories such as playing as a pacifist, or a cannibal, or a law man. Come in and keep the right mind set and you'll not only have fun, but create it for others.

is a game that makes you care.
From the beginning, it starts off with a rather simple premise. The retro-looking graphics helps to sell that premise, letting the casual person to look at it and assume the story it offers is just as simple. And it is... at first.
The main 'schtick' of the game being 'an RPG where you don't have to destroy anyone' made me ponder for a moment
it's even a gimmick in the first place. RPGs are those games where you kill monsters, get gold and xp, become stronger and save the world, right? Admit it, it's what most people think of when they hear 'RPG', and I wasn't any different.
What marks
as an RPG is that it doesn't diverge from that aspect at all, but instead adds something else. You can, if you truly desire to, kill monsters, get gold and xp, and so on. Obviously the monsters won't enjoy it when you do that to their friends and the story you create changes. Choices matter, and the game will remember what you do, what you don't do, and can be rather startling on how it reminds you of your past decisions.
The characters of
is where the game can make or break it for you. The game tries to instill some compassion for them and make you care for them. Now, I know it sounds bad for some, but it's not overly clumsy or heavy-handed in its approach. It does its best to make you smile. Or cry. Or both, if you're a big softy like me.
The monsters are diverse, funny, quirky, and so on (having drawn a large amount of inspiration from games like Earthbound) ranging from the meek and not-very-terrifying Whimsun to some rather violent and scary monsters. The battle mechanics are just as diverse, requiring good reflexes and judgement. Battle is turn-based, and you have to dodge attacks like a bullet-hell game... most of the time. Depending on the monster, the rules of the battle can change.
sometimes breaks the fourth wall, but it does so tastefully. The plot actually revolves around the fact that Undertale
, and it benefits greatly from not shying away from this fact. After all, this game does quite a bit to change your expectations of what to expect from this 'RPG'.
Who likes 8-bit games with pretty cool music
Who likes diverse, funny NPCs and monsters, and possibly having unexpected feels for them
Who likes having their expectations suddenly subverted in surprising ways
Who likes dodging, platforming, solving puzzles
Who likes being a soft-hearted saint or a cold-blooded murderer... or something in between
Having an appreciation for anime, bad puns, annoying dogs, spiders, skeletons, yelling for emphasis, ghosts, robots, and making friends would be nice, but not necessary. Also, strongly resist any urge to look up a guide until after your first playthrough. Spoilers would wreck a great deal of the experience this game has to offer.
Probably shouldn't let small children play it, though; I'd say kids 13+ wouldn't have a problem playing through it. It's not an overly-long game; a couple of hours and you'd be done unless you're scouring the game for secrets or something. Undertale has quite a few secrets as well, so take some time to smell the flowers.
There's a demo for the game (so you can try before you buy) as well as several YouTubers already having done playthroughs of the game. I'd recommend searching for 'StephenPlays First 20' of Undertale if you'd rather watch someone play the demo without too many spoilers, instead of playing it yourself.

So, Undertale.
The core game elements themselves are on the unremarkable-carcinogenic scale. The graphics and sound are decent, so far as 8-bit styles go, but I actually didn’t find them as remarkable as I thought I would (maybe I’m just biased against the game). The gameplay involves standard RPG running around, talking to people, and random encounter battles. Should you choose not to fight directly (which I imagine most people do, since that’s what the game sells itself on), you go through various “bullet hell” sequences while you try to figure out which set of actions properly pacifies the monsters. Pretty annoying.
So, yes, the game lives and dies by story elements alone. Now then.
To me, Undertale seems to be trying to sell you on the point that maybe you haven’t thought about the morality of killing monsters indiscriminately, without thought for their perspective.
It’s something to think about, sure. But once you
aware of it, it’s hard to be impressed by the message, especially when it sticks itself in your face instead of remaining calm and subtle. It’s even harder to be impressed when you consider the circumstances.
Your player character is almost God, in the sense that they are incredibly powerful and can kill almost effortlessly. “Don’t kill monsters” isn’t a very powerful message when you consider that the circumstances make such a principle not only plausible, but relatively easy and beneficial. Or when you consider that you’re alone, the only human you know of around, and that the monsters aren’t exactly on the verge of, e.g. murdering other humans.
Good and evil always exists on both sides of any halfway realistic conflict, at least in the sense that both sides have sympathetic motivations, regardless of how justifiable they are. Undertale seems to present one lone human who is encouraged to take the side of “misunderstood” monsters against faceless evil humans.
The irony is almost sickening.
---
On the same note, Undertale heavily relies on you, as the player, to stand in for the featureless protagonist.
The more story-driven a game is, the less acceptable I find this. I complain about this in series like Half-Life and The Legend of Zelda, but in those games, there is at least decent, sufficient gameplay (hint, hint) to at least partially override these grievances.
You could make the argument that Undertale is different because it explicitly breaks the fourth wall, such that you really are the protagonist, and that the avatar present in game is just an unfortunate limitation of the video game medium, rather than a stand-in (à la Gordon Freeman or Link).
But if that’s the argument, then the counter-argument is ridiculously simple: the fourth wall is open both ways.
Why
I care about what are effectively pixels on a computer screen? How is it in any way sane to equate the deletion of computer screen pixels to the deaths of real beings?
Because it’s a story, and we get drawn to characters in stories because of the sense of quasi-realism: no matter how fantastical the story or setting, it still feels “real” (plausible) - thanks to the fourth wall. I can watch a puppet show and feel for the characters (and rightly so), even though they’re really just sock heads on sticks.
But when you break the fourth wall like that, you violate the implicit agreement in place for experiencing stories. Which is fine in some cases, particularly when done for humor (again, going back to the puppet show example). When done for drama? If you’re telling me that the game world and the real world should be treated identically, in the literal sense - that is, no fourth wall - then I’m going to tell you that, hey, your “game world” characters are ♥♥♥♥ing pixels on a computer screen, who won’t know nor care what I do with them.
---
So, no, I can't recommend this game, not even as a curiosity.

I've first known about this game at the beginning of October.
Soon after everyone fell in love with it and i found my youtube main page full of commentaries and playthough of the game, but i didn't want to fall in the "best game ever hype" everyone seemed to be on because i wanted to experience it myself first.
First thing first. Don't get fooled by the graphics folks, this is a masterpiece of an RPG.
The game is made with GameMaker, so don't expect super hd graphics.
The lack of graphic appeal the game has (for me its fine, but for someone it's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics) is absolutely filled (with determination) with a well made story, and an original and clever gameplay.
Undertale makes you decide to kill or spare the enemy by using an "ACT" button.
With it you can decide not to kill a monster, by talking reasonably and interact with him in different ways, to make him change the idea he has of you.
This clever playstyle makes the game more fun, entertaining and immersive.
On a regular RPG battles don't mean anything right? (You kill enemies, level up, get stronger equipment, go in a dungeon, kill stronger enemies, get better equipment, go in more difficult dungeons, ecc....).
And if you kill an enemy nothing happends right? You just continue with the story without a worry.
In this game however, your actions have benefits and consequences.
The story changes with you, you can decide to make it a dating sim or a cruel horror story, a fun and cheery game or a sad game.
The game also makes you regret the wrong things and decisions you've made through it.
The characters are really well made, they all have different personalities. It's been so long since i felt like this towards the characters of a videogame.
Everything is enhanced by the amazing music.
Just go and listen to the OST of this game.
Not gonna lie, the game has some slightly boring parts (mainly the beginning part, first 20-30 mins), but don't quit playing it, it gets better and better.
The game is about 9-10 hours long.
The length is probably the only negative thing this game has; but you can play it again making different choices and see how the story changes, discover more about the characters personalities and the secrets of the game.
Undertale sure is one of the most enjoyable and emotional experience i ever had in an RPG.
Give this game a go, and don't judge it from the graphics, you won't regret playing it.
The game is fun, full of jokes and funny moments, so don't worry about the entertainment.

I've first known about this game at the beginning of October.
Soon after everyone fell in love with it and i found my youtube main page full of commentaries and playthough of the game, but i didn't want to fall in the "best game ever hype" everyone seemed to be on because i wanted to experience it myself first.
First thing first. Don't get fooled by the graphics folks, this is a masterpiece of an RPG.
The game is made with GameMaker, so don't expect super hd graphics.
The lack of graphic appeal the game has (for me its fine, but for someone it's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics) is absolutely filled (with determination) with a well made story, and an original and clever gameplay.
Undertale makes you decide to kill or spare the enemy by using an "ACT" button.
With it you can decide not to kill a monster, by talking reasonably and interact with him in different ways, to make him change the idea he has of you.
This clever playstyle makes the game more fun, entertaining and immersive.
On a regular RPG battles don't mean anything right? (You kill enemies, level up, get stronger equipment, go in a dungeon, kill stronger enemies, get better equipment, go in more difficult dungeons, ecc....).
And if you kill an enemy nothing happends right? You just continue with the story without a worry.
In this game however, your actions have benefits and consequences.
The story changes with you, you can decide to make it a dating sim or a cruel horror story, a fun and cheery game or a sad game.
The game also makes you regret the wrong things and decisions you've made through it.
The characters are really well made, they all have different personalities. It's been so long since i felt like this towards the characters of a videogame.
Everything is enhanced by the amazing music.
Just go and listen to the OST of this game.
Not gonna lie, the game has some slightly boring parts (mainly the beginning part, first 20-30 mins), but don't quit playing it, it gets better and better.
The game is about 9-10 hours long.
The length is probably the only negative thing this game has; but you can play it again making different choices and see how the story changes, discover more about the characters personalities and the secrets of the game.
Undertale sure is one of the most enjoyable and emotional experience i ever had in an RPG.
Give this game a go, and don't judge it from the graphics, you won't regret playing it.
The game is fun, full of jokes and funny moments, so don't worry about the entertainment.

Clearly 11/10 GOTY, nothing else to add. There is no way you won't like this game.
There are 3 main paths through the game:
1. True pacifist path - you don't kill any single creature. I very much advice you to follow this path at your first playthrough.
2. Neutral path - you killed some, but not everyone. Even if it's called "path" basically it means that you failed both other paths, so try again.
3. Genocide path - you killed everyone, not a creature left alive. Everyone will run away from you in fear, they won't recognize you as human. You are the angel of death and you will go to hell for it, have fun.
This game might not look the best, but everything else (music, gameplay, writing) easilly makes up for its visuals. You won't regret buying this game, I promise.

Undertale is at first an unassuming game that appears to be of the RPGMaker variety, but the overwhelming level of buzz about this game is not in the least incorrect: there's a lot more to this game than the first location might suggest.
The number of innovations to RPG mechanics, as well as callbacks to both the cliches and narrative structures of typical games of the past is just wonderful, and it is a credit to the author's writing that the characters encountered in this game are at once familiar, but not at all tired; a difficult balance to achieve.
