The original Legacy Rust was a great game but I feel it fell into the clunkiness of early access survival games, Thankfully this was not the case - They had noticed the errors the original faced and rather than give up like many, The rust team started over. While the new Rust faced, what was in my opinion, a terrible start the game now is fantastic. The graphical and overall running performance are both increasing with every other patch and the content in each patch is much more frequent than It was at the beggining. Rust is now a fantastic game with its only flaw being the community, Any new player to Rust will quickly notice that it will be "Kill fresh spawns then when they complain in chat or ask why the almighty line of 'Welcome to Rust' will be seen" overall I'd rate this a 8/10
Pros
-Fantastic Building system
-Very immersive landscape (Large clan bases with sniper tower guards are amazing to see.....from afar)
-Easy to understand crafting system
-Servers for everyone (standard, High gather, RP, BR, Pure PvP etc...)
-Frequent updates with good content
-Alternate clothing on Marketplace for easy team recognition (Required if you have a sizable clan)
cons
-Large amount of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ players (Same with every title within this genre though)
-Still some performance issues for low-end PCs
-Not much PvE content (Only really Helicopters at this point (could also include auto turrets))

In the middle
-Vehicles still in development (have been expected for a while now but understandable)
-Progression feels a bit quick within the game (There are many Melee weapons that you'll never really use for anything but opening Barrels)
-Some servers are completely dominated by Large clans but if you're in one of them that it would only enhance the gameplay
-Very harsh game for new players, You will die and get raided ALOT until you figure out the best way to get started and make some friends in-game to join you (some of these 'friends' will turn on you too, prepare yourself.)

DayZ is a game based off an amazing concept. The game forces us to employ great thinking to every move we make. If you prefer fast-paced games, however, DayZ may not be for you. DayZ is going from town to town, searching under beds and through shelves for beans and Spite. The real fun begins when you interact with another survivor.
With two hundred and twenty-five KM squared of map, coming across another survivor is quite uncommon. Except for when at a high PvP area (e.g. major cities or airfields), in which case you will probably be dead before you know they were there.
DayZ is a constant struggle and demands the player of excessive hours of gameplay. From travelling, looting and waiting - waiting while scouting an area for movement, or waiting because you know you are pinned down and can't move. In DayZ players need to keep an open mind, whether it be thinking ahead for your health (rationing food and water), or checking possible advantage points people may have over you in a distant town or field. Players will have to battle zombies, bandits, weather (cold and rain), hunger (and then possible sickness or poisoning) and thirst. DayZ is not like a FPS such as Call of Duty where bullet's project from a players head, but from the gun itself and after the bullet leaves the gun, time, gravity and distance takes into affect.
DayZ Standalone is at it's very earliest developing stages and for what reasons I cannot fathom, the developers chose to allow early access to the game. Of course people are going to complain, even after every time they must play DayZ a warning popup appears on their screen "This is an early access version of DayZ" and so on... The game has a super load of potential and anyone who is interested in this genre of gaming, will know that DayZ is the best game out there in it's generation. In my experience there are few bugs. The most annoying but less common one, is if your character's data is wiped.
DayZ is currently (approx.) twenty-eight euros and for what is being offered, I do believe this is a very high price. The game is merely complete but yet they are asking the full price of other games on Steam which are complete... In my opinion though, I don't see this price going down - rather it going UP. DayZ is improving with each update, and that means happier players, and even more players. I thought to buy the game at early access so I could really experience it through it's stages and creation. More than that, in the future, who knows, DayZ could rocket in price!
I would recommend DayZ Standalone to all people, all day long. This is a game where you make the fun. DayZ can be quite tedious without having a goal, otherwise you are just travelling along from barn to barn and water pump to water pump filling up your canteen bottles... have a character story. Have a DayZ story. Capture a hostage. Hunt down a bandit. Create a group of Chernarus Police. Become a legendary sniper. Become a gunslinger. Do whatever you would do in a Zombie Apocalypse to survive. But just know every time you die, a new life begins - and the insanity begins.

Different enemies will change the difficulty of the battle and make the tactics of winning different. The music of this game is very good! I absolutely love this game. The battle will be different and so will the outcomes. One of the best parts is... there's also a lot of secrets ;)
The only con I can think of is the storyline. It's a bit strange... Another thing is I wish there were more places to buy items, especially when you get close to boss battles...
Overall, I would recommend this game to EVERYONE!!! This game is unique and fun! I could play this game at least 5 times and still not be bored! I will for sure play this game at least 2 times! Well.
Where to begin with this one?
I consider myself a very generalized gamer, enjoying anything from Plants vs. Zombies to Destiny. And when my sister kept pushing me to buy this RPG that everyone on Tumblr was talking about, I thought, how bad could it be? I played it for about an hour the day I bought it, slept on it, and decided to pick it up the next day.
I finished it that day.
Undertale is a very stylized, turn-based RPG that incorporates elements of a top-down shooter in its 'combat' system. However, this game is much more than battles. Thorough, charming characters, a small but rich world, and an AMAZING soundtrack that fits any mood imaginable. But the best part is the cause/effect system. Literally anything you do, from killing, sparing, or befriending a monster to choosing different dialouges can thoroughly change the plot and ending. (By the way, the ending is one of the best I have seen in...well...ever. It will mess with you.) Unless you have a heart of stone, or more likely, reinforced concrete, you will have a barrage of emotions from playing this short and sweet experience. Yes, it's short. 10 hours maximum. But there are so many possible events in this world that you will not feel cheated out of your eight dollars in the slightest.
The storyline is surprisingly original, full of twists and turns that you really have to think about (or maybe just look online) to fully understand. The art is phenomenal, considering it was done by, like, two people. It ranges from monochrome 8-bit to full, smooth 16-bit graphic styles, and sometimes uses modern smooth animating techniques. The only problem I have with it is the character sprite...it just feels a bit off. And of course, this game isn't for EVERYONE. Just look at the 300 negative reviews. But it's for anyone who's looking for a rich storytelling expirience to laugh or cry at.
Put simply, it's a freakishly fun game that will frequently fill you full of feels.
8.75/10 would feel again
P. S. My advice? Don't kill anything. :)
P. P. S. Once you finish one ending, look up how to get them all. There's a lot of them.

TL;DR
Rust is a great game, it is worth the money. But it falls short on speed, stability, and is very laggy. 7/10.
If you dont know, Rust is an Early Alpha Survival game. Like much SURVIVAL games, you SURVIVE. But this is almost half a crafting game. You need to build a base, big or small, to survive.
PROS ARE HERE, CONS ARE BELOW!
With my experience of both legacy (the old, abandoned alpha of the game) and the current alpha, I have quite some backround. There are a range of tools, weapons, guns, and a guitar.
The map is big, and unlike DayZ, it's hard to recall any familiar places (You deicde if this is good or bad). There are 3 biomes to live in; Forest, Desert, and Arctic. Each place needs different type of clothing. For the Desert, you have to walk around in almost nothing to not burn to death, and the opposite with the Arctic. There are also Radtowns, abandoned areas with barrels to open, crates to search, and a bunch of other phat lootz. With the word RAD in it, the places sometimes have radiation. Fortunately, there are a lot on this big map, unlike Legacy, so there are many without building around it.
You can be a friendly person who takes anyone in their team, scavanging and searching radtowns. You can be a gang of builders, just building GIANT skyscrapers. You can be a lone wolf, killing anyone who walks near you. You can be a group of raiders, blowing up doors with C4 annd rockets! Or naked men. You can be any group you want.
PvE (Player vs Environment) is where there is not people killing each other, only the world.
PvP (Player vs Player) is where players are fight other players.
This game is both. You can use guns, bows, crossbows, rocks, spears, axes, and more to kill people or animals with.
The game has many prey, such as horses, pigs, deer, chicken, and other people. It also has predators, such as bears, wolves, and other people. You also have to fight cold, heat, and hunger.
PROS

If your going to buy an Early Access game make it this one! Tons of fun, very addictive, and very few game breaking bugs or glitches (me and my friends have encountered 1). Don't have to worry about this being DayZ where it will die in Early Access limbo, every week they have a develop talking about what they are working on, what's coming in the game, what's going out, possible ideas and concept art they have, and sometimes even polls for content or content changes.
Play it with a friend, if I had a dollar for every moment we busted out laughing or just had a big grin on our face, or even yelled over Skype "what just happened, that experience was worth the game" then I would have enough money to buy Fallout 4 for all of my friends.
What kind of moments could I be talking about? We joined a high population server, rich get richer, poor get killed. A rebellion started, the "Naked Men Rebllion" which was 10 guys in a wood hut. We joined them and one by one convinced them to kill each other until we were top dogs.
That's just one of many moments I cherish and think will be a found gaming memory for years to come.
TL;DR: Worth every penny, epically if you can play with friends.

This game has changed me dramatically, it has just become my all time favorite and I don't think that's going to change cause of how much of an impact it has made on me. The stories, the characters, the "humerus" jokes, and the fact that anything you do will change one of the biggest factors of this game is something that a lot of people need to try at least once to get a taste of.
Now looking back on it all, I'm glad I got into it. I'm so happy that my brother had bought it for me, because.. I know this is going to sound odd.. But it makes me feel better about myself, and some of the things I do. I feel like I'm being a whole lot more friendlier than how I used to be before I got into the whole world of Undertale.
So, please give this game a try. It doesn't matter what you see about it online, this game is about your OWN experience. Do your own thing, and see where it leads you in the game.. And in life. ( If it impacts you like it did me.. )

Possible Spoilers if you haven't played through this game at least once:
Wow. Just wow. No RPG in my life has ever convinced me to play it twice, even if it is only 6 hours for the first playthrough. However, if you do not play this game twice, with the second playthrough being a true pacifist run and doing the additional things that give you the true pacifist ending, you are missing out on one of the most incredibly scripted and written stories in video-gamedom. I am blown away.
Not to say that this game isn't flawed, it's way of communicating it's full story is not user-friendly. If you don't look at a guide, it's a hassle that has you traversing the same parts of the game multiple times. The game's morale about friendship is one that says that you offer unbounded mercy even when your enemy threatens to end the life of your friends. Additionally, it seems to communicate that the option to fight people always hurts more than it helps.
In the end though, if you are willing to deal with the crap it sometimes throws your way, you will be rewarded with a wonderful ending. One that perhaps, is all the more meaningful because of the hassle you need to go through to obtain it.
At this point, I have no intention of doing the genocide run, and I don't think I have the heart to do it even if I had the motivation to do another playthrough.
Ending impression: Incredible.

There is no way to describe the feeling you get when you just spent 2-3 hours gearing up and you are searching houses almost finished and you hear that first crack of a gunshot wiz by your head. So you quickly scramble for cover and this is when you decide what kind of DayZ player you are. Do you combat log and become the coward? Do you flank around and try to get a vantage point and make the poor basterd pay for his mistakes? Or do you just runaway and live to fight another day and be a survivalist? Is this game worth buying or recommending? Yes it definitely is one of the best games survival games and one of the best heartdropping intense pvp games you will play.
IMO- Use the new inventory system you get way better frames if you have a laptop and if you have a desktop. I run lowest settings at all times and still get 12-15 fps on the old inventory system but using the new one I get 20-30 fps solid. To get the new inventory system you go to your launch options and type -newui and launch DayZ. You're welcome for giving you frames ;)

The fanbase can be a bit ... excessive. But please, don't hold that against the game.  Try to judge Undertale on the EXP it gives you, and not off the fanbase LOVE. Try to go in as blind as possible and observe for yourself.   Experiencing the payoffs of Undertale are worth the time investment and, if you are that kind of person, the replays.
If you read/watch the Steam description or video preview of the game, you're gonna have a bad time.
If you read reviews (user OR critic), you're gonna have a bad time.
If you see video names or possibly even thumbnails from Youtubers, you're gonna have a bad time.
Go in blind. Either get the demo, or set your alarm clock for a few minutes before 2 hours and start the Steam game.  If you don't like it by then, simply savescum reality and request a refund.  Worst-case, It's only $8-$10 that gets returned after only a few days anyways.
==========================================================
I had been considering Undertale for about two months before buying it.  I've been a big fan of RPGs since the late NES/early SNES era. Having finally played Undertale, I can say it's a great game and the experience is worth your money.
At first, I held off under fears of potentially wasting my money on what could turn out to be merely the next flavor of the month variety of Youtube bait.   And sure, Undertale is LOADED with memes and randomness. So that audience will enjoy it.  But what about the rest of us?  What about me?  There's more to Undertale than JUST the memes.  The presentation is simplistic.  But in that simplicity lies it's genius.  What it lacks in highLV tech and budget, it makes up for in love.
Each character's dialogue box gets a unique sound for their text, giving the feeling and emotion of a voice without the cringeness or lack of imagination that standard voice acting can sometimes do.  There's a couple OMG moments when you finally put two and two together concerning character "voices," though you may not notice until your second playthru.
I am an absolute SUCKER for games that use recurring musical themes. Even if I don't consciously notice it during the game, it creates such a feeling of nostalgia to the work by the end of the first playthru.  Whether it be Ori, the old FFs, or the Pokemon Mystery Dungeon games (seriously, Time Gear and it's variants in Explorers). And let me tell you, Toby Fox absolutely ABUSES leitmotifs left and right in Undertale. In a good way.
The bullethell aspect might sound tacked on, but it is absolutely integral to the Undertale. First off, it makes grinding unneeded as players' skill determines their defensive capability, instead of the RNG gods.  Secondly, it makes mutli-enemy fights more interesting as they all combine to attack you at once, instead of waiting forever between multiple attacks. Third, it [spoiler deleted]. Fourth, the bullethell aspects simply OOZE personality both from boss and common mobs alike. Fighting a frog? Prepare to dodge flies or a hopping frog.  Some less aggressive enemy may stay stationary, just dancing or sleeping, doing their own thing during their "attack" phase. And so on.
You may have noticed I haven't said much about the actual "RPG" elements of the game itself.  The narrative, the wonderful cast, the combat (outside of explainign that the bullethell is a POSITIVE addtion even to someone who loves turn based), etc.  This is intentional. I want to say more.  But I believe the best way to experience Undertale is going in completely blind. I... never had that chance.
I want to say more, I really do.  I want to spoil SO MUCH to make sure you get this game.  But
My expectations...
My loneliness...
My fear...
For you, my child...
I will put them aside.
==================================================

I've waited a long time to make a review on this game, so I'll be as honest and heartfelt as I can:
Pros:
- This game has given me more individual memories between my friends and I than any other game, the sheer potential of a game that relies completely on player interaction in such an intimately violent medium is vast. Rust essentially gives you all the tools you ever need to be a bad person, and a player's value is determined by his refusal to become this bad person, or his ability to trancend into a next level of hatred, who ambushes strangers, plotting day and night for no end except that his target will suffer. The essential effort of Rust is to be so ruthlessly and creatively a degenerate that your opponents will stop playing Rust. When I started this game, naked in the woods with a rock, I admired a game with no tutorial, only wonder of what my ability was. Thats the great part, you never know the end of your ability. It was not long after I learned to craft my first spear that the power got to me, thus beginning my two year spiral into hateful despise of all my fellow man. Soon I was sticking up the non-opportuned with crude weapons just to hear how upset they were, looking at how to backhandedly kill every person that stumbled my way in the desert and wood. I built an empire from the cracked skulls of the countless hordes that fell before me, each one more butthurt than the last. But as Rust evolved, so did it's community, it's idea. Soon there were bigger fish. The previous sessions of my pals and I cutting down the poor were rustled apart by a new age of war where armored men with assault rifles ruled the land, and my tactical prowess could not compensate for their brute force and firepower. I became a scavenger, poking about the rusted shell of my former empire to hopefully slaughter the weak and destitute that fell in the wake of those stronger, scrapping by and hiding from vicious people who walked the Earth. Like Rust, I eventually evolved. The same massive encampments that had harmed me and kept me in hiding would unkowingly make me a force to be reckoned with. With large numbered forces ruling the game I was forced into a life of guerrilla warfare, and everything changed, the weak were now quick to bond with each other and the powerfull had become content. In no time I could band together a group of fighters with bows and arrows and a lot of hate, attacking in the dark and from multiple directions, abusing spawnpoints, throwing desperate bodies at the enemy. Blood laden assault rifles clattered to the ground under the weight of a thousand naked bodies, before the poor began to replicate the enemies stolen goods. All of the goodness had been stolen from my people, and only hatred filled demons walked the Earth. We killed all in sight and ushered in an age of crippling violent paranoia the likes of which have never been seen. The world has been weakened now, made even, and the line between success and extermination has become forever blurred by inconsistent chaotic violence. I walk Rust now, 390 hours into hell, and remember every moment, that I cant turn back from here.
- The game is very aesthetically pleasing, with good lighting effects and attention to small animation details and events.
- Progress in game developement has been consistently effortful, and players have been kept up to speed by developers
- Game has given me two years of enjoyable play with various friends without ever becoming too stale.
- Every player has lost their mind and will listen to outlandish ideas if you just role-play them.
- Map design does a great job at forcing players to compete for resources, instand proximity chat communication makes for good player interaction and seemless transition from talking♥♥♥♥♥♥to panicked shooting.
- The volatile nature of the combat system makes it possible for someone with 1 hour of gameplay to best someone with 400, making the game always keep you on your toes.
Cons:
- Character model is not customizable. Armor and clothes make character identification and uniforming relatively easy, but I would be able to mentally invest more of myself into make character if I could build him/her from scratch. Although the Somalian-pirate like nature of my code generated character and his abnormally large genitals have lead to some funny interactions, I just love a game more when I can make my identity.
- The frequency of server wiping updates can demotivate players against large projects, but the game is in Alpha, and that is completely understood.
Notes: The game is very difficult to progress through on your own, this game has been great for me being in the military, because people are forced into situations where I have hours to explain my Rust eploits and win them over to it. But if you are less of a social gamer, try to team up with people in game using proximity chat, and work with low level people first. Starting the game working with powerful people will hurt your skills in the long run, Rust is all about journey rather than destination. I wish the best of luck to anyone who plays this. It's been the source of many "HELL ♥♥♥♥ING YEAHS!!!" and "GOD DAMMMMIIITS!!!" for me, and I hope it can give you as much of a ride. Also, there are a lot of over experienced players in Rust, where my 400 hours seems like small potatos compared to a lot of players.
Pro tip: The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Eoka Pistol can fire shotgun shells. Be wary.

An interesting experience that many people dismiss for it's indie background. I'll try to keep this review as impartial as I can.
The story is an interesting one, that can change drastically or just barely depending on what you do. The creator took the time to put in little details here and there that compliment what you do.
In terms of gameplay, I guess it's more akin to a visual novel with some gameplay. A lot of people who praie the game will tell you wonders about story but not so much about the gameplay. Like in most RPGs you scout the world and have random encounters. The game then shifts it's theme drastically as the enemies's attacks are represented in a bullet hell fashion. You can dodge their attacks, and complete the turn without taking damage, just like you could die in a few seconds if you're not carefull. Though what I'm saying might make it sound like hardcore games like touhou or Ikaruga, the game is doable, even for people who are not familiar with what a bullet-hell game is. The challenge scalates as you progress, so there's that.
Now, on your end you can chose to either attack and defeat the enemy, like most RPG's, or you can "play nice" by ACTING. What this does is that, thorugh various methods, you're rejecting the idea of hurting the enemies, eventually, this will give you the option to SPARE them(I.E. end the fight).
The trailer and even the game itself tell you about this mechanic, whether you do it or not is up to you, but it will affect some of the story.
The only point left, I think, would be the music and replayability. Music is quite good actually, It fits the ocassion and doesn't feel off. As for the other point, well, I mentioned that the story can and will change depending on your actions. For me at least, it's an interesting way to try and get you to play it again, as the changes are quite a lot.
In the end, Undertale is an experience that it's maybe best to live by oneself. There is a demo that you can try if you still need something else that helps you decide whether you pick this game or not.

Undertale is a charming RPG that sucks you in with its interesting characters and warm atmosphere, not unless youd want to destroy all of that that is.
To kill or not to kill. The choices of the main character directly affect the game itself which makes you more attached to world and its denizens. You may choose to kill the enemy you encounter to gain experience and level up, or you may ACT and select a variety of interactions that differ from monster to monster. Through ACTing you can then SPARE the enemy if you meet its requirements, and this "wins" you the battle.
You can dodge enemy attacks via bullet hell segments, and these bullet hell attacks differ from every monster type you encounter and may prove very entertaining, funny and sometimes quite a challenge to avoid. Dodging these projectiles and various attacks are your only way of avoiding damage and may prove to be a challenge if you play the pacifist route, where in you dont "kill" any enemy you encounter thus you not being able to increase your stats due from not gaining experience from battles.
You may choose to gain experience and level up your stats to gain more powerful but this choice requires you to "kill" and will affect how the game goes. which in turn gives the game a ton of replayability as there may be multiple interactions, plot points and differing endings that may only appear if you do a certain act.
Some heavy choices may even affect your next playthrough and it may be permanent.
The art style is nice and the monster/boss battles are very creative. The music. Amazing. Writing is beyond my original expectations. I am a huge Earthbound fan and I really enjoy how close this hits to home. I proves to be challenging and blasts through your expectations, filled with surprises thatll surely warm the heart, or break it. Figuritavily and literally. Game is hard but do stay determined. Heavily recommend.

I've waited a long time to make a review on this game, so I'll be as honest and heartfelt as I can:
Pros:
- This game has given me more individual memories between my friends and I than any other game, the sheer potential of a game that relies completely on player interaction in such an intimately violent medium is vast. Rust essentially gives you all the tools you ever need to be a bad person, and a player's value is determined by his refusal to become this bad person, or his ability to trancend into a next level of hatred, who ambushes strangers, plotting day and night for no end except that his target will suffer. The essential effort of Rust is to be so ruthlessly and creatively a degenerate that your opponents will stop playing Rust. When I started this game, naked in the woods with a rock, I admired a game with no tutorial, only wonder of what my ability was. Thats the great part, you never know the end of your ability. It was not long after I learned to craft my first spear that the power got to me, thus beginning my two year spiral into hateful despise of all my fellow man. Soon I was sticking up the non-opportuned with crude weapons just to hear how upset they were, looking at how to backhandedly kill every person that stumbled my way in the desert and wood. I built an empire from the cracked skulls of the countless hordes that fell before me, each one more butthurt than the last. But as Rust evolved, so did it's community, it's idea. Soon there were bigger fish. The previous sessions of my pals and I cutting down the poor were rustled apart by a new age of war where armored men with assault rifles ruled the land, and my tactical prowess could not compensate for their brute force and firepower. I became a scavenger, poking about the rusted shell of my former empire to hopefully slaughter the weak and destitute that fell in the wake of those stronger, scrapping by and hiding from vicious people who walked the Earth. Like Rust, I eventually evolved. The same massive encampments that had harmed me and kept me in hiding would unkowingly make me a force to be reckoned with. With large numbered forces ruling the game I was forced into a life of guerrilla warfare, and everything changed, the weak were now quick to bond with each other and the powerfull had become content. In no time I could band together a group of fighters with bows and arrows and a lot of hate, attacking in the dark and from multiple directions, abusing spawnpoints, throwing desperate bodies at the enemy. Blood laden assault rifles clattered to the ground under the weight of a thousand naked bodies, before the poor began to replicate the enemies stolen goods. All of the goodness had been stolen from my people, and only hatred filled demons walked the Earth. We killed all in sight and ushered in an age of crippling violent paranoia the likes of which have never been seen. The world has been weakened now, made even, and the line between success and extermination has become forever blurred by inconsistent chaotic violence. I walk Rust now, 390 hours into hell, and remember every moment, that I cant turn back from here.
- The game is very aesthetically pleasing, with good lighting effects and attention to small animation details and events.
- Progress in game developement has been consistently effortful, and players have been kept up to speed by developers
- Game has given me two years of enjoyable play with various friends without ever becoming too stale.
- Every player has lost their mind and will listen to outlandish ideas if you just role-play them.
- Map design does a great job at forcing players to compete for resources, instand proximity chat communication makes for good player interaction and seemless transition from talking♥♥♥♥♥♥to panicked shooting.
- The volatile nature of the combat system makes it possible for someone with 1 hour of gameplay to best someone with 400, making the game always keep you on your toes.
Cons:
- Character model is not customizable. Armor and clothes make character identification and uniforming relatively easy, but I would be able to mentally invest more of myself into make character if I could build him/her from scratch. Although the Somalian-pirate like nature of my code generated character and his abnormally large genitals have lead to some funny interactions, I just love a game more when I can make my identity.
- The frequency of server wiping updates can demotivate players against large projects, but the game is in Alpha, and that is completely understood.
Notes: The game is very difficult to progress through on your own, this game has been great for me being in the military, because people are forced into situations where I have hours to explain my Rust eploits and win them over to it. But if you are less of a social gamer, try to team up with people in game using proximity chat, and work with low level people first. Starting the game working with powerful people will hurt your skills in the long run, Rust is all about journey rather than destination. I wish the best of luck to anyone who plays this. It's been the source of many "HELL ♥♥♥♥ING YEAHS!!!" and "GOD DAMMMMIIITS!!!" for me, and I hope it can give you as much of a ride. Also, there are a lot of over experienced players in Rust, where my 400 hours seems like small potatos compared to a lot of players.
Pro tip: The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Eoka Pistol can fire shotgun shells. Be wary.

I bet you've probably played a ton of games over the course of many years. You've seen the generel gist of them, you know how they tick and what to expect. Small things, that AAA game developers that work in huge teams often can't see. You usually know where the boundaries of such games lie and how to test the game until you hit that "wall", where the game doesn't allow you to procede, simply, because it isn't worthwhile to most game developers to program something, that the majority of the player base won't see. We've come to accept these boundaries, since that's just how video games are to us, today.
Now, what Undertale does, is take you by the throat and drag you beyond that wall into a realm where most of your expectations will be completely broken, twisted and far surpassed beyond that. Remember that feeling you had, when you played one of your favorites games for the first time? How everything seemed new, magical and meaningful, before you later learned of the true boundaries in games? That feeling, that everything matters, you can now experience once more, despite being a long-time gamer.
Be prepared, for this game will leave it's print on your soul.

So... Undertale.
It's an RPG, but instead of getting higher levels to breeze past bosses this game's combat takes a more active approach, requiring you to dodge projectiles for a brief time to not get hurt. This is a plus in my eyes already. Grinding until you beat things with higher numbers can be boring.
The overworld has a few puzzles but nothing you'll need a guide for. In fact, guides are bad for this game. Don't use them.
So I imagine you're asking yourself "So is this all that makes people so hyped about Undertale?"
It is not, but what, exactly, IS making people so hyped is hard to put into words.
Things as core to video gaming as saving and the fact you control a character are given plot significance in certain routes and some enemies break the game's rules entirely in a way that is, somehow, justified by narrative.
The game, somehow, managed to make me actually like these characters. I could never go through with a  "kill everyone" run simply because I now like the characters too much, and that says a lot given how apathetic I am to most RPG NPCs.
The humor is the sort of stuff I find funny, but given how different comedic tastes are not everyone will be in the same boat as I.
But truly, I'm afraid the only way to know if you'll like it is to give it a go. You can get a demo on the website for the game if you're on the fence. If you like that, the full game is more of it but better, and I'd absolutely recommend you experience it.

Rust teaches you that there are three kinds of people in this world. People who will offer you help and be kind to you, and not leave you as a limp lifeless corpse riddled with bullets. People who will, in fact, leave you as a limb lifeless corpse that is 56% Metal 44% Flesh and 100% Dead. And then there's the oh so magical third one. The kind of person that runs around with nothing but a pumpkin on their heads whilst screaming, "Stick it up my butt". I am usually the first kind of person (and sometimes the third), which as you can see makes you the most attractive to teenagers with Tommyguns and mafia fantasies. As you adjust to life after the Third World War (or after an unpopular team wins the super bowl), you will learn that living on your own is meaningless and boring. What fun is it to survive without friends? I eventually moved into a town, yes a THRIVING town known simply as "Smoke Town". The server I had chosen was TheRustyChicken (a server I highly recommend). Smoke Town was a thriving place...until the wipe where we proceeded to decimate the town with rocket launchers. THEN WE REBUILT THE TOWN, and everything was fine. That is until the mafia obsessed teenagers arrived. They annoyed our town by constantly re-spawning, stealing what they could, and going on Friday the 13th inspired rampages. Life was good in between those though. This game will teach you to be a better person, because in reality you don't want someone to break in to your home, steal everything from your kitchen, and smash you over the head with a rock they found in your garden. Either that or you'll eventually become a self-righteous hoarder who  says things like, "it's survival of the fittest, man". You'll then proceed to become a powerhouse, until the first people who set up stuff on the server notice you. They will raid you, take your stuff, and you're back to being a simple naked fellow with a pet rock. Rust is a game that I highly recommend (definitely try to play with friends if you can). Rust is a game that makes you wish the servers time out because if you log on before the people who held a gun to your head do, then you can loot their bodies and slay them in your sleep. 8/10.

After my pc broke about a week ago I really began to understand what it meant to take something for granted. By this I mean that since 2013 I've been blessed with a game that I would call divine in idea and creation, yet I've never written a damn review for said game. The game I speak of is... Nether! JK, although Nether would be fantastic if it still had populated servers. Enough about Nether, this review is about Rust. Rust is my favorite game in my steam library, if not my favorite game played ever. I would consider Rust a second life for the typical gamer. By that I mean when you get really into Rust it will be on your mind at least half the time you're doing other♥♥♥♥♥♥ Seriously, If you've never been lost in deep thought while making a poop and you want to, buy Rust. Some pros and cons I can think of off the top of my head:
Pros
-Looks beautiful. I consider Rust one of the prettiest games in my library. Even legacy has its charm IMO (a lot of people think it looks to dark/emo)
-Decent optimization. One of the most important things about games. Facepunch does it fairly well (at least you're not getting ARK lag), not exceptional, but they're getting there.
-Cheap... Considering the content and lifetime of Rust I would consider the $20 stipend pocket change.
-Addicting. ♥♥♥♥ heroin, Pass me the Rust. Rust isn't a game you're going to be forcing yourself to play.
-Diverse. Like building? Shooting? Melee? Socializing (eew)? Rust has something for everyone.
-Easy to have fun. DO NOT CONFUSE WITH EASY TO BE GOOD AT. Some of the funnest times I've had in Rust have been seconds after spawning on a server for the first time with nothing to cover my micro♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ a rock in my hand.
Cons
-Hackers. If experimental Rust hadn't usurped legacy as the preferred of the two we could bet that the game would still be overrun with hackers. I'm not saying there are no hackers, there are just a lot less.
-Unpredictable community. Some might say toxic ,I however prefer 'unpredictable'. I actually love the Rust community as is, that said I know people who don't play the game because they get instantly killed by players claiming to be friendly.
-Expensive. But earlier you said it was cheap, what heresy! To be clear, I consider $20 cheap for what Rust is now. Back in the days of legacy it was kind of a rip-off. That's right Facepunch, you dun just got called out.
All in all the most fun you'll ever have in Rust, let alone any game is when you're with friends. Whether they are covering your six in an adrenaline pumping firefight, or singing a song about getting man butt around a campfire, friends make Rust as fun as it is. I'll end this review with a shoutout to some of the best people I've ever met, whether they be personal friends of mine or other players whom I shared memories with.
To Mista and Farty two of my best friends IRL, ya'll have been with me since the beginning.
To Fireheart, one time you said something so memorable about Rust that I turned it into a playlist on Spotify. In the past day we've had four days worth of adventure.
To Liam, I don't care if you're a redcoat, you make memories like a yank.
To The old legacy crew, It's been ages since our fateful night of murder, and yes, everyone can hear you Software.
To The Gary's Town group, I'll admit I wasn't the best tenant but you guys were the best landlords.
To The New Rust crew, whether it be defending the pub or charging across fields we've had our share of fun and fury.
To Everyone I've♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, you all are the majority, congrats? I'm sincerely sorry, but that's the game.

You spawn in with a Torch and a Rock. From there you try to gather as many resources as you can. This is a game in which resources are key so acquiring them by any means necessary is fair game. Yes, that means you can kill the guy farming a tree for 5 minutes and take all his hard work. Or you can be killed by a guy while you're farming and subsequently lose all your hard work...or kill the guy farming then get killed by another guy. That is why you always want to use move around and look around while farming. To make sure you do not lose all of your resources, you must invest them into making a house. No house is ever 100% secure as enough explosives will break through just about anything. Clans are difficult to fight, but nothing is stopping you from gaining their trust, and then completely destroying them from the inside out. There is no such thing as "morally wrong" in Rust. You do what you must to survive, and survive what you must to continue doing so.
As for progress, how much have you hoarded so far and how many blueprints have you learned? The more you have learned - the more you have progressed. Eventually you will have all the blueprints studied - and you will have nothing better to do. At this point most clans just start wars with each other - this is the type of stuff you see in
. On most vanilla servers you will have blueprint wipe cycles the first of every month so all your blueprint progress is reset- and map wipes weekly or every two weeks whereas the map is cleaned of all houses and sleepers, without touching players' blueprint progress.  If you fancy permanent blueprint progression, less grinding or any other variation on normal gameplay - you are always free to play on modded servers that each offer their own mix of mods.
This game can be very unforgiving, but it is ultimately up to the player to decide whether or not they will persevere through the hardships and turn the tides of battle to their favor.

It's a clever game.  The story is simple, short, and vaguely interesting in what it addresses.  It has a few witty characters that give the game flavor and a sense of humor, which is great.  The systems in place for battle are well done and tie directly into the story, which is cool.  Its visual style is unique, which I can appreciate and dig to a certain extent, but it didn't blow me away.  Backtracking is a pain, especially later on in the game.  I find that odd considering the game's total length, but maybe that was entirely deliberate.  I avoided as much information about Undertale as I could before playing it, and I have to say that I find its soundtrack to be its most redeeming quality above all else.  Major props to Toby Fox and pals for putting together a game as painstakingly programmed as this in an RPG Maker, but I don't see it as a masterpiece or even an excellent game.  Maybe it doesn't have to be excellent, though.  It's a strange game, and it makes you think a little, and maybe that's all that really matters.

Rust teaches you that there are three kinds of people in this world. People who will offer you help and be kind to you, and not leave you as a limp lifeless corpse riddled with bullets. People who will, in fact, leave you as a limb lifeless corpse that is 56% Metal 44% Flesh and 100% Dead. And then there's the oh so magical third one. The kind of person that runs around with nothing but a pumpkin on their heads whilst screaming, "Stick it up my butt". I am usually the first kind of person (and sometimes the third), which as you can see makes you the most attractive to teenagers with Tommyguns and mafia fantasies. As you adjust to life after the Third World War (or after an unpopular team wins the super bowl), you will learn that living on your own is meaningless and boring. What fun is it to survive without friends? I eventually moved into a town, yes a THRIVING town known simply as "Smoke Town". The server I had chosen was TheRustyChicken (a server I highly recommend). Smoke Town was a thriving place...until the wipe where we proceeded to decimate the town with rocket launchers. THEN WE REBUILT THE TOWN, and everything was fine. That is until the mafia obsessed teenagers arrived. They annoyed our town by constantly re-spawning, stealing what they could, and going on Friday the 13th inspired rampages. Life was good in between those though. This game will teach you to be a better person, because in reality you don't want someone to break in to your home, steal everything from your kitchen, and smash you over the head with a rock they found in your garden. Either that or you'll eventually become a self-righteous hoarder who  says things like, "it's survival of the fittest, man". You'll then proceed to become a powerhouse, until the first people who set up stuff on the server notice you. They will raid you, take your stuff, and you're back to being a simple naked fellow with a pet rock. Rust is a game that I highly recommend (definitely try to play with friends if you can). Rust is a game that makes you wish the servers time out because if you log on before the people who held a gun to your head do, then you can loot their bodies and slay them in your sleep. 8/10.

As of last month, developers Facepunch (headed by Garry Newman of Garry’s Mod fame) declared that what was previously known as ‘Experimental Mode’ is now the definitive version of Rust. It now launches by default on Steam, with an option to play on the old ‘Legacy’ servers instead if you’re not ready for change. Unfortunately, I don’t think the game’s quite ready itself.
Spawning in Rust used to entail waking up in the wilderness hungry, naked and alone with only a rock and torch to make your way in the world. In the latest build you spawn alone, naked, hungry and thirsty, with just a rock. My first life started on a border between a forest and the recently added arctic biome. With the most interesting thing nearby being a deer, I did the logical thing and caved its head in. I went on to harvest a ludicrous amount of cloth and animal bones as well as, inexplicably, some wolf meat and a wolf skull – before ironically being eaten by an actual wolf shortly after. Rust is a mean place, even without its human denizens.
Now running in version 5 of the Unity engine, that mean place is certainly prettier. Like other survival games of its ilk, there’s a large amount of downtime in Rust, meaning atmosphere counts for a lot. Wandering the landscape, searching for resources and hoping for chance encounters with strangers forms the bulk of the game. This wasn’t previously the case: one of the largest changes made across engines is to the map itself. Instead of a relatively small area focused around structures and a single ring-road placed by the devs, each server now hosts its own massive, procedurally generated world. It has the potential to create moments of discovery that fixed environments can’t manage, but currently the generated worlds looks too repetitive to properly deliver on that front. It also makes meeting up with friends a nightmare.
The increased world size comes with an increase in max player count, with the official servers all hosting up to 500 players. However, on average there’ll only be about 50 other Rusters running around at the same time, resulting in the world feeling kinda lonely. In my first few hours with the game, I only encountered a couple of other people – and they were all sleeping (in what remains one of Rusts’ finer features, logged out players remain in the world unconscious). In lieu of anything more interesting to do I took their stuff, filled their pockets with wolf skulls and moved on.
In contrast, after ten minutes of playing on Legacy mode a kid had invited me to move into the cave next door to him and his friend. After another ten minutes I’d fended off a naked attacker as he shouted gibberish down his mic, and would in quick succession go on a hunting trip in which I accidentally shot an arrow through my new acquaintance’s chest, and be forced at gunpoint to tea-bag a sleeping person we’d happened across in the wilderness. Ten minutes after that I was dead, shot in the back of the head by a stranger as my new friends and I sheltered around a campfire.
The change of pace might be deliberate, but I’m not sure it’s welcome. Legacy feels relentless, but new Rust can feel placid. This isn’t to say that it doesn’t also introduce numerous improvements. Perhaps most notably, better anti-cheat software has solved the hacking problem that plagued the old game. The second person I met in Legacy mode demonstrated this by enthusiastically flying 100 feet into the air. Depressingly, when I asked him why he cheated he said it was to protect himself from other hackers.
The devs are also expanding the survival elements of the game, adding new status effects such as ‘wet’. I owed one of my early deaths to hypothermia after I attempted to swim across an icy river. There’s still a long way to go: the only way to satisfy the new ‘thirst’ metre is just to eat as normal. As befitting an early access title, the systems are also in a constant state of flux, with some fun mechanics being patched out for the sake of balance. The ability to open an alive players inventory was recently removed, for example, resulting in me having to kill every sleeping player I see and ruining my ability to replace all their stuff with wolf skulls.
Crafting remains largely the same, though there are significant changes in the pipeline. The blueprint system is still in effect, where plans for items not in the basic set have to be found and learnt, but can then be built by subsequent characters after you die – providing you stick to the same server. It lends a sense of achievement that persists across otherwise doomed playthroughs. However, there’s worrying talk of introducing blueprints through random Steam drops that can then be traded. Despite the developer’s reassurances, it’s hard not to imagine the system rewarding larger wallets over invested playtime. The other side of crafting, base building, has been streamlined. It’s easier to quickly gather the resources needed to make a basic shelter, and to put it together. It can still be a daunting task though, as I found when I got bludgeoned to death from behind while my guard was down. Attempting to steal a house went little better.
I’d spawned next to a basic hut, warmth and light emanating from the inside thanks to a lit bonfire. Someone was home! Without any equipment to break my way inside, I figured my best bet was to wait outside and ambush the guy as he came out. I crept into some nearby bushes and settled in – only to realise someone else had had the same idea. Fortunately he’d logged off, leaving me free to take out his sleeping body and instantly acquire a good set of gear. After a bit more skulking, I realised that now I could probably just break in.
It took me two minutes to get through the roof. I dropped down, taking out my freshly pilfered spear in expectation of a fight – but the guy had vanished. His stuff was scattered around as if he’d purposefully dropped it before somehow disappearing. It didn’t matter to me: within five minutes I’d scored two inventories worth of loot and an entire house. All I needed to do was replace the code-locked door with my own. After an age of chopping, I’d destroyed the previous tenant’s handiwork. The door’s code-lock, however, remained hovering in place: bugged out. Without any way to build over it or destroy it, my move-in was thwarted.
Rust clearly has potential. Swapping to Unity seems to have been the right move for the devs, as in the long-term procedural worlds and larger server counts should bear fruit – but it’s too unstable in its current state to be enjoyed properly. As well as that glitch with the lock, I found animals frequently wouldn’t attack me, my framerate would slow to a crawl, and occasionally servers would simply disconnect me. Performance issues at least have been acknowledged on the regularly updated dev blog, so there’s reason to think the problems will be addressed and that, with more time, Rust may yet achieve the compelling blend of stranger management and freeform construction it’s aiming for.

I haven't been this happy with a game purchase in ages. There is so much love put into this game it shows, from little details about the characters, the deep lore, the comical undertones, and an incredibly detailed system where your actions and words can greatly alter the game encouraging multiple playthroughs. In fact, it's heavily recommended you do play this game at least three or four times to get the full experience.

Hmm.... HMMMM! I'll just do my normal pros and cons. Though, there's one con that's not in the game, but directly relates to it.
*updated because I tried the genocide route*
PROS:
+You'll feel for the characters. Instead of trying to tell a story about events, this game goes for full on character development. It reminds me a lot of Spec Ops: The Line, where my actions had meaning, and in the end, they ALL mattered, and the game pulls a "This is all on you, a-hole" message. And just like Spec Ops: The Line, the game made me think about gaming as a medium.
+You remember that part in Batman: Arkham Asylum when the fear gas made you think the game crashed? Undertale does that. Very. Well.
+The setting for the game isn't all that grand. Monsters down there, humans up there, human falls down, and human decides what to do. It really isn't anything to write home about. However, the characters really make the game.  Seriously, the game should have been called "Character Tale" because that's all you'll care about.. is the characters!
+The art direction is perfect. Perfect. The monsters look neat, but, again I am going on about them, the characters are animated really well, and look nice.
+Everything about Mettaton. You'll get it when you play it. Just don't... Well, look below.
+Overally, the game made me feel fuzzy inside.
(NEW!) +I my original review, I complained about the friendship stuff as a drag sometimes until one of the characters would say or do something that'd make me entertained. You, as the player, can just go on a murderous rampage and, let me tell you, it changes things. It changes a lot of things. This game really is what Spec Ops: The Line is for all games rather than just games about war.
+I personally like some of the user-made content for this game, such as fanart, music videos, animations, etc. See CONS for more on this subject matter.....
MIXED:
+/- Regardless of whether or not you do a FIGHT or ACT run, the combat itself will be exactly the same: You move a little heart around, dodging objects. It's INCREDIBLY creative, but at the same time, it can be INCREDIBLY frustrating. There are some fights you'll repeat 30 times. Ironically, the game has a set piece which explains why the player (yes, the player, not the character) would repeat this over and over. Just go play the damn game!
+/- Do yourself a massive favor and use your xbox 360, Steam Controller (like me!), or find any controller to use with this game. You can use the keyboard with it, but it plays better with a controller.
CONS:
-....From what I've been told, the community is from Tumblr. Need I say more, especially after that thing happened with Steven Universe fanart? Maybe I'm just overly cautious, but whenever a game amasses a following from Tumblr, a place where overly-sensitive morons breed and multiply, I get extra cautious. For example, look at Mettaton. I can't really talk about him without spoiling it, but imagine if someone took a character which resembled Ziggy Stardust and added a massive amount of stereotype to it, while ignoring character traits which make the character a self-obessed vane monster. Maybe it's just me. I don't know, but fandoms nowadays bother me.
-Ya, there isn't anything that stands out as bad for the game itself. It's doesn't set out to be something more than it already is and succeeds at it.
CONCLUSION:
This game is worth the buy. It stands along side other titles such as The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Spec Ops: The Line, The Stanley Parable--all games that made me think about the story and intrepret its meaning. Except Undertale stands above those games because of its low budget look and reliance on art direction and witty story than flashy cutting edge graphics.

This game was a creative joy road down Feels Alley with a few stops at WTF town, Mind Blown Lane, and Comedy Street. Toby Fox and co. made a brilliant game. Fallout 4 be damned, once I fired this up I couldn't stop till I was done.
What I liked about it (aside from the obvious heaps of creativity lovingly dumped all over every aspect of the game) was the way it turned the whole RPG system on it's head with the ACT system and then how it had a consistent story with foreshadowing, hints, and teasers that tied everything in. It also addresses the player being able to Save and reload saves by working this into the game in a fascinating, and at one point terrifying, way.
I'd recommend this game to everyone. It is a must play and should be Game of the Year for 2015.

UNDERTALE...(by Toby Fox)
So one day I'm scrolling through I Can has Cheezburger again, and I saw some fanart that caught my eye, and it confused me... "Why did they re-design Sue? Why do Mimigas now have horns? Why would Pixel do that... Unless... OH MY GOD IS THERE A CAVE STORY 2? QUICK CHECK THE TAGS- "Undertale"?... As in an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? No, I've played too much Dust: An Elysian Tail... Oh. Well cool, this character looks cute. I like her." Then I began to hear that name with more frequency... Undertale, Undertale, Undertale. Then one of my friends on Skype recommended it and I caved and asked what it was about, and he told me "It's an RPG where you don't have to kill anything." And that intrigued me just enough... Now a Neutral ending and a Pacifist ending later, I love the game.
It's a basic RPG with a Bullet-Hell Nonshooter battle system, which is interesting. The music is great, capturing a retro feel, while simultaneously capturing the grand scape of actual instruments (though synthetic). and the retro-SNES style graphics are very well done and charming. I won't go into the story because I feel it's best to be experienced yourself, how ever that said, the music, story, and graphics are the best parts about this game.
Looking at it from an RPG standpoint, it is missing a lot of basic features. Like maps, or a party system, or more than just one attack. Looking at it from a Bullet-Hell standpoint, it's lacking even worse. If you want an RPG with much more content and features that are now of days labelled as "basic needs", or a good Bullet Hell Shooter, I'd recommend Epic Battle Fantasy 4, or Epic Battle Fantasy 4.4: Bullet Heaven 2 (both by Matt Roszak) respectively. That's not my only flaw with the game however, But first I must issue a SPOILER ALERT!
DO NOT READ PAST IF YOU DON'T WANT POTENTIAL SPOILERS.
Upon completing a Genocide run you are greeted by the first human to fall, Chara. She then jumpscares you and crashes the game, upon reloading, you must wait 10 whole minutes before anything at all happens. She then tells you she can restore the game at the cost of Frisk's soul. Saying no will result in another crash, and 10 more minutes of nothing before she asks again. After selling Frisk's soul, the ending to the Pacifist run is slightly altered just to hammer in that you already got the worst ending, and you will never live it down. Now, if this was a one time thing, then I'd be fine. But it's not. It's a permanent change. ALL Pacifist endings are forever altered... Unless you file dive. Which if this game is ported to consoles, is not an option. There is no in-game way of undoing it, and yes it was nearly a deal breaker to me. I nearly hated this game as much as I loved it, and twice as fast. This warrants a patch, but I highly doubt Toby Fox will remove it.
SPOILERS END HERE,
If you are looking for a good, quick story, then you have got almost nothing to lose. If you are looking for a Standard grade RPG, look elsewhere. It's definitely not "The Best game of All time", but it's worth it's sale price of $7.99
6/10. And if the above mentioned patch happens, 7/10.

I haven't been this happy with a game purchase in ages. There is so much love put into this game it shows, from little details about the characters, the deep lore, the comical undertones, and an incredibly detailed system where your actions and words can greatly alter the game encouraging multiple playthroughs. In fact, it's heavily recommended you do play this game at least three or four times to get the full experience.

Hmm.... HMMMM! I'll just do my normal pros and cons. Though, there's one con that's not in the game, but directly relates to it.
*updated because I tried the genocide route*
PROS:
+You'll feel for the characters. Instead of trying to tell a story about events, this game goes for full on character development. It reminds me a lot of Spec Ops: The Line, where my actions had meaning, and in the end, they ALL mattered, and the game pulls a "This is all on you, a-hole" message. And just like Spec Ops: The Line, the game made me think about gaming as a medium.
+You remember that part in Batman: Arkham Asylum when the fear gas made you think the game crashed? Undertale does that. Very. Well.
+The setting for the game isn't all that grand. Monsters down there, humans up there, human falls down, and human decides what to do. It really isn't anything to write home about. However, the characters really make the game.  Seriously, the game should have been called "Character Tale" because that's all you'll care about.. is the characters!
+The art direction is perfect. Perfect. The monsters look neat, but, again I am going on about them, the characters are animated really well, and look nice.
+Everything about Mettaton. You'll get it when you play it. Just don't... Well, look below.
+Overally, the game made me feel fuzzy inside.
(NEW!) +I my original review, I complained about the friendship stuff as a drag sometimes until one of the characters would say or do something that'd make me entertained. You, as the player, can just go on a murderous rampage and, let me tell you, it changes things. It changes a lot of things. This game really is what Spec Ops: The Line is for all games rather than just games about war.
+I personally like some of the user-made content for this game, such as fanart, music videos, animations, etc. See CONS for more on this subject matter.....
MIXED:
+/- Regardless of whether or not you do a FIGHT or ACT run, the combat itself will be exactly the same: You move a little heart around, dodging objects. It's INCREDIBLY creative, but at the same time, it can be INCREDIBLY frustrating. There are some fights you'll repeat 30 times. Ironically, the game has a set piece which explains why the player (yes, the player, not the character) would repeat this over and over. Just go play the damn game!
+/- Do yourself a massive favor and use your xbox 360, Steam Controller (like me!), or find any controller to use with this game. You can use the keyboard with it, but it plays better with a controller.
CONS:
-....From what I've been told, the community is from Tumblr. Need I say more, especially after that thing happened with Steven Universe fanart? Maybe I'm just overly cautious, but whenever a game amasses a following from Tumblr, a place where overly-sensitive morons breed and multiply, I get extra cautious. For example, look at Mettaton. I can't really talk about him without spoiling it, but imagine if someone took a character which resembled Ziggy Stardust and added a massive amount of stereotype to it, while ignoring character traits which make the character a self-obessed vane monster. Maybe it's just me. I don't know, but fandoms nowadays bother me.
-Ya, there isn't anything that stands out as bad for the game itself. It's doesn't set out to be something more than it already is and succeeds at it.
CONCLUSION:
This game is worth the buy. It stands along side other titles such as The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, Spec Ops: The Line, The Stanley Parable--all games that made me think about the story and intrepret its meaning. Except Undertale stands above those games because of its low budget look and reliance on art direction and witty story than flashy cutting edge graphics.

Undertale is work of art for those who enjoy games. For those who didn't play them, it is an enigma. How could a game with such graphics in today's time capture such an audience so as to become a culture on its own?
Like a great literature, it is
to describe one's experience in Undertale by utter words. But as I feel the need to contribute to one of the most influential game I have ever played, I will try my best to write this simple love letter:
The game has an incredible plot that does not force on you, rather, how much you take in depends on how much you care. Everything is there for a reason. Just like real life, if you simply take a glimpse at the scenery, you only saw a beautiful picture, not the cold wind that embrace your skin nor the sound of nature. In this game, if you are of inquisitive mind, you will soon discover more than what were delivered. A welcome change from the bombardment of to-the-face content that the various AAA titles with their fancy CGI gives you. True, it rewards those with more commitment but the most beautiful thing was how without realizing, the game is able to embrace you, slowly and without force. Before long, you simply cared.
It is first and foremost an RPG game. With standard interface and traditional RPG combat based on action selection found in most JRPGS like pokemon or earthbound. Despite so, Undertale's combat is one of the most ingenious system i've ever experienced.
The combat is exhilarating and manage to include components that seems to try its best in exploring the various possibilities that lies within the system. It is also able to seamlessly incorporate story elements so much as that the gap  between the gameplay and the story is very much nonexistant. As a result, each combat feel more alive. For a combat concept that is based on random-encounters, this is an impressive feat.
Each of the OSTs are masterfully crafted. It doesn't matter if they are reiterations of a few molds, each music conveys the meaning perfectly for different situations. Every time you hear it, nostalgia will overwhelm you, you will remember the best moments of this game. Every time you hear it, your feelings will come.
At the end of the day you would realize how much effort was put into this masterpiece.
This is the standard and quality that we should strive for. This should be the message we gamers send. We want content that not only look beautiful, but also feel and sound beautiful. Games should be crafted with most care, not about profits they earn but about the impacts that they deliver. After all, gamers learn and will happily give their money away to reward those that manage to create a wonderful world for us.
Toby fox created a game that has gamers not just to have fun, but also has gamers thinking, dreaming and have each and every membrane of imagination dwell in it. Thank you, Toby Fox.

When I first saw Undertale, I was filled with...
Skepticism, uncertainty, doubt
The first time I peered through the reviews of Undertale on the Steam store page the sheer amount of pretentiousness was something that I couldn't grasp. Weeks later after I saw that page I saw more and more Undertale everywhere, people were frantic about it on the internet, my close friends talked about it, people in my University were into it. The Undertale phenomenon was massive.Everyone who I have met AND I MEAN EVERYONE, has said either one of two things about Undertale:
1) That is was the best game they have ever played
2) That the game is perfect
I never really believed in perfection in games, let alone perfection in this world. The more I heard about Undertale, the more I gave into it. I played the demo and I heard the music. Finally, weeks later I was gifted the game by a friend, and finally tried out Undertale, and this is what I have to say:
Undertale in one of the best indie games I have ever played in my life
The way this game is designed, how it plays tricks with your mind, predicts your moves, and how the game tells its story through it's gameplay and how every action does affect the outcome of the story unlike other games that claim to do the same. What Toby Fox has achieved here with Undertale is short of masterful game design and the game has every right to be called an Indie master piece.
Now Undertale is not a perfect game and there's many things that I don't like about it. I don't like the visuals, while they are nice pixel art they aren't that appealing to me, I didn't like how certain minor enemy encounter's were random and how much of the game's style and influence comes from the wretched bowl's of the Tumblr culture, which, while Tumblr has many nice artists, I don't like a lot of what comes out of it. And while the game is enjoyable, I didn't find it super enjoyable, maybe it's because of my current state in life, maybe.
In conclusion, Undertale is a great game. I know there isn't much to say about the game but that's kind of how the game works, telling you anything would spoil the experience. Just as the Stanley Parable is that kind of virtual experience where talking about what happens spoils the experience. Undertale is that kind of game,now for me personally Undertale is not my favorite Indie game, that title belongs to Hotline Miami, Undertale moved me emotionally, but not as emotionally as The Walking Dead Season 2's ending, and it's definitely not the best game I have ever played, but it is a very, very special game
All in all, my first impression of Undertale made me filled with skepticism, uncertainty, and doubt
But after finishing the game on the pacifist playthrough (which I highly recommend only playing, MY GOODNESS ME THAT ENGING)
made me filled with...
Determination

As of last month, developers Facepunch (headed by Garry Newman of Garry’s Mod fame) declared that what was previously known as ‘Experimental Mode’ is now the definitive version of Rust. It now launches by default on Steam, with an option to play on the old ‘Legacy’ servers instead if you’re not ready for change. Unfortunately, I don’t think the game’s quite ready itself.
Spawning in Rust used to entail waking up in the wilderness hungry, naked and alone with only a rock and torch to make your way in the world. In the latest build you spawn alone, naked, hungry and thirsty, with just a rock. My first life started on a border between a forest and the recently added arctic biome. With the most interesting thing nearby being a deer, I did the logical thing and caved its head in. I went on to harvest a ludicrous amount of cloth and animal bones as well as, inexplicably, some wolf meat and a wolf skull – before ironically being eaten by an actual wolf shortly after. Rust is a mean place, even without its human denizens.
Now running in version 5 of the Unity engine, that mean place is certainly prettier. Like other survival games of its ilk, there’s a large amount of downtime in Rust, meaning atmosphere counts for a lot. Wandering the landscape, searching for resources and hoping for chance encounters with strangers forms the bulk of the game. This wasn’t previously the case: one of the largest changes made across engines is to the map itself. Instead of a relatively small area focused around structures and a single ring-road placed by the devs, each server now hosts its own massive, procedurally generated world. It has the potential to create moments of discovery that fixed environments can’t manage, but currently the generated worlds looks too repetitive to properly deliver on that front. It also makes meeting up with friends a nightmare.
The increased world size comes with an increase in max player count, with the official servers all hosting up to 500 players. However, on average there’ll only be about 50 other Rusters running around at the same time, resulting in the world feeling kinda lonely. In my first few hours with the game, I only encountered a couple of other people – and they were all sleeping (in what remains one of Rusts’ finer features, logged out players remain in the world unconscious). In lieu of anything more interesting to do I took their stuff, filled their pockets with wolf skulls and moved on.
In contrast, after ten minutes of playing on Legacy mode a kid had invited me to move into the cave next door to him and his friend. After another ten minutes I’d fended off a naked attacker as he shouted gibberish down his mic, and would in quick succession go on a hunting trip in which I accidentally shot an arrow through my new acquaintance’s chest, and be forced at gunpoint to tea-bag a sleeping person we’d happened across in the wilderness. Ten minutes after that I was dead, shot in the back of the head by a stranger as my new friends and I sheltered around a campfire.
The change of pace might be deliberate, but I’m not sure it’s welcome. Legacy feels relentless, but new Rust can feel placid. This isn’t to say that it doesn’t also introduce numerous improvements. Perhaps most notably, better anti-cheat software has solved the hacking problem that plagued the old game. The second person I met in Legacy mode demonstrated this by enthusiastically flying 100 feet into the air. Depressingly, when I asked him why he cheated he said it was to protect himself from other hackers.
The devs are also expanding the survival elements of the game, adding new status effects such as ‘wet’. I owed one of my early deaths to hypothermia after I attempted to swim across an icy river. There’s still a long way to go: the only way to satisfy the new ‘thirst’ metre is just to eat as normal. As befitting an early access title, the systems are also in a constant state of flux, with some fun mechanics being patched out for the sake of balance. The ability to open an alive players inventory was recently removed, for example, resulting in me having to kill every sleeping player I see and ruining my ability to replace all their stuff with wolf skulls.
Crafting remains largely the same, though there are significant changes in the pipeline. The blueprint system is still in effect, where plans for items not in the basic set have to be found and learnt, but can then be built by subsequent characters after you die – providing you stick to the same server. It lends a sense of achievement that persists across otherwise doomed playthroughs. However, there’s worrying talk of introducing blueprints through random Steam drops that can then be traded. Despite the developer’s reassurances, it’s hard not to imagine the system rewarding larger wallets over invested playtime. The other side of crafting, base building, has been streamlined. It’s easier to quickly gather the resources needed to make a basic shelter, and to put it together. It can still be a daunting task though, as I found when I got bludgeoned to death from behind while my guard was down. Attempting to steal a house went little better.
I’d spawned next to a basic hut, warmth and light emanating from the inside thanks to a lit bonfire. Someone was home! Without any equipment to break my way inside, I figured my best bet was to wait outside and ambush the guy as he came out. I crept into some nearby bushes and settled in – only to realise someone else had had the same idea. Fortunately he’d logged off, leaving me free to take out his sleeping body and instantly acquire a good set of gear. After a bit more skulking, I realised that now I could probably just break in.
It took me two minutes to get through the roof. I dropped down, taking out my freshly pilfered spear in expectation of a fight – but the guy had vanished. His stuff was scattered around as if he’d purposefully dropped it before somehow disappearing. It didn’t matter to me: within five minutes I’d scored two inventories worth of loot and an entire house. All I needed to do was replace the code-locked door with my own. After an age of chopping, I’d destroyed the previous tenant’s handiwork. The door’s code-lock, however, remained hovering in place: bugged out. Without any way to build over it or destroy it, my move-in was thwarted.
Rust clearly has potential. Swapping to Unity seems to have been the right move for the devs, as in the long-term procedural worlds and larger server counts should bear fruit – but it’s too unstable in its current state to be enjoyed properly. As well as that glitch with the lock, I found animals frequently wouldn’t attack me, my framerate would slow to a crawl, and occasionally servers would simply disconnect me. Performance issues at least have been acknowledged on the regularly updated dev blog, so there’s reason to think the problems will be addressed and that, with more time, Rust may yet achieve the compelling blend of stranger management and freeform construction it’s aiming for.
