The only bad part I can think of is a boss battle against a character near the end, where it really seems sloppily done and doesn't fit in with the environment of the area nor the tone of the game as a whole. The combat is marvelous overall though, normal JRPG mechanics with an interesting Bullet Hell system to let you avoid any attacks, it sounds easy, but in reality, it can be quite a challenging game. Honestly, if you think you'll like this game, you probably will.
If you like RPGs and games with a good sense of humor, then you should give this a try.

Ah,  this game has given me so many feelings.
Depression, suicidal ones, sadness, disgust, and on a very small occasion(0.00001% of the time) joy.
If you're looking for a fun wasteland-zombie apocalypse themed game, this is not the game for you.
The game is basically an unfinished team death match arena, with the addition of zombies trying to kill you by dodging walls and everything that's material, and a slightly over-scale arena, designated to burn your CPU.
The community could be described as a collective record of every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that ever existed, because most of the time you'll find either clueless new guys who ask for help, or complete numb ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that will kill you with 100 different tools.
Yes, the game mostly focuses on tools to kill others rather than the survival aspect of things.
If you're a man that has a job, and a life, this is not the game for you. Why? Most of the time you'll be walking around the map for a few hours(3-5 hours min. in order to get some proper gear) and then, after  you've spent so much time, some 'tard with a shovel will bash your head in as you are spawning in.
Most of the places you'll find will be looted to the ground, aside from some towns nobody ever checks, because people log out at one spot, and join another server because every server knows where you last were, so all the hotspots will either be camped by people or looted by 100 people before you.
Alongside all of these, there are countless bugs which include, but are not limited to; Zombies running through doors, walls, ceilings, across 500m of you in 0.5 seconds.

It keeps on getting worse.
It used to be so fun 1.5 years ago, it wasn't grindy, gunplay was pretty good, the game itself looked good and felt snappy, and It had pretty good performance.
Then the lead dev changed.
The game now requires more grind than ever before, barrels have almost no loot in them, you only get components that you can't use anyway because you have no BPs. The workbenches cost a lot to get all 3 of them you need 1800 scrap, gettings scrap for them requires a ton of looting/recycling. Just smashing barrels insn't an option since barrels only give a single scrap.
Finding AKs is harder than ever before, in the old BP system you used to be able to find them everywhere even in barrels. You didn't have to build near a radtown to get stuff, now you pretty much have to build near launchsite/mil tunnels since these are the only radtowns where you can find AKs and other high level equipment.
Rockets can only be obtained by the heli, you have to kill a heli, otherwise you can't rocketraid, this is really hard for small groups on big servers. Rockets used to drop from every other barrel. Rocketlaunchers can be looted from bradley (requires c4 tho) chopper and from elite crates. Elite crates spawn every 2 hours on 2 different radtowns, I haven't seen a rocketlauncher since the new system was implemented.
Items/bps that were standard/common in oldschool BP are now rare, getting BPs in general require you to camp launch/mil tunnels. Some of the radtown that used to be good are now trash. Sattelite has the same loot as 20 metres of road, it used to spawn military crates.
Servers still die within 2 days, they used to live a minimum of 3 days up to 4 weeks. Official/Rustafied servers eat up all the population, these are the only servers that are alive for more than a week. On wipedays they usually get a queue of about 300 people.
Over the past year gunplay worsened a lot, you used to have a lot of recoil and a high accuracy, you had to tap at mid ranges with the AK. Some people complained about gunplay being RNG reliant, so the dev who's name shall not be mentioned thought  it was a genius idea to rework the gunplay. He lowered the recoil and decreased to overall accuracy. ♥♥♥♥in great, now everyone can "control" the recoil and hitting somebody on range is pretty much pure luck.
Tons of player including PvP streamers complained about it decreasing the skill ceiling of the game.
The dev just brushed it off as "vocal minority" as he does it with every problem he doesn't want to touch any further.
Some months of♥♥♥♥♥♥gunplay have passed and he finally decided to rework the gunplay once more, it got better but it still is way too easy to control. Triple headshotting people with an AK over 100 metres is. The AK has less recoil than the semi auto pistol. The MP5 has 5 times the horizontal recoil of the AK, even though it is a mid range SMG.
The implementation of the stance "recoil" was a letdown as well, it was intended to stop players from standing and strafing while full autoing an AK. What it essentially did was make shots inaccurate while tapping and strafing, which is essential since you don't want to stand still while shooting.
When complaining about gunplay in this game, the dev who's name shall not be mentioned keeps comparing it to other games like call of duty or battlefield, even though you can't compare any of these games. In none of these game you lose literal hours of  of farming when dying, RNG shouldn't be such a big factor in gunplay. RNG recoil was ok because you were able to control it just fine, it took a lot of practice but it was okay.
Performance used to be pretty good, getting over 100 fps on a server that is several days old wasn't uncommon. The game had little to no inputlag. When comparing 144 fps on july2016 to 144 fps today you can see a big difference, july 2016 looks way smoother and feels way snappier.
This weeks patch ♥♥♥♥ed my performance a lot, I lost over 40 fps this patch and my game keeps freezing.
Nights currently are a big mess, you can't see anything inside your base at night and you can barely see anything when going out, a lot of people use a third party program to see better at night, it is somehow acceptable to use a cheat now to actually see something. This has been a big problem for a long time and the devs refuse to comment on the subject.
The game has gotten worse and worse over the past year, I forced myself to play this game in the last 2 months but I just can't play it and be happy, I want to enjoy this game like I used to.

Ok, so you've all heard the hype and decided, "Eh, why not? I guess I'll try this game." You play through the game, being a pacifist, as is the norm for most people. I mean, at this point, everyone's heard the whole, "No one has to die" spiel, and you think you're a pretty decent person so you do it. You play the game with no mistakes, everyone loves you at the end. You play through it again and all your friends are there cheering you on. You finish the game, you think, "Wow, that was a pretty decent story for a game with such crappy mechanics and terrible puns. I guess it was worth it." And you feel satisfied, but slightly let down that it didn't emotionally wreck you more.
And that's the end of your experience with the game.
So you go back to your everyday life. You interact with the people at your job maybe, or perhaps your friends at school. You enjoy yourself. The day ends. You go to your home and see your family. your 6 or 7 dogs, or maybe you live alone. You eat dinner and sleep. The night ends. You wake up. You do it all again.
And then it hits you: "Is this the right way to be living?"
This was how I felt after playing this game. You play it the sterile way, making no one unhappy and everyone loves you at the end. You have fun playing it too, you love terrible puns after all and it did have a decent, if not generic, message and all. "No one has to die." But in reality, it's more than that. This game is so much deeper, and playing it that way, to please the system, is not what the creator intended. He wanted you to slip up, to think, "God, this freaking Tsundere airplane is so annoying! It'd be so much easier to just fight her and get it over with." And then you slip up, and they're dead. You don't think much of it. The game doesn't make much of a big deal of it. You just move on. Maybe a character will treat you strangely. But it doesn't faze you, because you befriend them anyways. Then after the game is over, you feel an overwhelming feeling of guilt. Of frustration! Of anger! It was just one airplane, but the game doesn't let it go. You don't let it go. And it eats away at you. But then you're offered a chance. Not to redeem yourself, because the damage has already been done. But to start over. To start over and do it right this time. This is what this game is about. It's about realizing the true gravity of your actions. Because Toby Fox may not know how to let a joke go, but he sure as hell never lets you forget your actions. Ever.

Possibly the long-lost video game of my childhood has finally emerged; at the perfect time in my life where I can take in all the fantastic characters and gameplay of Undertale. I will play and talk about this game for the rest of my life just as much as I play and talk about Zelda and Earthbound.

Undertale is a quirky RPG in the vein of the SNES game EarthBound. You never gain any other party members, and the RPG elements aren't that heavy (you only get two inventory slots, and there is no magic.) The game has two central gameplay mechanics.
1. Defense. Rather than just a text box saying the enemy attacks you and deals X damage, you control a small red heart inside a box and must avoid projectiles and other things, making it possible to not get hit at all.
2. Pacifism. It's possible to complete the game without hitting anyone (except Asgore, and Mettaton, but only in defense). After you complete the main game and get the Neutral ending, you can play again for a Pacifist run, extending the game beyond the normal final boss. Or you can just go for the Genocide ending.
The game is short, but sweet, longer if you go for the multiple endings. It's full of memorable characters and unique enemies. The soundtrack is amazing (like Waterfall, and the battle theme of Mettaton and Asgore). I do highly recommend this, and it's one of the best games of the year.

It is difficult to describe Undertale because the core experience of playing it is different from the surface level features. Nevertheless, I'll try.
On the surface, Undertale is an homage to the style of mid-80's Japanese role-playing games like Final Fantasy or Dragon Warrior: you fight monsters in a turn-based battle system to gain experience and gold that allow you fight more monsters until you get to the end of the game. Usually, these games have a story about saving the world, but it's usually just provides context and immersion between encounters.
What makes Undertale different is that its mechanics allow you to resolve fights without killing your opponents or even using violence against them. The game will critique you for using force, yet it will never prevent you from using it if you decide to. As you go forward on your quest, you might encounter scenarios where there doesn't seem to be a way out, but it's up to you to decide what to do. In some ways, this allows the player to step back from the mechanics of the game and think about their decisions outside of it. I'm being somewhat vague because I don't want to provide examples that would spoil the game's events.
While some of the events are serious, most of them are humorous tounge-in-cheek references to the rediculous mechanics of vintage JRPGs. It's also well-paced and can be completed in about 5-6 hours.
If you're still on the fence, there's a demo floating around on the internet. It features the first chapter to the game and introduces you to the mechanics, plot, and themes of the game in about 30 minutes. If that doesn't convince you that Undertale is worth considering, you might want to look elsewhere.

It is difficult to describe Undertale because the core experience of playing it is different from the surface level features. Nevertheless, I'll try.
On the surface, Undertale is an homage to the style of mid-80's Japanese role-playing games like Final Fantasy or Dragon Warrior: you fight monsters in a turn-based battle system to gain experience and gold that allow you fight more monsters until you get to the end of the game. Usually, these games have a story about saving the world, but it's usually just provides context and immersion between encounters.
What makes Undertale different is that its mechanics allow you to resolve fights without killing your opponents or even using violence against them. The game will critique you for using force, yet it will never prevent you from using it if you decide to. As you go forward on your quest, you might encounter scenarios where there doesn't seem to be a way out, but it's up to you to decide what to do. In some ways, this allows the player to step back from the mechanics of the game and think about their decisions outside of it. I'm being somewhat vague because I don't want to provide examples that would spoil the game's events.
While some of the events are serious, most of them are humorous tounge-in-cheek references to the rediculous mechanics of vintage JRPGs. It's also well-paced and can be completed in about 5-6 hours.
If you're still on the fence, there's a demo floating around on the internet. It features the first chapter to the game and introduces you to the mechanics, plot, and themes of the game in about 30 minutes. If that doesn't convince you that Undertale is worth considering, you might want to look elsewhere.

Rust is a game that has gotten many improvements throughout its development. The optimization is still patchy, but is significantly better than the Early access competition. Rust has a level of polish that is impressive for an EA title made by a small studio.
However, somewhere along the way, Rust lost its soul, and is not quite the same as the game we played during Legacy. Much of the voice chat and relationships you build with neighbors and randoms is gone, replaced by the cold silence of massive discord servers.
Interactions with other players during Legacy were often brutal, but had a healthy dose of humanity to them. Today, Rust's mechanics favor large groups of people working together with copious amounts of free time. Many of these players have never known what it is like to solo play, and many do not even know what their voice chat key is.
The Rust we have today is a very different animal from what we had during Legacy. There are more features for community interaction than ever, but fewer people willing to enjoy them. Gmod: The Survival game has become Dayz with crafting.

The humor and the graphics might not be your style, and I can understand if they might put you off, but, in my experience, the story, the characters, and the music are enough to make this a great experience anyway. And if they are your style, then even better.
Pros:
-Great soundtrack
-Great story
-Good pacing
-Emotional weight (there's a good chance you will cry, and I say this as someone who almost never does)
-Likeable/relatable characters
-Several dogs
-Several pettable dogs
-Nonbinary protagonist (!!!!!)
-Actually, multiple nonbinary characters
-Multiple LGBT characters in general, to be honest (I mean, I know most people probably don't really care about this, which is fine, but it was a selling point to me)
-Can go on at least 2 dates
-Very good replay value (I guarantee you missed something the first time)
-Engaging battle system (this is another personal taste thing, though)
-Good difficulty balance (People who are very good at bullet hells may find it too easy, and people who are very bad may struggle a little to progress, but the game has ways (different armors) to make battles easier or harder if you want to, and I think that the balance is right for the average player)
-Can play mini golf for gold
-Is a good length for busy people (can finish a playthrough in a week if you play for an hour a day, or in one afternoon if you have a day off)
-Multiple layers to the game (secret rooms, hidden characters, hidden plotlines?)
-More content coming (Kickstarter stretch goal reached)
-Very nice pixel art
-Fun to mess with appdata files
-Does not require a good computer to play
-Affordable
-Homestuck references
-Filled me with DETERMINATION (I'm sorry, I had to. It's kind of true, though?)
Cons:
-Style might not appeal to everyone (to be fair, that applies to literally everything ever)
-Left me wanting more?
-Not enough cats
-Can't ride a horse
-No horses at all, actually?
-This is truly a problem
-Music gets stuck in your head
-Writing can be a bit cheesy at times (not necessarily bad)
-At least 2 typos
-If you really try, you can make it glitch
-Homestuck references
-Distracted me from the things I really should have been doing instead (but probably wouldn't have, anyway)
Overall, great game, 10/10. You should play it. Even if you don't end up loving it, it's worth the $10.

This unique RPG is taking the indie-gaming world by storm, and for good reason. You play as small child who must navigate through the "Underground,"a world teeming with monsters each with their unique personailty and quirks, in order to reach the surface. The fighting aspect of the game has a "Touhou-esque" bullet hell feel, but in fact, you can complete the game by not fighting any monsters at all. The game features a variety of good qualities like clever writing, various and unique characters (ranging from a shy, weeaboo reptile to a quite fabulous robot), and an atmostphere that is sure to blow you away. With that said, the game surely is not for everyone, because Undertale is, in a word..."weird." But for those looking for a game in which you will fall in love with the characters, or able to choose to be good or the villain, or just an overall memorable experience, Undertale is for you.
Hands down the best game ever created. (In my opinion) Thank you Toby Fox for this wonderful masterpiece!

ALPHA -
After playing the ALPHA DayZ for about a year now, I can honestly say it's been a hell of a rollercoaster ride of joy, frustration, anger, fear, friendship, betrayal, and exasperration.
Even though sometimes other players, glitches, or boredom make me want to uninstall, I take a couple days away and come back to it like a baby to its mother's teats.  Yes the game is glitchy, yes other players can ruin your day, yes it can be frustrating dealing with new stuff the developers are attempting to get 'right'...  But overall, this is one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I've ever had.
This is the most realistic gaming experience I've come across in terms of scavenging, weather, and atmosphere.
I have feared at night to create a fire to warm myself hoping bandits don't see the light and hunt me down.
I have shot another person out of sheer deparation of thinking they are only going to shoot me or steal my food.
I have had to climb on top a building and jump, killing myself because I was so badly injured there was no chance of healing.
I have hunted deer, cooked the meat over a campfire that I have created and made a backpack out of the leather.
I have had to beat a zombie down with my bare fists out of desparation of not being able to find a weapon.
And I have killed a person on sight simply because I wanted to.
This is Chernarus, there is only one rule.  Survive.
I can't imagine real life being much different from this.
ALPHA - 8/10
I can only hope when it's finished it's worthy of 10/10
EDIT: June 2017 - So more than 2 years after posting this review and I'm STILL playing it regularly.  They went nearly a year & a half of absolutely NO progress, but recently have made some HUGE changes like optimization (the main big one!) that have really made this game a true winner.  It's about to go into BETA shortly and I am very excited to see what Chernarus has to offer over the next several months.  Sure there are some bugs (nothing game breaking at all) and sure, there are some WTF moments that come with an alpha/beta game.
Overall, I urge anyone reading this (long) review to ignore most of the thumbs down (as most people posting negative reviews ignore things like "minimum system requirements" and don't understand much, if anything, about the genre that DayZ is satisfying.
The game is worth it, and getting it through Steam Sales (-15% off!) is a hell of a deal, considering it literally never goes on sale.

Honestly, I think this game is all but dead in the water.
Rust currently offers nothing extra to this genre despite nearly two years in "alpha" and one complete redesign that seems to have simply set it back more than anything. Facepunch is a very small studio and I applaud what they did to help popularize this genre. However, with bigger and more fleshed out games like ARK and H1Z1 approaching goalposts that Rust can't even see yet, I don't think there's much hope for it.
The worlds are very empty and boring. Wildlife is rare and even more rarely is it dangerous. Legacy Rust actually did better than the current build in both respects and even that is still uninteresting compared to newer games in the genre.
Worst of all, the game is still very poorly optimized. Despite maximum settings being visually underwhelming, they will tank most computers. Even on the flat and ugly medium settings you'll need a decent gaming rig to avoid perfomance hits.
As it currently stands...
If you're looking for a survival game with a heavy crafting/building element, you're better off going with ARK. ARK also offers a much more interesting "Player vs Environment" experience.
If you're looking for a post-apocalyptic survival game with a classic town-scavenging mechanic and/or zombies (a` la Day Z), get H1Z1.
Best of wishes to Facepunch, but I think Rust is a textbook case of "too little, too late".
Rust is the reason I will never buy another Alpha.

Undertale is a very fun game, with well written characters and an enjoyable story. I love me a good dose of bad puns, so characters like Sans are automatically amazing! But the game also knows how to play with your emotions, when two particular fights near the end force you to fight, even if you were going down the pacifist route. (For the sake of avoiding big spoilers, I'll say no more. But don't worry, these fights don't hurt your run.)
The connection you can build with characters is, in my opinion, both a good thing and a bad thing, because you only have one save file, so if you want to attempt the genocide route, you HAVE to delete the previous file.
However, as much as I enjoy this game, and it deserves a lot of the praise it's given, there is one thing in particular I take issue with; the game's attitude towards corrupted game files. To my understanding, if your file corrupts, you are met with a dog dancing to music on an otherwise blank screen with no context given. My initial reaction to this was "did I die too much or something? What's going on?" It wasn't until I heard from other people that my file corrupted, and the day I spent playing was wasted.
From what I've heard, this is supposed to be a form of punishment to those who use cheat codes or Flowey's time machine, but I wasn't using any of that! The dancing dog felt like an insult, and it's made me apprehensive about picking the game up again.
It's a real shame, because I love the game itself, but this one thing, while not ruining the game for me (I'm not that over dramatic) has left a bad taste in my mouth. By all means, try Undertale out for yourself, but beware the dancing dog.

I have not had the desire to make a review for any game I've played for a long time...
...
.
The name has popped up everywhere. Seems like the big viral game that everyone's playing, right? Countless YouTubers are playing it, a large fanbase has formed, and everyone's talking about it. Seems characteristic for famous indie games, doesn't it? It'll soon pass on, and we'll forget about it. Just like big viral games of the past: Slender, Flappy Bird and Five Nights at Freddy's.
You...are wrong. I was wrong. I truly hope, and believe, this game will have staying power. While it likely won't appeal to everyone, if this has ended up being reccomended to you on Steam, I implore you...please purchase this game. The developer deserves every cent.
While the graphics are a simple 8-bit style, that ends up being insignificant in the face of the fantastic story that's offered to you, the interesting characters you really end up caring about; and the fantastic "fights," that often had me on the edge of my seat in the more intense battles. The music is also an absolute delight to the ears, sometimes upbeat and quirky, other times large, epic, and possibly even tragic.
And you know what? If you find yourself truly determined to see the quest through as best you can...you may just find yourself shedding tears. I certainly know I had plenty to share.
But enough of my unending praise, what IS this game about?
You play a young human, who has fallen into the world of monsters. The term "monsters" alone may make you think this poor child is in danger...but not at all. The inhabitants of the underground don't really want to fight you.
But the question you must ask yourself early on...do you fight these monsters? Or will you show them mercy? Whichever you choose will certainly hold consequences, on either path you take.
While I still have yet to fully complete the game, only seeing the Neutral Ending, I know I'll see this through to the end...
But enough of my stereotypical ranting about this game--just buy it. You won't regret it. If you don't...

Undertale is a game that uses a set of deliberate, albeit functionally adequate systems to hand craft a thoroughly entertaining adventure through a land of monsters.  As a warning to those who have been recommended this game, this game is not one with particularly deep systems. Though parts of the systems are engaging and scenarios clever, if you're looking for a game with intricate systems that drive optimization and offer avenues for player expression, you'll not find them in Undertale.
To be perfectly clear, the reason to play Undertale is to consume the story and experience the adventure. If the story doesn't hook you in the manner of the theater absurd or the characters do not evoke any emotions, you'll probably have a boring time playing through Undertale. That being said, I found the writing in Undertale to have a surprising amount of dimension considering the absurdity of the context. Basically, events occur where the player's character falls down a mountain in lands in a world of monsters. The tone dips from unnervingly creepy to absurdly humorous to wholesomely heartwarming to quietly somber. The mood constantly shifts and cycles through various states of ambiance as new locations come into focus. Although somehow confined beneath a mythical mountain, there are plenty of venues from oddly purple hued ruins to little snow villages to technoindustrial factories. The chip-tun-esque music adds its own charm to the atmosphere, blending well with scene and aesthetic.
Undertale, if nothing else, is a great adventure filled with clever writing and great characters. I will caveat that Undertale is not for everybody. Personally, I think the writing and story are worth the price of admission alone. The actual systems in the game could be more developed, but admittedly the game is not about the systems. Even with the battle system and fights, I liken Undertale to more of a classical point-and-click adventure game than a traditional JRPG or RPG for that matter. I think people who've played the old Sierra adventure games or some of the new Telltale adventure games will get a supreme kick out of the story and be surprised at some of depth of the characters. A lot of the far reaching outcomes of the player's choices during combat won't be made known until late in the game which Telltale fans may recognize some similarities in story structure although you won't get a message saying "Flowey will remember that." Additionally, there are some deconstructive elements that occur during the story, a little bit in line with games like The Stanley Parable or Spec Ops: The Line, though not quite as much the focus and only at certain points. If adventure games or video game deconstructions hit your fancy, you'll find something in Undertale to like.
Now, I value when a game drives me to optimize for best possible outcomes and Undertale does not drive me to optimize my play. The systems only care about the outcome, not the path. In particular, the battle system drives little compulsion for the most optimal play since any path taken results in indistinct classes of short term consequence. As such, there is not much variance in outcome whether playing well or playing poorly. Instead, the choice is binary, meant to give agency that asks nothing about performance, only intent.
That being said, Undertale does a good job of creating a handcrafted adventure, evident through its writing and meticulous attention to detail. Though there are few systemic determinations made to judge and measure the player, the writing picks up the slack with special cases written for exploring and discovering various different endpoints in the exploration space. Few games can boast such fine attention to detail, and that attention to detail written in lieu of systemic reactions to outcomes, makes Undertale highly recommended if nothing for the sheer breadth of discovery laden in the story and interactions in the game.
I will mention once more that if you're into games for mastering nuanced systems and exploring interesting decision spaces, this game can be lacking after you look pass the story and writing or the writing simply doesn't grab you. You'll probably beat the game once and never play again. However, if you're in the game for the stories and the discovery, Undertale will charm and charm again with a meticulously crafted adventure.

Now, to the meat and potatoes:
This game is well-done for being an indie (developers correct me). While visually not impressive, the concept of the game and the characters, as well as the OST are another story.
UnderTale is about your character who falls into the underground and has to brave the terrors of the monsters lurking within, either fighting, acting or fleeing each battle.
The gameplay is very unique since not many games give the option of acting and trying to make peace with your opponent. It is very well applied to the game since your character is a CHILD, and you should have that option with such innocence. The minigames you have to go through while fighting (even though annoying sometimes) are very fun and make you put effort and thought into how you play and help you learn a new system since it is not blow for blow.
The characters are half and half, some are memorable like Toriel, Flowy, Sans and Papyrus to name the most memorable, while others can easily be forgotten. Personality and AI wise? They are really well done, creating interesting characters for yours to meet up with, talk to and have some fun with based off of text or their combat.
And the musical score is on great terms, perfectly fitting the dynamic of the game.
Overall, if I could give it a number score instead of the overwhelmingly negative to overwhelmingly positive, this would be an 8.3/10 since it does lack in certain aspects and needs some touch-ups to be perfected.

Honestly, I think this game is all but dead in the water.
Rust currently offers nothing extra to this genre despite nearly two years in "alpha" and one complete redesign that seems to have simply set it back more than anything. Facepunch is a very small studio and I applaud what they did to help popularize this genre. However, with bigger and more fleshed out games like ARK and H1Z1 approaching goalposts that Rust can't even see yet, I don't think there's much hope for it.
The worlds are very empty and boring. Wildlife is rare and even more rarely is it dangerous. Legacy Rust actually did better than the current build in both respects and even that is still uninteresting compared to newer games in the genre.
Worst of all, the game is still very poorly optimized. Despite maximum settings being visually underwhelming, they will tank most computers. Even on the flat and ugly medium settings you'll need a decent gaming rig to avoid perfomance hits.
As it currently stands...
If you're looking for a survival game with a heavy crafting/building element, you're better off going with ARK. ARK also offers a much more interesting "Player vs Environment" experience.
If you're looking for a post-apocalyptic survival game with a classic town-scavenging mechanic and/or zombies (a` la Day Z), get H1Z1.
Best of wishes to Facepunch, but I think Rust is a textbook case of "too little, too late".
Rust is the reason I will never buy another Alpha.

Undertale is a game that uses a set of deliberate, albeit functionally adequate systems to hand craft a thoroughly entertaining adventure through a land of monsters.  As a warning to those who have been recommended this game, this game is not one with particularly deep systems. Though parts of the systems are engaging and scenarios clever, if you're looking for a game with intricate systems that drive optimization and offer avenues for player expression, you'll not find them in Undertale.
To be perfectly clear, the reason to play Undertale is to consume the story and experience the adventure. If the story doesn't hook you in the manner of the theater absurd or the characters do not evoke any emotions, you'll probably have a boring time playing through Undertale. That being said, I found the writing in Undertale to have a surprising amount of dimension considering the absurdity of the context. Basically, events occur where the player's character falls down a mountain in lands in a world of monsters. The tone dips from unnervingly creepy to absurdly humorous to wholesomely heartwarming to quietly somber. The mood constantly shifts and cycles through various states of ambiance as new locations come into focus. Although somehow confined beneath a mythical mountain, there are plenty of venues from oddly purple hued ruins to little snow villages to technoindustrial factories. The chip-tun-esque music adds its own charm to the atmosphere, blending well with scene and aesthetic.
Undertale, if nothing else, is a great adventure filled with clever writing and great characters. I will caveat that Undertale is not for everybody. Personally, I think the writing and story are worth the price of admission alone. The actual systems in the game could be more developed, but admittedly the game is not about the systems. Even with the battle system and fights, I liken Undertale to more of a classical point-and-click adventure game than a traditional JRPG or RPG for that matter. I think people who've played the old Sierra adventure games or some of the new Telltale adventure games will get a supreme kick out of the story and be surprised at some of depth of the characters. A lot of the far reaching outcomes of the player's choices during combat won't be made known until late in the game which Telltale fans may recognize some similarities in story structure although you won't get a message saying "Flowey will remember that." Additionally, there are some deconstructive elements that occur during the story, a little bit in line with games like The Stanley Parable or Spec Ops: The Line, though not quite as much the focus and only at certain points. If adventure games or video game deconstructions hit your fancy, you'll find something in Undertale to like.
Now, I value when a game drives me to optimize for best possible outcomes and Undertale does not drive me to optimize my play. The systems only care about the outcome, not the path. In particular, the battle system drives little compulsion for the most optimal play since any path taken results in indistinct classes of short term consequence. As such, there is not much variance in outcome whether playing well or playing poorly. Instead, the choice is binary, meant to give agency that asks nothing about performance, only intent.
That being said, Undertale does a good job of creating a handcrafted adventure, evident through its writing and meticulous attention to detail. Though there are few systemic determinations made to judge and measure the player, the writing picks up the slack with special cases written for exploring and discovering various different endpoints in the exploration space. Few games can boast such fine attention to detail, and that attention to detail written in lieu of systemic reactions to outcomes, makes Undertale highly recommended if nothing for the sheer breadth of discovery laden in the story and interactions in the game.
I will mention once more that if you're into games for mastering nuanced systems and exploring interesting decision spaces, this game can be lacking after you look pass the story and writing or the writing simply doesn't grab you. You'll probably beat the game once and never play again. However, if you're in the game for the stories and the discovery, Undertale will charm and charm again with a meticulously crafted adventure.

Now, to the meat and potatoes:
This game is well-done for being an indie (developers correct me). While visually not impressive, the concept of the game and the characters, as well as the OST are another story.
UnderTale is about your character who falls into the underground and has to brave the terrors of the monsters lurking within, either fighting, acting or fleeing each battle.
The gameplay is very unique since not many games give the option of acting and trying to make peace with your opponent. It is very well applied to the game since your character is a CHILD, and you should have that option with such innocence. The minigames you have to go through while fighting (even though annoying sometimes) are very fun and make you put effort and thought into how you play and help you learn a new system since it is not blow for blow.
The characters are half and half, some are memorable like Toriel, Flowy, Sans and Papyrus to name the most memorable, while others can easily be forgotten. Personality and AI wise? They are really well done, creating interesting characters for yours to meet up with, talk to and have some fun with based off of text or their combat.
And the musical score is on great terms, perfectly fitting the dynamic of the game.
Overall, if I could give it a number score instead of the overwhelmingly negative to overwhelmingly positive, this would be an 8.3/10 since it does lack in certain aspects and needs some touch-ups to be perfected.

A beautiful game ruined by hackers
The first time you awake on a beach with nothing but a torch and your trusty rock, you start to feel how immersive this experience is going to be. You scramble for food and shelter for the first few hours while trying not to die. As you progress deeper you build a base and start crafting better gear to the point where wandering outside at night becomes second nature. When you add a friend or several, this experience is unforgettable.
Unfortunately all of this is ruined by hackers. From the moment you first step on that beach you may see a character flying through the air at exhilarating speeds. They may even kill you, but in the beginning what you lose is paltry compared to later. Later a hacker or two will soar past you and kill you instantly, while you lose a couple hours’ worth of progress in the form of weapons and armor. That’s not so bad. What is inexcusable is when you spend 70 + hours building a base only to have it hacked in and all your hard work stolen. It is one thing if players do it legitimately, but it’s another when they destroy the exact walls to reach your most valuable sections. You see, on top of flying characters and aim bots; you also have a fun little hack that allows you to see what’s on the other side of walls.
For this reason I don’t recommend this game to anyone. It’s a great experience, but there is zero reason to invest time, because someone else is going to cheat you out of your hard earned time anyway.

That kind of busy work is my kryptonite, the game jerked me around too much near the end, i died over and over and the game acknowledged that fact. it told me of alt endings before i finished the true ending and im deflated. Im not sure if im locked out of an ending because of some order or person i forgot to know to talk to seconds before a fight on the other side of the game. Ill never know because it drained me and im not going back. Near the end my patience was gone and what emotions it tried to pluck failed because at that point i wanted to turn evil. To know all my work was undone after i strained to not murder only to find i failed and get an empty ending is the last straw.  This game made me happy for a day but truly wore out its charm as you put up with another bullet hell, attempt another talk or backtrack to get another burger. I started off wanting to make friends but after someone kills you 3 times you have no mercy left. Many people think this game is just another earthbound ripoff with cheap characters.
Tell me, how many have actually played the game?
I hear you asking:"What makes this game so great?"
Well...first off: The soundtrack
This game's soundtrack is easely one of the best i have heard in quiet a while.
Despite being a retro-styled game, the music isn't just retro beeps, but it contains actual instruments as well.
Notable music tracks are 'Spider dance' and 'Megalovania'.
Second: The characters
The characters in Undertale are simply loveable, and there's a good reason why.
Let me explain some of the main characters for you.
There's Flowey, who, despite looking very innocent, might as well be the devil himself, because he doesn't have feelings like love, depression, etc, which is explained as you play.
There's Sans, who is a laid-back skeleton that loves to joke around, and older brother of Papyrus, who tries very hard to capture a human in order to join the royal guard.
And then there's the game mechanics
First of all, you should know that this game has several types of runs.
There's the Pacifist run, where you kill nobody. Not even the bosses.
There's the neutral run, where you kill some monsters, but not all of them.
And there's the Genocide run, where you murder EVERYTHING!
I don't recommend the Genocide run for the newer players, because not only is this game mode significantly harder, you will also affect the pacifist run permanently.
Why would it affect the pacifist run?
Well...lets just say that, even after you reset your game, the characters remember everything you've done.
Every action, every kill, every choice you made, EVERYTHING.
The only way to delete their memory is by doing a true reset.
Last, but not least: The story
The story, depending on what run you're doing, is AMAZING!
I'm not gonna spoil it for you, because you have to experience it for yourself.
But...one important aspect of the story is that the characters seem to know that they're in a game.
Flowey, for example, know that you have the power to 'SAVE' (which he also has).
Sans is aware that even if they escape the undeground, the player (you) will just reset the game, leaving them without memory of them escaping in the first place (we're talking about the true reset), which is why he is so careless about everything (or it could just be an excuse to be lazy).
Do i recommend this game?
Absolutely!
Do i recommend you buying the soundtrack?
Hell yeah!
Is it worth the 10 bucks?
It's worth double the value.

The thing is that I didn't mind the art style because I like the look of old school stylized games, but again the combat at first wasn't at all appealing to me. I didn't want to kill anything, I wanted friends and helping people. Every-time you go into an encounter no matter how big or small you never felt something this emotional before; every encounter matters in this story which I've never experience in a RPG. I wanted to be this kid, I wanted to make these friends, and it really felt I was making all these amazing friends. The connections just felt so real I cried too much during this game.

Honestly, I think this game is all but dead in the water.
Rust currently offers nothing extra to this genre despite nearly two years in "alpha" and one complete redesign that seems to have simply set it back more than anything. Facepunch is a very small studio and I applaud what they did to help popularize this genre. However, with bigger and more fleshed out games like ARK and H1Z1 approaching goalposts that Rust can't even see yet, I don't think there's much hope for it.
The worlds are very empty and boring. Wildlife is rare and even more rarely is it dangerous. Legacy Rust actually did better than the current build in both respects and even that is still uninteresting compared to newer games in the genre.
Worst of all, the game is still very poorly optimized. Despite maximum settings being visually underwhelming, they will tank most computers. Even on the flat and ugly medium settings you'll need a decent gaming rig to avoid perfomance hits.
As it currently stands...
If you're looking for a survival game with a heavy crafting/building element, you're better off going with ARK. ARK also offers a much more interesting "Player vs Environment" experience.
If you're looking for a post-apocalyptic survival game with a classic town-scavenging mechanic and/or zombies (a` la Day Z), get H1Z1.
Best of wishes to Facepunch, but I think Rust is a textbook case of "too little, too late".
Rust is the reason I will never buy another Alpha.

A beautiful game ruined by hackers
The first time you awake on a beach with nothing but a torch and your trusty rock, you start to feel how immersive this experience is going to be. You scramble for food and shelter for the first few hours while trying not to die. As you progress deeper you build a base and start crafting better gear to the point where wandering outside at night becomes second nature. When you add a friend or several, this experience is unforgettable.
Unfortunately all of this is ruined by hackers. From the moment you first step on that beach you may see a character flying through the air at exhilarating speeds. They may even kill you, but in the beginning what you lose is paltry compared to later. Later a hacker or two will soar past you and kill you instantly, while you lose a couple hours’ worth of progress in the form of weapons and armor. That’s not so bad. What is inexcusable is when you spend 70 + hours building a base only to have it hacked in and all your hard work stolen. It is one thing if players do it legitimately, but it’s another when they destroy the exact walls to reach your most valuable sections. You see, on top of flying characters and aim bots; you also have a fun little hack that allows you to see what’s on the other side of walls.
For this reason I don’t recommend this game to anyone. It’s a great experience, but there is zero reason to invest time, because someone else is going to cheat you out of your hard earned time anyway.

It's my first review and Undertale is something I'm pretty passionate about, so please forgive me if I blabber.
Undertale is... it's something else.
I'm not an avid gamer, mind you, but I do love myself some stories from time to time, and like to believe I can recognize them when they appear. Undertale's story in its full scope will take at least two or maybe three playthroughs to fully catch and appreciate, because the choices you make affect the gameplay so heavily, you will be presented only pieces of the universe depending on the route you are on.
The dev's meticulous attention to easter eggs and subtle to not-so-subtle breaking of the fourth wall will sometimes leave you in chills (the most iconic 4th wall instance coming from No Mercy route
). They've paid so much attention to it, it's as if the characters themselves respond to what you do (the most iconic of this one coming from neutral/pacifist run
). Actions that you may think insignificant may draw responses from the characters. The game itself really reflects the many years' work Toby and devs put into the game.
The gameplay is your standard bullet-hell (and trust me, it does get hellish depending on what route you do), very similar to how Touhou is played--if you know what that is. The graphics aren't the best around either, but it has this inexplicable appeal with its simplicity. But what I found most pleasant about the graphics is that its simplicity did not--or could not--contain the intricacy of the story or the beauty of it.
The Metacritic score on the side is very well-deserved. I would buy this twice if I could, maybe even more. I'm just glad I was around to witness something like Undertale and its universe.

I fully recommend Rust to anyone looking for a survival game that actually works. If you want a more in-depth look, then continue reading!
Generally, with survival games, there are three main problems that people have:
1) The Art
2) The Mechanics and Gameplay
3) The Optimization
OLD RUST:
A year ago, I wouldn't recommend Rust if I was valuing each of the above as requirements. The Art was sub-par and animations just weren't good. The User Interface was slow and ugly to look at.
The gameplay was decent. There was content in the form of base raiding and defending. It wasn't necessarily great, but it was there. The hitboxes weren't smooth and reasonable and fighting was a pain.
There were quite a few visual bugs and poor FPS in high-density areas. Overall Legacy Rust was fun for groups who only looked to raid and defend but past that, it didn't offer much.
NEW RUST:
I don't hesitate to♥♥♥♥♥♥on old Rust now because new Rust is just so much better. The biggest improvement is the visuals in my opinion. The game just flat out looks impressive. The developers have been putting out devblogs with continuous detail over every aspect of the game and my favorite section is when the artists discuss their process. The animations are a million times better as well.
The gameplay is more than just raiding a large clan with your clan. Because of the beautiful vistas and new construction, it's satisfying to be a builder and explorer. It's fun to run around collecting materials because it's fun to look at everything. They made it harder to raid bases and that lead to more creative forms of fighting and interacting with players.
The optimization is the best it has ever been. My PC isn't high end. It's a mid-range PC that is getting dated quickly. Legacy Rust ran very poorly for me on decent settings and that greatly impacted my love for the game. New Rust was actually the same half a year ago. I couldn't run on high settings in dense areas without my FPS diving below 10. But the dev team has made great strides to further improve the optimization of the game and even on my mid-range PC I can run the game on max settings and be above 30 FPS consistantly.
Obviously Rust is the same as any other multiplayer survival game. In that your experience is entirely dependent on how you play. Meaning the server you choose, the people you play with, and the role you want to fill. I'd say that Rust fills the space of Mutliplayer Survival Game in a way that Ark, DayZ, H1Z1, and others just don't. I recommend it!

Review Date: 21 September 2015
I want to like this game... I really do. I have played off and on since it first hit Steam back before the current re-launch. I have sunk hour after hour learning to play as efficiently as possible. But there are still so many issues with this game that it has essentially become an exercise in futility. The idea behind the game is great but the execution has left far too much to be desired. Here are the items that I feel truly make this game either unplayable or a waste of your time and energy.
Cheats: I won't dignify them by calling them hacks since most people that are abusing the game are using premade kits that don't require any computer skill further than downloading and installing (Don't believe me? Just check YouTube). There has been a consistent issue with cheats since the very first iteration of the game and the same ones can still be seen in-game years later. Aimbots continue to be popular, along with speed hacks, vision hacks, flying (which is not exactly flying but weird air jumping), and anything else that can give an advantage to someone who evidently feels that they are simply inadequate or just want to grief other players who follow the rules. Dozens of hours of personal time invested in a game can vanish in 3 minutes to one individual using a cheat and there is nothing to offset the loss.
End-Game: There is none. The initial goals are to establish basic supplies, build a base, and then work on gathering additinal resources and blueprints. But there really is no point to it. You eventually get to a point (barring cheaters) that you have built up a sufficiently strong base that can ward off anyone who doesn't have 100 C4 charges. There is nothing else to do, therefore you wind up with bored individuals with automatic weapons and armor who have nothing to do but harass new naked players who are only armed with a rock. Sometimes these individuals are solo but you will often find a group of 2 or 3 (occasionally with 1 running a cheat) who simply roam the entire map griefing anyone that they find.
Rascim and Gay Bashing: With the introduction of signs in the game you will now see a wide variety of hate messages posted throughout the world. I have encountered just about every variation including anti-semitic messages and the typical poorly spelled rascist insults. I don't know why I wouldn't expect this in any game these days, but the point is that I have never seen any attempts by an admin to lock down on this type of behavior (even on servers that state that they do). The use of local voice communications is typically used for anything other than simple chat. 95% of all speech I have heard is beyond hateful and some would result in criminal charges if taken to law enforcement. Once again, I have rarely seen any admin take steps to offset this.
Ultimately, the community in this game is leaning more and more towards the toxic extreme. People playing the game quickly learn to be distrustful of anyone that approaches them. Preemptive retaliation becomes the norm and this is the worst part of the game. It will teach you to be distrustful of everyone around you.

Undertale is a role-playing game that was developed by Toby Fox. The game came out in September 15th, 2015, and has received a lot of good reviews and popularity since then. At first I thought that the game was overhyped, and I thought that it was based around another FNAF like fanbase, especially since one of my friends was obsessed with the game. I decided to buy it, and I now know why she loves it so much. In Undertale, you are a human who has fallen to the Underground after a great war. This place is filled with friendly and menacing monsters. All of your choices impact the characters and the story of the game. When fighting an enemy, you can either kill them and get it over with, or show them mercy.  People will remember who you killed, and hate you for it. Depending on your actions, future playthroughs will also be effected. I will not go into spoiler territory, but this game really made me question my morals. The game is pretty short. It took me 8.5 hours to beat my first play through. The game has a lot of replayability value, since there are many different endings. Even though I don't really like RPGs, I still had a blast with this game. If you like a good story, lovable characters, and crying, then I highly recommend this game.

The BETA is not scheduled to be released until the late quarter of 2015. That means we will most likely not see a finished official product until early to mid 2016.

For those of you that don't understand what Persistence means. It is essentially taking the game to a whole new level. Server restarts will no longer eat up items you leave on the floor, it will also NO LONGER SPAWN CONSTANT LOOT.
This is a massive game changer. To be explicit, the massive cities that are just little PVP areas because of there massive amount of loot spawns will no longer be spawning loot. Once a server has begun being hosted and it is open for the first time. The loot will be fresh, most things -should- be pristine (in condition) or very usable at the least.
However as little bambies start to loot up these urban areas over time. The areas in question will quickly become baron. Eventually cities will become empty loot-wise and just full of zombies and poor starving bambies. You will no longer be able to run through a city and run out of it fully geared. Cities will quickly become wastelands, more dangerous then the notorious NWAF we all know and love. The hordes of zombies (that are planned to be in the hundreds eventually) and starvation will now be your biggest threat.
Entire playstyles will quickly become obsolete as players will HAVE TO learn how to use the environment outside of the cities to survive. Even now on persistent servers (not all servers are persistent for the moment) people are often starving to death within an hour of playing. Which in the mind of a Veteran DayZ players is fantastically horrifying while a massive leap in the right direction! The game is starting to actually be about SURVIVAL. Strategy is now everything, risk and reward situations just got taken up a notch and the game is going to be a harsh, harsh mistress.
So many of you will be thinking by now "Well f*** that.. Sounds way too hard!"
Well if you're thinking that then you honestly shouldn't bother getting the game. To those people that read this and think "F*** YES! FINALLY!!" then keep on reading, it only gets better!
The crafting system in the game is finally being paid sincere attention. Let me do a little list of perfect examples:
Can't find any guns? - Craft a bow and make arrows for it with either bones from animals or sharpened sticks.
Can't find apples or berries? - Get some seeds and farming tools. Because you can now make your own sustenance! (Pumpkins FTW!)
Can't find a ghillie suit? - MAKE YOUR OWN! Customize it to your liking, maybe you only want a certain part of it? Sure go ahead.
Ran out of bandages? - Tear up clothes to bandage yourself.
Broken leg but no morphine? - Use the rags from your torn up clothes to use a stick to make a splint (Works on legs AND arms)
Can't find farming equipment? - Just get the right materials and you can go make a fishing rod OR a fishing trap!
The list goes on and I'm sure by now I have made my point. Survival is finally being taken seriously!!
Verdict:
I have never spent so much time in a game (Besides the DayZ mod itself) and probably never will. The unique experiences DayZ brings are unmatchable and no matter how many other rip-offs *Cough* H1Z1 *Cough* are released. They will always be second to DayZ. DayZ is for all intents and purposes, The Godfather of this unique genre.
Does that mean you should buy it?
No.
Not unless you actually understand how broken so many different aspects of the game are. If you are veteran of DayZ you will remember the glitches and bugs that ARMA 2 gave us. The ARMA 3 engine is no different. BUT... The experiences DayZ offers still come very often, heart-pumping scenarios are a daily occurrence no matter how much of a veteran you think you are. The problem is quite often servers will crash mid-way through those scenarios. Sometimes there are just those times when you are on TS and say "Well boys... I think I just got DayZed"
The key is.. You gotta decide for yourself if it is worth it.
I know for damn sure it was worth it for me.

DISCLAIMER: A large portion of this review covers the "behind the curtain" reasons DayZ is in the current state it is, and why. I feel that people need to understand what early video game development is.
I see many reviews ranting on about the state of the game being things like "broken" and "unnacceptable" when it comes to functionality. Blaming the devs for bugs in an alpha is like blaming JIF Peanut Butter for your peanut allergy. On DayZ's steam page you can see two things before purchasing:
1. "WARNING: THIS GAME IS EARLY ACCESS ALPHA. PLEASE DO NOT PURCHASE IT UNLESS YOU WANT TO ACTIVELY SUPPORT DEVELOPMENT OF THE GAME AND ARE PREPARED TO HANDLE WITH SERIOUS ISSUES AND POSSIBLE INTERRUPTIONS OF GAME"
2. What the developers have to say:
“DayZ Early Access is your chance to experience DayZ as it evolves throughout its development process. Be aware that our Early Access offer is a representation of our core pillars, and the framework we have created around them. It is a work in progress and therefore contains a variety of bugs. We strongly advise you not to buy and play the game at this stage unless you clearly understand what Early Access means and are interested in participating in the ongoing development cycle.”
They tell you twice that they reccommend you NOT buy the game, and that it will be full of bugs. This is how game development works. The most commonly known stages of development being "alpha" and "beta."
Alpha is about adding game assets. Putting in planned content, building all of the base content and features that you are going to see in the game. Generally, games are not released to the public in this state. Why? Because it's not a ready or finished product. As new things are coded and added into a game, bugs are going to show up, it just happens. It wouldn't be logical to go and pin down every problem as soon as it comes up. New bugs are just going to present themselves later anyway.
Think of beta like a dishwasher. You wouldn't put each individual dish in it and wash them one by one as you use them. You pile them up and fill the whole machine, and then rinse and clean them all at once. Game development is the machine, and the content are the dishes, the dirty dishes being bugs/glitches/performance etc.
Hopefully with this information you can understand why DayZ is the way it is.
_________________________________
On a seperate note, I think we as gamers are starting to be conditioned to the sort of thing larger companies are doing, Where we are seeing games yearly from companies like EA and Ubisoft, or the Call of Duty franchise. We expect to have full working games by the end of a single year. The truth is that games take a long time to make. For a company to decide what they want in the game, what they are going to do with it, and how they are going to go about takes a great deal of time. Three years is a pretty common and GOOD amount of time for games.
DayZ has been in development for some time. I personally see about a four year total development time, and see it coming to completion somewhere in 2016. That is my guess, not fact. Four years is a considerable time, yes. Remember that it is a standalone game from a mod, which Bohemia is now working on. Surely the sudden popularity and demand for a game from them shoved it's way into other plans of theirs. Now they are working on DayZ which they picked up out of the blue, so having an extended dev cycle is understandable. It sure is better than rushing it out and leaving it broken in the future... Just saying, some of you gamers are quite hard to please.
I bought DayZ when it was $20 USD. That wasn't a sale, that was the price at the time. I do not agree that it is now $35 USD. Early access should be free and then require purchase once full release hits. Paying for early access is an iffy way for devs to take money and run, it's not a guaranteed method and I don't really like it, we've already had some bad cases from this type of game release.
_________________________________
On an actual topic of DayZ, and the gameplay:
DayZ is a fun game for a certain type of person. If you enjoy slower, but intense PvP that really gets the adrenaline going, DayZ may be a good fit for you. Currently, DayZ is a poorly optimized game with framerate issues in many areas, lag, server and client crashes being common. Hackers are agonizing. I'm basically echoing the steampage at this point, you shouldn't buy this game if you can't handle these sorts of things, for the time being, they are going to happen. I feel that once this game is complete, it will definitely be worth the money.

Undertale is a role-playing game that was developed by Toby Fox. The game came out in September 15th, 2015, and has received a lot of good reviews and popularity since then. At first I thought that the game was overhyped, and I thought that it was based around another FNAF like fanbase, especially since one of my friends was obsessed with the game. I decided to buy it, and I now know why she loves it so much. In Undertale, you are a human who has fallen to the Underground after a great war. This place is filled with friendly and menacing monsters. All of your choices impact the characters and the story of the game. When fighting an enemy, you can either kill them and get it over with, or show them mercy.  People will remember who you killed, and hate you for it. Depending on your actions, future playthroughs will also be effected. I will not go into spoiler territory, but this game really made me question my morals. The game is pretty short. It took me 8.5 hours to beat my first play through. The game has a lot of replayability value, since there are many different endings. Even though I don't really like RPGs, I still had a blast with this game. If you like a good story, lovable characters, and crying, then I highly recommend this game.

Undertale is an unforgettable classic turn based RPG game with tons of unique gameplay and replay-ability. This game is great for anyone who enjoys RPG, turn-based, action and adventure games. It has great artwork and music with many twists and turns in the story and in your backtracking.
The story of this game is the part that appeals to me the most, as I love all the characters and the choices you can make. I especially love how each character has their own unique characteristics and personality. You get attached to these characters and feel as if you truly know them (if you choose to take the pacifist route).
The games difficulty is just enough to make it challenging and fun at the same time. The uniqueness of the mercy option and ability to dodge attacks yourself instead of using pure luck is a great idea, and it is used perfectly in this game. It isn't forced upon the player to kill or spare enemies and the amount of damage you take is based off of your own skill instead of chance. You are given tons of freedom in your choices.
Undertale is a fun, unique, and interesting experience with tremendous replay-ability. It never gets boring, and you can easily put hours upon hours into this game without even noticing it.
Truly, I believe this is the very best game of 2015.

After about 70h of gameplay, I feel I can give a decent review of this. First, I'd like to mention that this is an "early access" review.
The simple idea of surviving in a zombie apocalypse is not original, but it's rarely BAD. In DayZ, you can't build your own home, although with creativity and ingeanuity you can use buildings to settle in, create camp fires and more, but it's usually better to stay on the move in DayZ.
The world of Charnaus isn't that big compared to many games, but it might seem like it and despite the size there's still a lot to explore, including but not limited to: Ruined castles, military bases, hospitals, factories and much more. Of course, before you can actually explore, it's vital to loot the things needed for survival.
When you start the game and join a server, you start of at a random spawn point (usually along the coast), without food, water or a way to store things you find. A single flashflight (batteries included) is all you have, as well as some color of jeans (4 pockets), a T-shirt and shoes (I recommend tearing the T-shirt into rags and keeping them, you might need them soon). Your first objective is to find the items mentioned earlier, which is a part of the exploration as well. You will eventually learn what buildings usually have inside, as some will often have clothes, some are more likely to contain food, and so on.
And of course, the zombies. That creature we often refer to as "undead". In DayZ, this is because of some virus, but that's not important yet (since it's just an early access game). To start off, DON'T fight them if you don't have a weapon. Using your hands is like hitting a brick with a spoon - it will eventually crack, but it (in DayZ, YOU) might break (die) first. You have many options, from running from them (it's possible) to searching for proper weapons to fight them. Eventually you might find some ammo, or a gun of some kind, but one thing is important to take note: The zombies are just like they are depicted in most games: they respond to sound easily, so shooting a gun will probably just attract more than the one you just killed. But don't worry, your very unlikely to be facing a horde of them, usually no more than 3.
This is all the PvE part, but there is also other players in Charnaus trying to survive. Most them are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that will KOS (Kill On Sight), but some (including me) will help others if they can (despite usually getting myself killed by others because of this). Players can do more than just kill your character: they can bind you and then force feed you stuff, experiment with medical equipment or even just leave you with your hands bound.
You don't have to play alone against everyone else of course, some times people will band together in small groups and help each other out, but unless you know them IRL it might get ugly... And when you DO play with friends, you might spawn on opposite sides of the map, and even when you spawn not-so-far away from each other, unless you're using maps online (just search DayZ Standalone Map on google) you WILL struggle to find one another. Finally, even if you know where you are, and where your friends are, you might die from various reasons before you can enjoy the game.
Personally, if there was a way for some servers to have PvP OFF for real, I would have enjoyed the game much, much more, but that's neither here nor there.

This game is how I got introduced to survival games. I really liked it for a time before the problems started to take hold over me and made me stop playing.
Hackers -  There are hackers in this game. They are in almost every survival game. I think they'll get fixed in time but I'm including it in the review to let potential buyers know what they are getting into.
Bugs - Numerous times I have walked over a rock to be thrown across the map, insta death. Falling off stairs. Switching weapons when nothing is clicked was the biggest upset. Idk if it was fixed but one of the most detrimental things I've seen in-game.
But lets disregard bugs/hackers and get to the main point.
The engine was originally called RV. Then they 'ripped out alot, and rewrote a ton". They called it Enfusion. But to me, it still played and looked the same.
The movement is extremely clunky. Its hard to make precise movements. You will stop pushing movement keys and your character will sometimes keep moving in the last pushed direction. This causes deaths, and unnecessary frustration.
Its feels like you're weighted down by gear and other means....But in reality its just plain crappy movement.
There is no bullet drop. This is another major point for me in a shooter. Its all hit scan. If your reticule is on them, it will surely hit. There are ranges sure, but no drop.
There are some good things about the game though -
Realistic animations, Running, sprinting, firing.
Visually the range is nice.
Some people say the game is crap because of development time. And some the bugs/hackers. None of this matter to me.
**The game is built on a flawed foundation of an engine. Its clunky and unresponsive and that is why i cannot recommend this game.**

I used to hate this game and the mod it's based on. And by used to, I mean that was my opinion a week ago. The game is glitchy; zombies run through walls, dropping items sometimes makes them disappear (goodbye, bandages and shotgun...), and my friend has broken his leg and died by looking at a potato on the floor of a house.
However, I had decided to go ahead and give it another try. If so many people can play and love this game despite the bugs, why can't I? And now I have found out why.
Many players have the shoot-on-sight mentality. See a player, defensless or heavily armed, and kill him without asking any questions. I'm proud of myself to be able to say that in every single one of these types of games, I have always been able to push back bandit thoughts and help others if possible, or at the very least shoo them on their way.
Today was one of those days. Exiting a hospital in one of the towns, I saw a man, completely unarmed, running straight toward me. "Hey, stop there!" I yelled to him as he got close. He stopped when he saw me, raised his hands in the air, and typed out "ZOMBIE!!!" He was being chased, and with a shot of my beautiful Blaze rifle, took the zombie down. He still stood there with his hands up, watching me as I backed away from him. "Just don't get near me and we'll be alright." I rounded a corner and ran toward a group of buildings to go back to searching for supplies.
Not much longer later, I see a man standing in a little shack with an axe on his back, bleeding profusely. It was the same guy! I took a deep breath and moved towards him, bandaging him as well as I could with the server acting up. "Hey, thanks, man." "Yeah, no problem." Just then, a rifle shot was heard from a distance. "You hear that?" He asked. "Yeah. There's been a lot of shooting around here for the past ten minutes or so." I let him follow me, keeping a close eye on him. Not once does he reach for his axe, or get too close to me. But it was when a sniper from one of the buildings shot me and knocked me unconscious that I knew this man was a friend.
After a few seconds of thinking I was dead, my character actually woke up, with my new friend standing over me with bandages. "Damn, thanks! Come on, let's get out of here!" We ran across the street and through some buildings, trying to lose the seemingly endless amount of bad guys in the area. "Hey man. If we don't make it, thanks for not shooting me on sight." He told me. "Yeah, thanks to you, too. But hey...we're gonna make it. Stay positive." We kept on moving. And then...I lost him. I heard more shots, and thought for sure he was dead. I was upset, and wished that I could have done something. As fate would have it, though, I ended up turning into a building to see him standing inside. I honestly felt relief and happiness. We talked for a while, and he was hurt, so I taught him how to rip up clothes for rags to bandage himself with. We tried to figure out a plan when we heard moving around outside.
"Hey, there's someone near here." He told me as I looked out the window in time to see someone sticking their head around. I raised my gun. "Hey, you friendly out there?" The response was the shattering of the window as he fired off his weapon at me, and I shot my last round at him. I couldn't tell if he got hit or not, but I yelled out to my ally that they were out there. I saw him bolt out just as I turned to run up the stairs, and as I did, I heard more gunshots, and my heart sunk...
"You cool in there?" One of the voices asked me. "Me? Am I cool?" I asked, incredibly nervous and angry. "Yeah, are you cool?" Another guy asked. "Yeah, I'm cool. But what about you? Did you just shoot my friend?" "Yes we did. He ran at us and tried to kill us." "Because you shot at us, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!" I retorted. "Hey, you better watch your attitude. If you come downstairs, I'll put a bullet in your head like I did your friend." I didn't answer. I wish I could say I heroically went downstairs, swinging my axe and avenged my friend. But I didn't. I stayed upstairs, preparing for them to come up (which they didn't), and then walked outside to find the body of James. I survived, and he didn't.
I have never felt this amount of intensity in a game before. Excitement, drama, death, happiness and sadness. It was just plain awesome, and I'm already excited to take back my bad opinions about it and play it even more.

This game is how I got introduced to survival games. I really liked it for a time before the problems started to take hold over me and made me stop playing.
Hackers -  There are hackers in this game. They are in almost every survival game. I think they'll get fixed in time but I'm including it in the review to let potential buyers know what they are getting into.
Bugs - Numerous times I have walked over a rock to be thrown across the map, insta death. Falling off stairs. Switching weapons when nothing is clicked was the biggest upset. Idk if it was fixed but one of the most detrimental things I've seen in-game.
But lets disregard bugs/hackers and get to the main point.
The engine was originally called RV. Then they 'ripped out alot, and rewrote a ton". They called it Enfusion. But to me, it still played and looked the same.
The movement is extremely clunky. Its hard to make precise movements. You will stop pushing movement keys and your character will sometimes keep moving in the last pushed direction. This causes deaths, and unnecessary frustration.
Its feels like you're weighted down by gear and other means....But in reality its just plain crappy movement.
There is no bullet drop. This is another major point for me in a shooter. Its all hit scan. If your reticule is on them, it will surely hit. There are ranges sure, but no drop.
There are some good things about the game though -
Realistic animations, Running, sprinting, firing.
Visually the range is nice.
Some people say the game is crap because of development time. And some the bugs/hackers. None of this matter to me.
**The game is built on a flawed foundation of an engine. Its clunky and unresponsive and that is why i cannot recommend this game.**
